chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: A green and yellow parrot hung in a cage outside the door and kept repeating, over and over:
“Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That’s all right!”

He could speak a little Spanish. He also spoke a language nobody understood, unless it was the mockingbird hanging on the other side of the door, which whistled its fluty notes out into the breeze with maddening persistence.
Mr. Pontellier could not read his newspaper in any comfort. He got up with a look and an exclamation of disgust.

He walked down the gallery and across the narrow “bridges” that joined the Lebrun cottages to one another. He had been sitting in front of the door of the main house. The parrot and the mockingbird belonged to Madame Lebrun, and they had every right to make all the noise they liked. Mr. Pontellier had the right to leave their company once they stopped being entertaining.

He stopped at the door of his own cottage, the fourth from the main building and next to the last. A wicker rocker stood there, and he sat down in it and went back to reading the newspaper. It was Sunday, and the paper was a day old; the Sunday papers had not yet reached Grand Isle. He already knew the market reports, so he ran a restless eye over the editorials and bits of news he had not had time to read before leaving New Orleans the day before.
Mr. Pontellier wore glasses. He was forty, of medium height, rather slender, and a little stooped. His brown hair was straight and parted on one side, and his beard was kept neat and close.

Now and then he took his eyes off the newspaper and looked around. There was more noise than ever over at the house. The main building was called “the house” to tell it apart from the cottages. The chattering and whistling birds were still going. Two young girls, the Farival twins, were playing a duet from “Zampa” on the piano. Madame Lebrun bustled in and out. Whenever she was inside the house she gave orders in a high voice to a yard-boy, and whenever she was outside she gave directions in an equally high voice to a dining-room servant. She was a fresh, pretty woman, always dressed in white with elbow sleeves, and her starched skirts crinkled as she came and went. Farther down, in front of one of the cottages, a lady in black walked demurely up and down, telling her beads. A good many of the guests at the pension had crossed over to the Chênière Caminada in Beaudelet’s lugger to hear mass. Some young people were out under the water-oaks, playing croquet. Mr. Pontellier’s two children were there, sturdy little fellows of four and five, and a quadroon nurse followed them about with a faraway, meditative air.

At last Mr. Pontellier lit a cigar and started to smoke, the paper dangling forgotten from his hand. His gaze settled on a white sunshade inching its way up from the beach. Between the gaunt trunks of the water-oaks and over the stretch of yellow camomile he could see it plainly. The gulf looked far off, melting hazily into the blue of the horizon. Still the sunshade came on, slowly. Beneath its pink lining were his wife, Mrs. Pontellier, and young Robert Lebrun. They reached the cottage and sat down facing each other on the top step of the porch, each leaning on a post, looking rather worn out.
“What folly, to go bathing at such an hour, in such heat!” exclaimed Mr. Pontellier. He himself had taken a plunge at daylight, and that was why the morning seemed so long to him.

“You are burnt beyond recognition,” he added, regarding his wife as a man regards a valuable possession that has come to some harm. She held up her hands, strong and shapely, pushed her fawn sleeves back from the wrists, and examined them critically. The sight reminded her of her rings, which she had handed to her husband before going to the beach. Silently she reached out a hand, and he, understanding, took the rings from his vest pocket and let them fall into her open palm. She put them back on her fingers. Then, hugging her knees, she looked across at Robert and began to laugh, and the rings sparkled. He answered her with a smile.

“What is it?” Pontellier asked, glancing lazily and with some amusement from one to the other. It was some utter nonsense, an adventure out there in the water, and both of them tried to tell it at once. Told aloud, it did not seem half so funny. They saw that, and so did Mr. Pontellier. He yawned and stretched, then got to his feet and announced that he had half a mind to walk over to Klein’s hotel for a game of billiards.
“Come with me, Lebrun,” he said to Robert. Robert answered, quite frankly, that he would rather stay put and talk with Mrs. Pontellier.
“Well, when he bores you, Edna, send him packing,” her husband instructed as he got ready to go.
“Wait, take the umbrella,” she said, and held it out. He took the sunshade, lifted it over his head, went down the steps and off.

“Will you be back for dinner?” his wife called. He stopped a moment and shrugged. He felt in his vest pocket, where a ten-dollar bill lay. He could not say. Maybe he would be back for the early dinner, and maybe not; it all hung on the company he found at Klein’s and the stakes of “the game.” He did not say so, but she understood, and she laughed and nodded him good-by.
When the children saw their father setting off, both wanted to go with him. He kissed them and promised to come back with bonbons and peanuts for them.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Mrs. Pontellier had quick, bright eyes, a yellowish brown close to the color of her hair. She would swing them suddenly onto something and hold them there, as if she were lost in some inward maze of contemplation or thought.

Her eyebrows were a shade darker than her hair, thick and nearly level, and they deepened the look of her eyes. She was more handsome than beautiful. Her face drew people by its frankness, and by a subtle play of features that contradicted it. Her manner was engaging.

Robert rolled a cigarette. He smoked cigarettes, he said, because he could not afford cigars. He had a cigar in his pocket that Mr. Pontellier had given him, and he was saving it for his smoke after dinner.

This seemed quite fitting and natural in him. His coloring was much like hers, and his clean-shaven face made the likeness stronger than it would have been otherwise. His open face carried no trace of care, and his eyes took in the light and languor of the summer day and gave them back.

Mrs. Pontellier picked up a palm-leaf fan from the porch and began to fan herself while Robert breathed light puffs of smoke from his cigarette. They chattered nonstop. They talked about what was around them; about their funny adventure out in the water, which had grown amusing again; about the wind, the trees and the people who had gone over to the Chênière; about the children playing croquet under the oaks, and the Farival twins, who were by now playing the overture to “The Poet and the Peasant.”

Robert talked a good deal about himself. He was very young and did not know any better. Mrs. Pontellier talked a little about herself, for the same reason. Each was interested in what the other said. Robert spoke of his plan to go to Mexico in the autumn, where a fortune was waiting for him. He was always planning to go to Mexico but somehow never got there. In the meantime he kept his modest position in a mercantile house in New Orleans, where he was worth no small amount as a clerk and correspondent because he knew English, French and Spanish equally well.

He was spending his summer vacation at Grand Isle with his mother, as he did every year. Long ago, before Robert could remember, “the house” had been a summer luxury for the Lebruns. Now a dozen or more cottages stood beside it, always full of exclusive visitors from the “Quartier Français,” and together they let Madame Lebrun keep up the easy, comfortable life that seemed to be hers by birth.

Mrs. Pontellier told him about her father’s plantation in Mississippi and the home of her girlhood in the old Kentucky blue-grass country. She was an American woman with a small drop of French that seemed to have been lost by dilution. She read out a letter from her sister, who was away in the East and had become engaged. Robert was interested. He wanted to know what sort of girls the sisters were, what their father was like, and how long their mother had been dead.
By the time Mrs. Pontellier had folded the letter, it was time to dress for the early dinner.
“I see Léonce is not coming back,” she said, glancing toward the place where her husband had vanished. Robert thought not, since so many New Orleans club men were over at Klein’s.

Mrs. Pontellier left him and went into her room. The young man went down the steps and wandered over to the croquet players, and there, in the half hour before dinner, he entertained himself with the little Pontellier boys, who were very fond of him.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: It was eleven o’clock that night when Mr. Pontellier got back from Klein’s hotel. He was in splendid humor and high spirits, and very talkative. His wife, who had been in bed fast asleep, woke when he came in. While he undressed he talked to her, passing on anecdotes, news and gossip he had picked up during the day. He pulled a fistful of crumpled bank notes and a good deal of silver coin from his trouser pockets and piled it on the bureau, jumbled in with keys, knife, handkerchief and whatever else his pockets held. She was drowning in sleep, and she answered him in little half-sentences.
It was very discouraging, he thought, that his wife, the one object of his existence, took so little interest in what concerned him and thought so little of his conversation.

Mr. Pontellier had forgotten the bonbons and peanuts for the boys. Still, he loved them dearly, and he went into the next room, where they slept, to look at them and be sure they were resting comfortably. He did not like what he found. He turned the youngsters over and moved them about in bed, and one of them began to kick and talk about a basket full of crabs.
Mr. Pontellier went back to his wife and told her that Raoul had a high fever and needed attention. Then he lit a cigar, sat down by the open door, and smoked it.

Mrs. Pontellier was quite certain that Raoul had no fever. He had gone to bed perfectly well, she said, and had been fine all day. Mr. Pontellier knew the signs of fever too well to be wrong. He assured her the child was burning up even then in the next room.

He scolded his wife for her inattention, for neglecting the children as she always did. If looking after children was not a mother’s place, then whose on earth was it? He himself had his hands full with his brokerage business. He could not be in two places at once, earning his family’s living down on the street and staying home to see that nothing harmed them. He went on in a flat, insistent voice.

Mrs. Pontellier jumped out of bed and went into the next room. She soon returned and sat on the edge of the bed, laying her head down on the pillow. She said nothing, and when her husband questioned her she would not answer. When his cigar was finished he went to bed, and half a minute later he was sound asleep.

By now Mrs. Pontellier was wide awake. She began to cry a little, and she wiped her eyes on the sleeve of her peignoir. She blew out the candle her husband had left burning, pushed her bare feet into a pair of satin mules at the foot of the bed, and stepped out onto the porch. There she settled in the wicker chair and began to rock gently to and fro.

It was past midnight, and the cottages were all dark. One faint light shone from the hallway of the house. Nothing could be heard outside but the hooting of an old owl at the top of a water-oak and the everlasting voice of the sea, which at that soft hour did not rise. It broke upon the night like a mournful lullaby.

Tears came so fast to Mrs. Pontellier’s eyes that the damp sleeve of her peignoir was no longer any use for drying them. With one hand she gripped the back of her chair; the loose sleeve of her raised arm had slid almost to the shoulder. She turned and pressed her face, steaming and wet, into the crook of her arm, and there she kept on crying, no longer caring to dry her face, her eyes, her arms. She could not have told why she was crying. Such episodes were not unknown in her married life. Until now they had never seemed to count for much against her husband’s abundant kindness and a constant devotion that had come to be silent and taken for granted.

An indescribable oppression, which seemed to well up from some unfamiliar part of her consciousness, filled her whole being with a vague anguish. It was like a shadow, like a mist drifting across the summer day of her soul. It was strange and unfamiliar; it was a mood. She did not sit there blaming her husband in her heart, or lamenting the Fate that had set her feet on the path they had taken. She was simply having a good cry all by herself. The mosquitoes made merry over her, biting her firm, round arms and nipping her bare insteps.
The little stinging, buzzing imps managed to drive off a mood that might have kept her there in the darkness for half the night longer.

Next morning Mr. Pontellier got up early to catch the rockaway that would carry him to the steamer at the wharf. He was returning to the city and his business, and they would not see him on the Island again until the next Saturday. He had recovered his composure, which seemed to have suffered somewhat the night before. He was impatient to be off, looking forward to a lively week in Carondelet Street.
Mr. Pontellier handed his wife half the money he had carried away from Klein’s hotel the evening before. She liked money as well as most women do, and she took it with no little satisfaction.
“That will buy a handsome wedding present for Sister Janet!” she said, smoothing the bills and counting them one by one.
“Oh, we’ll do better than that for Sister Janet, my dear,” he laughed, bending to kiss her good-by.

The boys were tumbling about, clinging to his legs and begging him to bring back all sorts of things. Mr. Pontellier was a great favorite, and ladies, men, children, even nurses, were always on hand to say good-by to him. His wife stood smiling and waving, and the boys shouted, as he disappeared down the sandy road in the old rockaway.

A few days afterward a box came for Mrs. Pontellier from New Orleans. It was from her husband. It was packed with friandises, luscious and toothsome morsels: the finest fruits, patés, a rare bottle or two, delicious syrups, and bonbons in abundance.

Mrs. Pontellier was always very generous with the contents of such boxes; she was well used to receiving them when away from home. The patés and fruit went to the dining-room, and the bonbons were handed around. The ladies chose with dainty, discriminating fingers, and a little greedily, and every one of them declared Mr. Pontellier the best husband in the world. Mrs. Pontellier had to admit she knew of none better.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Mr. Pontellier could not have said, to his own satisfaction or anyone else’s, just how his wife failed in her duty to their children. He felt it more than he saw it, and he never put the feeling into words without regretting it afterward and making generous amends.

If one of the little Pontellier boys fell down while playing, he would probably not go running and crying to his mother for comfort. He would be more likely to get up, wipe the water from his eyes and the sand from his mouth, and carry on with his game. Tots though they were, they stuck together and stood their ground in childish battles, with fists doubled and voices raised, and they generally beat the other mother-tots. The quadroon nurse was looked on as a huge encumbrance whose only use was to button up waists and drawers and to brush and part hair, for it seemed to be a law of society that hair must be parted and brushed.

In short, Mrs. Pontellier was not a mother-woman. That summer at Grand Isle the mother-women seemed to be everywhere. They were easy to spot, fluttering about with outspread, protecting wings whenever harm, real or imagined, threatened their precious brood. They idolized their children and worshiped their husbands, and they thought it a holy privilege to efface themselves as individuals and sprout wings as ministering angels.

Many of them were delicious in the part, and one of them was the embodiment of every womanly grace and charm. If her husband did not adore her, he was a brute and deserved to die by slow torture. Her name was Adèle Ratignolle. No words can describe her except the old ones that have so often pictured the heroine of romance of long ago and the fair lady of our dreams. Nothing about her charms was subtle or hidden; her beauty was all there, flaming and plain to see: the spun-gold hair that neither comb nor pin could hold down; the blue eyes that were like nothing but sapphires; the two pouting lips, so red that looking at them one could think only of cherries or some other delicious crimson fruit. She was growing a little stout, but this did not take an iota from the grace of every step, pose and gesture. No one would have wanted her white neck a mite less full or her beautiful arms any slimmer. Never were there hands more exquisite than hers, and it was a joy to watch them as she threaded her needle, or slipped her gold thimble onto her tapering middle finger, while she sewed away at little night-drawers or made a bodice or a bib.

Madame Ratignolle was very fond of Mrs. Pontellier, and she would often pick up her sewing and go sit with her in the afternoons. On the afternoon of the day the box came from New Orleans she was there again. She had the rocker, and she was busy sewing a tiny pair of night-drawers.

She had brought along the pattern of the drawers for Mrs. Pontellier to cut out. It was a marvel of construction, designed to enclose a baby’s body so well that only two small eyes would peer out of the garment, like an Eskimo’s. They were meant for winter, when treacherous drafts came down the chimneys and sly currents of deadly cold crept in through keyholes.

Mrs. Pontellier’s mind was quite at rest about her children’s present material needs. She saw no use in looking ahead and making winter night garments the subject of her summer thoughts. But she did not want to seem unfriendly and uninterested. So she had brought out some newspapers and spread them on the floor of the gallery, and under Madame Ratignolle’s direction she had cut out a pattern for the impervious garment.

Robert was there, sitting as he had sat the Sunday before, and Mrs. Pontellier again held her old place on the top step, leaning listlessly on the post. A box of bonbons stood beside her, and every so often she offered it to Madame Ratignolle.

That lady seemed unable to choose. At last she settled on a stick of nougat, wondering whether it was too rich and whether it could possibly hurt her. Madame Ratignolle had been married seven years. She had a baby about every two years. At that time she had three babies and was beginning to think about a fourth. She was always talking about her “condition.” Her “condition” showed in no way, and no one would have known anything about it if she had not kept making it a subject of conversation.
Robert began to reassure her, saying he had known a lady who had lived on nougat through the entire — but he saw the color rise in Mrs. Pontellier’s face, stopped himself, and changed the subject.

Mrs. Pontellier had married a Creole, but she was not completely at home among Creoles; she had never before been thrown so closely among them. That summer at Lebrun’s there were only Creoles. They all knew one another and felt like one large family, with the friendliest of relations among them. One trait set them apart, and it struck Mrs. Pontellier most forcibly: they had no prudery at all. Their freedom of speech was at first beyond her understanding, though she had no trouble reconciling it with a lofty chastity that in the Creole woman seems to be inborn and unmistakable.

Edna Pontellier would never forget the shock she felt on hearing Madame Ratignolle tell old Monsieur Farival the harrowing story of one of her accouchements, holding back no intimate detail. She was getting used to shocks like this, but she could not keep the color from rising in her cheeks. More than once her arrival had interrupted the droll story Robert was telling to some amused group of married women.

A book had been making the rounds of the pension. When her turn came to read it, she read it in profound astonishment. She felt moved to read it in secret and alone, though none of the others had, and to hide it when she heard footsteps. At table it was openly criticized and freely discussed. Mrs. Pontellier gave up being astonished and decided that wonders would never cease.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: They made a congenial group, sitting there that summer afternoon. Madame Ratignolle sewed away, often stopping to tell a story or an incident, with much expressive movement of her perfect hands. Robert and Mrs. Pontellier sat idle, now and then exchanging a word, a glance or a smile that showed a certain advanced stage of intimacy and friendship.

For the past month he had lived in her shadow, and no one thought anything of it. Many people had predicted that Robert would devote himself to Mrs. Pontellier the moment he arrived. Every summer at Grand Isle since he was fifteen, eleven years back, Robert had appointed himself the devoted attendant of some fair lady or young girl. Sometimes it was a young girl and sometimes a widow; but as often as not it was some interesting married woman.

For two seasons in a row he lived in the sunlight of Mademoiselle Duvigne’s presence. But she died between summers, and then Robert played the inconsolable one, throwing himself at the feet of Madame Ratignolle for whatever crumbs of sympathy and comfort she might care to grant.
Mrs. Pontellier liked to sit and look at her fair companion as she might look at a faultless Madonna.

“Could anyone fathom the cruelty under that fair exterior?” Robert murmured. “She knew I once adored her, and she let me. It was ‘Robert, come; go; stand up; sit down; do this; do that; see whether the baby sleeps; my thimble, please, which I left God knows where. Come and read Daudet to me while I sew.’”
“Par exemple! I never had to ask you. You were always under my feet, like a troublesome cat.”
“You mean like an adoring dog. And the moment Ratignolle appeared on the scene, then it was like a dog. ‘Passez! Adieu! Allez vous-en!’”

“Perhaps I was afraid of making Alphonse jealous,” she put in, with great naïveté. That made them all laugh. The right hand jealous of the left! The heart jealous of the soul! But then, the Creole husband is never jealous; in him the gangrene passion has shrunk from lack of use.

Meanwhile Robert, speaking to Mrs. Pontellier, went on about his hopeless passion of long ago for Madame Ratignolle: the sleepless nights, the consuming flames that made the very sea sizzle when he took his daily plunge. And the lady at the needle kept up a running, contemptuous commentary:
“Blagueur — farceur — gros bête, va!”

He never struck this half-comic, half-serious note when he was alone with Mrs. Pontellier. She never knew quite what to make of it, and just then she could not guess how much was jest and how much earnest. It was understood that he had often spoken words of love to Madame Ratignolle without ever expecting to be taken seriously. Mrs. Pontellier was glad he had not played the same part with her. She would have found it unacceptable and annoying.

Mrs. Pontellier had brought her sketching materials, with which she sometimes dabbled in an unprofessional way. She liked the dabbling. It gave her a kind of satisfaction that no other occupation gave her.

She had long wanted to try her hand at Madame Ratignolle. Never had that lady looked a more tempting subject than now, sitting there like some sensuous Madonna, the gleam of the fading day enriching her splendid color.

Robert crossed over and sat on the step below Mrs. Pontellier to watch her work. She handled her brushes with an ease and freedom that came not from long acquaintance with them but from natural talent. Robert followed the work intently and let slip small cries of approval in French, which he addressed to Madame Ratignolle.
“Mais ce n’est pas mal! Elle s’y connaît, elle a de la force, oui.”

In his oblivious attention he once rested his head quietly against Mrs. Pontellier’s arm. She gently pushed him away. He did it again. She could not help believing it was thoughtlessness on his part, but that was no reason for her to put up with it. She did not protest, except to push him away again, quietly but firmly. He offered no apology. The finished picture looked nothing like Madame Ratignolle. She was greatly disappointed to find that it did not resemble her. But it was a fair enough piece of work, and in many respects satisfying.
Mrs. Pontellier plainly did not think so. She studied the sketch critically, then dragged a broad smudge of paint across it and crumpled the paper in her hands.

The youngsters came tumbling up the steps, the quadroon trailing behind at the respectful distance they required her to keep. Mrs. Pontellier had them carry her paints and things into the house. She tried to hold them back for a little talk and some play. But they were in deadly earnest; they had come only to look into the bonbon box. Without a murmur they took whatever she chose to give them, each holding out two chubby hands, cupped like scoops, in the vain hope of getting them filled; and then off they went.

The sun hung low in the west, and the breeze from the south was soft and languorous, heavy with the seductive scent of the sea. Children in fresh frills were gathering to play under the oaks, their voices high and piercing.

Madame Ratignolle folded up her sewing, setting thimble, scissors and thread together in the roll and pinning it firmly shut. She said she felt faint. Mrs. Pontellier flew to get the cologne water and a fan. She bathed Madame Ratignolle’s face with cologne while Robert plied the fan far harder than was needed.
The spell was soon over. Mrs. Pontellier could not help wondering whether a little imagination was behind it, since the rose tint had never left her friend’s face.

She stood watching the fair woman go down the long line of galleries with the grace and majesty queens are sometimes supposed to have. Her little ones ran to meet her. Two clung to her white skirts; the third she lifted from its nurse and carried off in her own fond, encircling arms, with a thousand endearments. And this although, as everybody well knew, the doctor had forbidden her to lift so much as a pin!
“Are you going bathing?” Robert asked Mrs. Pontellier. It was less a question than a reminder.
“Oh, no,” she answered, sounding undecided. “I’m tired; I think not.” Her eyes strayed from his face toward the Gulf, whose sonorous murmur came to her like a loving but imperious entreaty.
“Oh, come on!” he insisted. “You mustn’t skip your bath. Come along. The water must be delicious, and it will not hurt you. Come.”

He reached up for her big, rough straw hat on its peg outside the door and set it on her head. They went down the steps and off toward the beach together. The sun hung low in the west, and the breeze was soft and warm.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Edna Pontellier could not have said why, when she wished to go to the beach with Robert, she first refused and then followed him, obeying one of the two contradictory impulses that drove her.
A certain light was beginning to dawn dimly within her, the light that, as it shows the way, forbids it.
At that early stage it only bewildered her. It carried her into dreams and thoughtfulness, and into the shadowy anguish that had come over her at midnight when she gave herself up to tears.

In short, Mrs. Pontellier was beginning to see her position in the universe as a human being, and to recognize her relations, as an individual, with the world within and around her. This may seem a ponderous weight of wisdom to settle on the soul of a woman of twenty-eight, perhaps more wisdom than the Holy Ghost is usually pleased to grant to any woman.
But the beginning of things, of a world especially, is bound to be vague, tangled, chaotic and very disturbing. How few of us ever get out of such a beginning! How many souls are lost in its tumult!
The voice of the sea is seductive, never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander awhile in abysses of solitude, to lose itself in mazes of inward contemplation.
The voice of the sea speaks to the soul. The touch of the sea is sensuous, folding the body in its soft, close embrace.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Mrs. Pontellier was not a woman who confided in people, and in this she had always been true to her nature, which was not confiding. Even as a child she had lived her own small life entirely inside herself. Very early, and by instinct, she had grasped that there are two lives: the outward one that conforms, and the inward one that questions.

That summer at Grand Isle she began to loosen, a little, the cloak of reserve she had always worn. There may have been influences, subtle and obvious, working in their various ways to bring this about. There must have been. But the most obvious was Adèle Ratignolle. At first it was the Creole’s extraordinary physical charm that drew her, for Edna was sensually responsive to beauty. Then there was the candor of the woman’s whole existence, open for anyone to read and so striking a contrast to Edna’s own habitual reserve. That may have made a link. Who can say what metals the gods use to forge the subtle bond we call sympathy, and might just as well call love?

One morning the two women went down to the beach together, arm in arm, under the huge white sunshade. Edna had persuaded Madame Ratignolle to leave the children behind. She could not get her to give up a tiny roll of needlework, though, which Adèle begged to be allowed to slip into the depths of her pocket. Somehow, and they could not have said how, they had given Robert the slip.

It was a fair walk to the beach, along a long sandy path. On both sides a straggling, tangled growth kept creeping in over the path, now and then without warning. Acres of yellow camomile stretched away on either hand. Farther off there were vegetable gardens, with small plantations of orange or lemon trees scattered among them. Even from a distance the dark green clusters glistened in the sun.

Both women were fairly tall, but Madame Ratignolle had the more feminine, matronly figure. The charm of Edna Pontellier’s body crept up on you without your noticing. Its lines were long, clean and symmetrical, and now and then it fell into splendid poses. It had nothing of the trim, stereotyped look of a fashion plate. A casual, undiscerning observer, passing by, might not have looked at her twice. But someone with more feeling and judgment would have seen the noble beauty of its modeling, and the graceful severity of its poise and movement, which set Edna Pontellier apart from the crowd.

That morning she wore a cool muslin, white with a waving vertical line of brown running through it, along with a white linen collar and the big straw hat she had taken from the peg outside the door. The hat sat at any angle on her yellow-brown hair, which waved a little, was heavy, and clung close to her head.

Madame Ratignolle took more care of her complexion and had wound a gauze veil around her head. She wore dogskin gloves with gauntlets that protected her wrists. She was dressed in pure white, in a fluff of ruffles that suited her. The draperies and fluttering things she wore went with her rich, luxuriant beauty in a way that a plainer line could never have done.

Along the beach stood a number of bath-houses, roughly but solidly built, each with a small sheltering gallery facing the water. Every house had two compartments, and every family at Lebrun’s had one of its own, fitted out with everything needed for bathing and whatever other comforts the owners wanted. The two women had no plan to bathe. They had simply walked down to the beach to stroll, to be alone, and to be near the water. The Pontellier and Ratignolle compartments lay side by side under one roof.

Mrs. Pontellier had brought her key down out of habit. She unlocked the door of her bath-room and went in. Soon she came out again with a rug, which she spread on the floor of the gallery, and two huge hair pillows covered in crash, which she propped against the front of the building.

The two sat down there in the shade of the porch, side by side, backs against the pillows and feet stretched out. Madame Ratignolle took off her veil and wiped her face with a rather delicate handkerchief. Then she fanned herself with the fan she always carried hanging somewhere on her person from a long, narrow ribbon. Edna took off her collar and opened her dress at the throat. She took the fan from Madame Ratignolle and began to fan them both. It was very warm, and for a while they did nothing but trade remarks about the heat, the sun and the glare. But a breeze was blowing, a stiff, choppy wind that whipped the water into froth. It fluttered the women’s skirts and kept them busy for a while adjusting, readjusting, tucking in, and fixing hair-pins and hat-pins. A few people were playing in the water some distance away. At that hour the beach was very quiet of human sound. The lady in black was reading her morning devotions on the porch of a neighboring bath-house. Two young lovers, having found the children’s tent empty, were sharing the yearnings of their hearts beneath it.

Edna Pontellier had looked all around and finally let her eyes rest on the sea. The day was clear, and the gaze could travel out as far as the blue sky went. A few white clouds hung idly over the horizon. A lateen sail showed in the direction of Cat Island, and others to the south seemed almost motionless in the far distance.

“Of whom — of what are you thinking?” asked Adèle. She had been watching her companion’s face with some amusement, struck by the absorbed look that seemed to have seized every feature and fixed it in statuesque repose.

“Nothing,” Mrs. Pontellier answered with a start, and at once added, “How stupid! But I think it is the answer we all give instinctively to such a question. Let me see,” she went on, throwing back her head and narrowing her fine eyes until they shone like two vivid points of light. “Let me see. I really wasn’t aware of thinking of anything. But perhaps I can retrace my thoughts.”
“Oh! never mind!” laughed Madame Ratignolle. “I’m not so demanding. I’ll let you off this time. It’s really too hot to think, especially to think about thinking.”

“But for the fun of it,” Edna insisted. “First, the sight of the water stretching so far away, and those motionless sails against the blue sky, made a delicious picture, and I just wanted to sit and look at it. The hot wind beating in my face made me think — I can’t trace any connection — of a summer day in Kentucky, and a meadow that seemed as big as the ocean to the very little girl walking through grass that was higher than her waist. She threw out her arms as she walked, as if she were swimming, beating at the tall grass the way you strike out in water. Oh, I see the connection now!”
“Where were you headed that day in Kentucky, walking through the grass?”

“I don’t remember now. I was just walking diagonally across a big field. My sun-bonnet blocked the view. All I could see was the stretch of green in front of me, and I felt I must walk on forever without coming to the end of it. I don’t remember whether I was frightened or pleased. I must have been entertained.
“As likely as not it was Sunday,” she laughed, “and I was running away from prayers, from the Presbyterian service, which my father read in such a gloomy spirit that it chills me yet to think of it.”
“And have you been running from prayers ever since, ma chère?” Madame Ratignolle asked, amused.

“No! oh, no!” Edna hastened to say. “In those days I was a little unthinking child, just following a misleading impulse without question. Quite the opposite, in fact: for one period of my life religion took a firm hold on me. That was after I was twelve and until — until — well, I suppose until now, though I never thought much about it, just driven along by habit. But do you know,” she broke off, turning her quick eyes on Madame Ratignolle and leaning forward so that her face came quite close to her companion’s, “sometimes this summer I feel as if I were walking through the green meadow again, idly, aimlessly, unthinking and unguided.”

Madame Ratignolle laid her hand over Mrs. Pontellier’s, which was lying near her. When the hand was not drawn away, she clasped it firmly and warmly. With her other hand she even stroked it a little, fondly, murmuring under her breath, “Pauvre chérie.”

At first the gesture rather confused Edna, but soon she gave herself readily to the Creole’s gentle caress. She was not used to affection expressed outwardly and in words, either by herself or by others. She and her younger sister, Janet, had quarreled a good deal, out of a habit that did neither of them any good. Her older sister, Margaret, was matronly and dignified, probably because she had taken on a matron’s and housewife’s duties too early, their mother having died when they were quite young. Margaret was not effusive; she was practical. Edna had had a girl friend now and then, but whether by chance or not they all seemed to be of one type, the self-contained. She never saw that the reserve in her own character had much to do with this, perhaps everything. Her closest friend at school had been a girl of rather exceptional intellectual gifts, who wrote fine-sounding essays that Edna admired and tried to imitate. With her Edna talked, and glowed, over the English classics, and sometimes argued about religion and politics.

Edna often wondered at one tendency that sometimes disturbed her inwardly, without any outward sign on her part. At a very early age (perhaps it was when she crossed the ocean of waving grass) she remembered being passionately in love with a dignified, sad-eyed cavalry officer who visited her father in Kentucky. When he was there she could not leave his presence or take her eyes from his face, which was something like Napoleon’s, with a lock of black hair falling across the forehead. But the cavalry officer faded imperceptibly out of her life.

At another time her affections were deeply taken by a young gentleman who was visiting a lady on a neighboring plantation. This was after they went to live in Mississippi. The young man was engaged to the young lady, and they sometimes called on Margaret, driving over in a buggy in the afternoons. Edna was a little miss just coming into her teens, and the knowledge that she herself was nothing, nothing, nothing to the engaged young man was a bitter affliction to her. But he, too, went the way of dreams.

She was a grown young woman when she was overtaken by what she took to be the climax of her fate. The face and figure of a great tragedian began to haunt her imagination and stir her senses. That the infatuation lasted gave it an air of genuineness. Its hopelessness colored it with the lofty tones of a great passion.

The tragedian’s picture stood framed on her desk. Anyone may own the portrait of a tragedian without raising suspicion or comment. (This was a sinister reflection, and she cherished it.) In front of others she spoke admiringly of his exalted gifts, passing the photograph around and dwelling on how true a likeness it was. When she was alone she sometimes picked it up and kissed the cold glass passionately.

Her marriage to Léonce Pontellier was purely an accident. In this it resembled many other marriages that masquerade as the decrees of Fate. She met him in the midst of her secret great passion. He fell in love, as men are in the habit of doing, and pressed his suit with an earnestness and ardor that left nothing to be desired. He pleased her, and his absolute devotion flattered her. She fancied that there was a sympathy of thought and taste between them, and in that fancy she was mistaken. Add to this the violent opposition of her father and her sister Margaret to her marrying a Catholic, and we need look no further for the reasons that led her to accept Monsieur Pontellier as her husband.

The height of bliss, which would have been marriage with the tragedian, was not for her in this world. As the devoted wife of a man who worshiped her, she felt she would take her place with a certain dignity in the world of reality, closing the doors forever behind her on the realm of romance and dreams.

But before long the tragedian had gone to join the cavalry officer, the engaged young man and a few others, and Edna found herself face to face with realities. She grew fond of her husband. She noticed, with a satisfaction she could not account for, that her affection had no trace of passion or excessive, false warmth in it, which might threaten to dissolve it.

She was fond of her children in an uneven, impulsive way. Sometimes she would gather them passionately to her heart; sometimes she would forget them. The year before, they had spent part of the summer with their grandmother Pontellier in Iberville. She felt sure of their happiness and welfare, and so she did not miss them, except for an occasional intense longing. Their absence was a sort of relief, though she did not admit this even to herself. It seemed to free her from a responsibility she had taken on blindly and for which Fate had not fitted her.

Edna did not reveal as much as all this to Madame Ratignolle that summer day as they sat with their faces turned to the sea. But a good part of it slipped out. She had put her head down on Madame Ratignolle’s shoulder. She was flushed, and felt intoxicated by the sound of her own voice and the unaccustomed taste of candor. It muddled her like wine, or like a first breath of freedom.

Voices approached. It was Robert, surrounded by a troop of children and looking for them. The two little Pontelliers were with him, and he carried Madame Ratignolle’s little girl in his arms. There were other children too, and two nurse-maids followed, looking disagreeable and resigned.

The women rose at once and began to shake out their draperies and loosen their muscles. Mrs. Pontellier tossed the cushions and rug into the bath-house. The children all scampered off to the awning, where they stood in a line staring at the intruding lovers, who were still trading vows and sighs. The lovers got up, with only a silent protest, and walked slowly off somewhere else.
The children took over the tent, and Mrs. Pontellier went over to join them.
Madame Ratignolle begged Robert to go with her to the house. She complained of cramp in her limbs and stiffness in her joints. As they walked she leaned on his arm, dragging.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: “Do me a favor, Robert,” said the pretty woman at his side, almost as soon as the two had started on their slow way home. She looked up into his face, leaning on his arm in the circle of shade under the umbrella he had raised.
“Granted. As many as you like,” he answered, glancing down into her eyes, which were full of thoughtfulness and some speculation.
“I only ask for one. Leave Mrs. Pontellier alone.”
Robert burst into a sudden, boyish laugh. “Tiens! Voilà que Madame Ratignolle est jalouse!”
“Nonsense! I’m in earnest. I mean what I say. Leave Mrs. Pontellier alone.”
“Why?” he asked, growing serious himself at his companion’s urging.
“She isn’t one of us. She isn’t like us. She might make the unfortunate mistake of taking you seriously.”

His face flushed with annoyance. He took off his soft hat and began beating it impatiently against his leg as he walked. “Why shouldn’t she take me seriously?” he demanded sharply. “Am I a comedian, a clown, a jack-in-the-box? Why shouldn’t she? You Creoles! I have no patience with you! Must I always be treated as one of the amusements on the program? I hope Mrs. Pontellier does take me seriously. I hope she has enough discernment to find something in me besides the blagueur. If I thought there was any doubt —”

“Oh, enough, Robert!” she cut into his heated outburst. “You aren’t thinking about what you’re saying. You speak with about as little reflection as we’d expect from one of those children down there playing in the sand. If you ever paid attentions to a married woman here meaning to be convincing, you wouldn’t be the gentleman we all know you to be, and you’d be unfit to keep company with the wives and daughters of the people who trust you.”
Madame Ratignolle had stated what she took for the law and the gospel. The young man gave an impatient shrug.
“Oh! well! That isn’t it,” he said, slamming his hat down hard on his head. “You ought to see that such things aren’t flattering to say to a man.”
“Should all our dealings with each other be an exchange of compliments? Ma foi!”

“It isn’t pleasant to have a woman tell you —” he went on, not listening, then broke off suddenly. “Now if I were like Arobin — you remember Alcée Arobin and that story about the consul’s wife at Biloxi?” And he told the story of Alcée Arobin and the consul’s wife. He told another about the tenor of the French Opera, who received letters that should never have been written, and still others, grave and gay, until Mrs. Pontellier, and her possible tendency to take young men seriously, seemed quite forgotten.

When they reached her cottage, Madame Ratignolle went in to take the hour’s rest she thought so helpful. Before leaving her, Robert begged her pardon for the impatience, which he called rudeness, with which he had met her well-meant warning.

“You made one mistake, Adèle,” he said, with a light smile. “Mrs. Pontellier could never possibly take me seriously. What you should have warned me about was taking myself seriously. Then your advice might have counted for something and given me food for reflection. Au revoir. But you look tired,” he added with concern. “Would you like a cup of bouillon? Shall I stir you a toddy? Let me mix you a toddy with a drop of Angostura.”

She agreed to the bouillon, which sounded welcome and good. He went to the kitchen himself, a building separate from the cottages, behind the house. And he himself brought her the golden-brown bouillon in a dainty Sèvres cup, with a flaky cracker or two on the saucer.
She put a bare, white arm out through the curtain screening her open door and took the cup from him. She said he was a bon garçon, and she meant it. Robert thanked her and turned toward “the house.”

The lovers were just coming into the grounds of the pension. They leaned toward each other like the water-oaks bending from the sea. There was not a particle of earth under their feet. Their heads might have been turned upside-down, so completely did they walk on blue ether. Creeping along behind them, the lady in black looked a little paler and more worn than usual. There was no sign of Mrs. Pontellier and the children. Robert searched the distance for any such figure. They would no doubt stay away until the dinner hour. The young man climbed to his mother’s room. It was at the top of the house, a room of odd angles and a queer, sloping ceiling. Two broad dormer windows looked out toward the Gulf and as far across it as a man’s eye could reach. The furnishings were light, cool and practical.

Madame Lebrun was hard at work at the sewing-machine. A little black girl sat on the floor and worked the treadle with her hands. The Creole woman takes no chances with her health that can be avoided.

Robert went over and sat down on the broad sill of one of the dormer windows. He took a book from his pocket and began to read it energetically, to judge by how precisely and how often he turned the pages. The sewing-machine made a resounding clatter in the room, being of a ponderous, old-fashioned make. In the lulls, Robert and his mother traded scraps of rambling conversation.
“Where is Mrs. Pontellier?”
“Down at the beach with the children.”

“I promised to lend her the Goncourt. When you go down, don’t forget to take it. You’ll find it on the bookshelf above the small table.” Clatter, clatter, clatter, bang! went the machine for the next five or eight minutes.
“Where is Victor going with the carriage?”
“The carriage? Victor?”
“Yes, down in front. It looks as if he’s getting ready to drive off somewhere.”
“Call him.” Clatter, clatter!
Robert let out a shrill, piercing whistle that could have been heard all the way back at the wharf.
Madame Lebrun flew to the window and called “Victor!” She waved a handkerchief and called once more. Down below, the young fellow climbed into the vehicle and set the horse off at a gallop.

Madame Lebrun went back to the machine, crimson with annoyance. Victor, her younger son and Robert’s younger brother, was a tête montée, with a temper that invited violence and a will no ax could break.
“Whenever you say the word I’m ready to thrash into him as much reason as he can hold.”

“If only your father had lived!” Clatter, clatter, clatter, clatter, bang! Madame Lebrun held it as a fixed belief that the running of the universe, and everything connected with it, would have been plainly more intelligent and on a higher order if Monsieur Lebrun had not been removed to other spheres in the early years of their marriage.

“What do you hear from Montel?” Montel was a middle-aged gentleman. For twenty years his vain ambition and desire had been to fill the void left in the Lebrun household when Monsieur Lebrun was taken away. Clatter, clatter, bang, clatter!

“I have a letter somewhere,” he said, looking in the machine drawer and finding the letter at the bottom of the workbasket. “He says to tell you he will be in Vera Cruz at the beginning of next month,” — clatter, clatter! — “and if you still mean to join him” — bang! clatter, clatter, bang!
“Mother, why didn’t you tell me this before? You know I wanted —” Clatter, clatter, clatter!

“Do you see Mrs. Pontellier starting back with the children? She’ll be late for luncheon again. She never begins to get ready for luncheon until the last minute.” Clatter, clatter! “Where are you going?”
“Where did you say the Goncourt was?”

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Every light in the hall was blazing, every lamp turned up as high as it could go without smoking the chimney or risking an explosion. The lamps were fixed at intervals along the wall, circling the whole room. Someone had gathered orange and lemon branches and made graceful festoons of them in between. The dark green of the branches stood out and glistened against the white muslin curtains that draped the windows. The curtains puffed, floated and flapped at the whim of a stiff breeze sweeping up from the Gulf.

It was Saturday night, a few weeks after the intimate talk between Robert and Madame Ratignolle on their way back from the beach. An unusual number of husbands, fathers and friends had come down to stay over Sunday, and their families were entertaining them suitably, with the material help of Madame Lebrun. The dining tables had all been moved to one end of the hall, and the chairs were arranged in rows and clusters. Earlier in the evening each little family group had had its say and traded its domestic gossip. Now there seemed to be a disposition to relax, to widen the circle of confidences and give the conversation a more general tone.

Many of the children had been allowed to stay up past their bedtime. A small band lay on their stomachs on the floor, looking at the colored sheets of the comic papers Mr. Pontellier had brought down. The little Pontellier boys were allowing it, and making sure everyone felt their authority.

The entertainments were music, dancing and a recitation or two, furnished, or rather offered. But there was nothing systematic about the program, no sign that it had been arranged beforehand, or even thought out.

Early in the evening the Farival twins were persuaded to play the piano. They were fourteen-year-old girls, always dressed in the Virgin’s colors, blue and white, since they had been dedicated to the Blessed Virgin at their baptism. They played a duet from “Zampa” and, at everyone’s earnest request, followed it with the overture to “The Poet and the Peasant.”

“Allez vous-en! Sapristi!” shrieked the parrot outside the door. He was the only one present candid enough to admit that this was not the first time that summer he had listened to these gracious performances. Old Monsieur Farival, the twins’ grandfather, grew indignant at the interruption and insisted that the bird be taken away and shut up in the dark. Victor Lebrun objected, and his decrees were as unchangeable as those of Fate. Fortunately the parrot gave the entertainment no further trouble. All the venom of his nature seemed to have been stored up and hurled at the twins in that one impetuous outburst.
Later a young brother and sister gave recitations. Everyone present had heard them many times at winter evening entertainments in the city.

In the middle of the floor a little girl performed a skirt dance. Her mother played the accompaniment while she watched her daughter with greedy admiration and nervous apprehension. She had no cause for apprehension. The child was mistress of the situation. She had been properly dressed for the occasion in black tulle and black silk tights. Her little neck and arms were bare, and her artificially crimped hair stood out over her head in fluffy black plumes. Her poses were full of grace, and her little black-shod toes twinkled as they shot out and upward with a speed and suddenness that was bewildering.

But there was no reason why everyone should not dance. Madame Ratignolle could not, so it was she who gaily agreed to play for the others. She played very well, keeping excellent waltz time and putting an expression into the music that was truly inspiring. She kept up her music for the children’s sake, she said. She and her husband both thought it a way of brightening the home and making it attractive.

Almost everyone danced except the twins, who could not be persuaded to separate for the short time that one or the other would be whirling around the room in a man’s arms. They might have danced together, but it never occurred to them.

The children were sent to bed. Some went quietly; others went shrieking and protesting as they were dragged off. They had been allowed to stay up until the ice-cream was served, which naturally marked the limit of human indulgence.

The ice-cream was passed around with cake, gold and silver cake arranged on platters in alternate slices. It had been made and frozen that afternoon behind the kitchen by two black women, under Victor’s supervision. It was pronounced a great success. It would have been excellent, people said, if it had only had a little less vanilla or a little more sugar, if it had been frozen a degree harder, and if the salt could have been kept out of parts of it. Victor was proud of his achievement. He went around recommending it and urging everyone to eat it to excess.

Mrs. Pontellier danced twice with her husband, once with Robert, and once with Monsieur Ratignolle, who was thin and tall and swayed like a reed in the wind as he danced. After that she went out on the gallery and sat on the low window-sill. From there she could see all that went on in the hall and also look out toward the Gulf. A soft glow showed in the east. The moon was rising, and its mystic shimmer threw a million lights across the distant, restless water.
“Would you like to hear Mademoiselle Reisz play?” Robert asked, as he came out onto the porch where she was. Of course Edna would like to; but she feared it was useless to plead with her.

“I’ll ask her,” he said. “I’ll tell her you want to hear her. She likes you. She’ll come.” He turned and hurried off to one of the far cottages, where Mademoiselle Reisz was shuffling about. She was dragging a chair in and out of her room, and now and then complaining about the crying of a baby that a nurse in the next cottage was trying to put to sleep. She was a disagreeable little woman, no longer young, who had quarreled with nearly everyone, because of a self-assertive temper and a habit of trampling on other people’s rights. Robert won her over without too much difficulty.

She came into the hall with him in a lull between dances and made an awkward, imperious little bow as she entered. A homely woman, she had a small, shriveled face and body, and eyes that glowed. She had no taste at all in dress. She wore a mass of rusty black lace, and pinned a bunch of artificial violets at the side of her hair.

“Ask Mrs. Pontellier what she would like to hear me play,” she told Robert. She sat perfectly still before the piano, not touching the keys, while Robert carried her message to Edna at the window. A general air of surprise and real satisfaction came over everyone as they saw the pianist come in. People settled down, and a feeling of expectancy filled the room. Edna was a little embarrassed at being singled out for the imperious little woman’s favor. She would not dare to choose, and begged that Mademoiselle Reisz please herself in what she played.

Edna was what she herself called very fond of music. Well-played music had a way of calling up pictures in her mind. She sometimes liked to sit in the room in the mornings when Madame Ratignolle played or practiced. There was one piece Madame Ratignolle played that Edna had named “Solitude.” It was a short, plaintive piece in a minor key. The piece had a different title, but she called it “Solitude.” When she heard it, the figure of a man came before her imagination, standing beside a desolate rock on the seashore. He was naked. His attitude was one of hopeless resignation as he looked toward a distant bird winging its flight away from him.

Another piece brought to mind a dainty young woman in an Empire gown, taking mincing dance steps down a long avenue between tall hedges. One reminded her of children at play, and another of nothing on earth but a demure lady stroking a cat.

From the very first chords Mademoiselle Reisz struck on the piano, a keen tremor ran down Mrs. Pontellier’s spine. She had heard an artist at the piano before. Perhaps this was the first time she was ready for one. Perhaps this was the first time her being was tempered to take the impress of the abiding truth.

She waited for the pictures she expected to gather and blaze in her imagination. She waited in vain. No pictures of solitude, hope, longing or despair came. Yet the passions themselves were stirred in her soul, swaying it and lashing it as the waves daily beat on her splendid body. She trembled and choked, and the tears blinded her.
Mademoiselle had finished. She rose, made her stiff, lofty bow, and left without waiting for thanks or applause. Passing along the gallery, she patted Edna on the shoulder.

“Well, how did you like my music?” she asked. The young woman could not answer. She pressed the pianist’s hand convulsively. Mademoiselle Reisz saw her agitation, and even her tears. She patted her on the shoulder again and said:
“You are the only one worth playing for. Those others? Bah!” And off she went down the gallery toward her room, shuffling and sidling.

But she was wrong about “those others.” Her playing had set off a fever of enthusiasm. “What passion!” “What an artist!” “I have always said no one could play Chopin like Mademoiselle Reisz!” “That last prelude! Bon Dieu! It shakes a man!”
It was growing late, and most people were ready to break up. But someone, perhaps Robert, thought of a bath at that mystic hour and under that mystic moon.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: In any case, Robert had proposed it, and nobody objected. Everyone was ready to follow wherever he led. He did not actually lead, though; he pointed the way. He himself dawdled at the back with the lovers, who had shown a wish to linger and keep to themselves. He walked between them, and whether he did it out of malice or mischief was not entirely clear, even to him.

The Pontelliers and the Ratignolles walked ahead, the women leaning on their husbands’ arms. Edna could hear Robert’s voice behind them and now and then make out what he said. She wondered why he did not join them. It was not like him. Lately he had sometimes kept away from her for a whole day, then doubled his attentions the next day and the day after, as if to make up for the lost hours. She missed him on the days when some excuse took him away, the way one misses the sun on a cloudy day without having given it much thought while it was shining.

The people strolled toward the beach in little groups, talking and laughing, and some singing. Down at Klein’s hotel a band was playing, and its strains came to them faintly, softened by the distance. The air was full of strange, rare odors: the smell of the sea tangled with weeds and damp, freshly plowed earth, and over it the heavy perfume of a field of white blossoms somewhere near. Yet the night rested lightly on sea and land. Its darkness had no weight, and nothing cast a shadow. The moon’s white light lay over the world like the mystery and softness of sleep.

Most of them walked into the water as if it were their natural element. The sea was calm now. It rose lazily in broad swells that melted into one another and broke only on the beach, in little foamy crests that curled back like slow, white serpents.

All summer Edna had tried to learn to swim. Both the men and the women had given her lessons, and in some cases the children had. Robert had kept up a system of lessons almost every day, and he was close to giving up, seeing how useless his efforts were. A kind of uncontrollable dread clung to her in the water, unless a hand was near that could reach out and reassure her.

But that night she was like a little child, tottering, stumbling and clutching, who suddenly finds out what it can do and takes its first steps alone, boldly and with too much confidence. She could have shouted for joy, and she did shout for joy when, with a sweeping stroke or two, she raised her body to the surface of the water.

Exultation took hold of her, as if she had been handed some power of great import over the working of her body and her soul. She became daring and reckless, and she overrated her strength. She wanted to swim far out, farther than any woman had swum before.
Her unexpected achievement was a source of wonder, applause and admiration. Each person congratulated himself that his own special lessons had brought about the result they all wanted.

“How easy it is!” she thought. “It is nothing,” she said aloud. “Why did I not find out before that it was nothing? Think of all the time I have lost, splashing about like a baby!” She would not join the groups in their games and races. Drunk with the power she had just won, she swam out by herself.

She turned her face to the open sea, to take in an impression of space and solitude. The vast sheet of water, meeting and melting into the moonlit sky, gave that impression to her excited fancy. As she swam, she seemed to be reaching for the unlimited, to lose herself in it.

Once she turned and looked back at the shore, toward the people she had left there. She had not gone very far — that is, not far for an experienced swimmer. But to her unaccustomed eyes the water behind her took on the look of a barrier that her own strength, with no help, could never overcome.
A sudden vision of death struck her soul and, for a second, appalled her and weakened her senses. But with an effort she rallied her staggering faculties and managed to get back to land.
She said nothing of her brush with death or her flash of terror, except to tell her husband, “I thought I should have perished out there alone.”
“You were not so very far, my dear; I was watching you,” he told her.

Edna went straight to the bath-house. By the time the others left the water, she was dressed in dry clothes and ready to go home. She set off alone. They all called and shouted after her. She waved a hand to say no and kept walking, ignoring their renewed cries to make her stay.
“Sometimes I am tempted to think that Mrs. Pontellier is capricious,” said Madame Lebrun. She was enjoying herself immensely and was afraid that Edna’s sudden leaving might spoil the pleasure.
“I know she is,” agreed Mr. Pontellier; “sometimes, not often.”
Edna had not covered a quarter of the way home when Robert caught up with her.
“Did you think I was afraid?” she asked him, without a trace of annoyance.
“No; I knew you weren’t afraid.”
“Then why did you come? Why didn’t you stay out there with the others?”
“I never thought of it.”
“Of anything. What difference does it make?”
“I’m very tired,” she said, in a complaining tone.

“You don’t know anything about it. Why should you? I never was so tired in my life. But it isn’t unpleasant. A thousand feelings have rushed through me tonight, and I don’t understand half of them. Pay no attention to what I’m saying; I am only thinking aloud. I wonder whether anything will ever stir me again the way Mademoiselle Reisz’s playing did tonight. I wonder whether any night on earth will ever be like this one. It is like a night in a dream. The people around me seem like uncanny, half-human creatures. There must be spirits abroad tonight.”
“There are,” whispered Robert. “Didn’t you know this was the twenty-eighth of August?”
“The twenty-eighth of August?”

“Yes. On the twenty-eighth of August, at midnight, if the moon is shining — and the moon must be shining — a spirit that has haunted these shores for ages rises from the Gulf. With its own piercing sight, it searches for some mortal worthy to keep it company, worthy to be raised for a few hours into the realms of the semi-celestials. Until now its search has always failed, and it has sunk back into the sea, disheartened. But tonight it found Mrs. Pontellier. Perhaps it will never quite release her from the spell. Perhaps she will never again permit a poor, unworthy earthling to walk in the shadow of her divine presence.”

“Don’t make fun of me,” she said, hurt by what seemed his flippancy. He did not mind what she asked, but her tone, with its delicate note of pathos, felt like a reproach. He could not explain. He could not tell her that he had seen into her mood and understood. He only offered her his arm, since she had admitted she was exhausted. She had been walking alone, her arms hanging limp, her white skirts trailing along the dewy path. She took his arm but did not lean on it. Her hand lay on it listlessly, as if her thoughts were elsewhere, somewhere ahead of her body, and she were trying to catch them up.
Robert helped her into the hammock, which hung from the post in front of her door to the trunk of a tree.
“Will you stay out here and wait for Mr. Pontellier?” he asked.
“I’ll stay out here. Good night.”
“Shall I get you a pillow?”
“There’s one here,” she said, feeling around, for they were in the shadow.
“It must be dirty; the children have been tumbling it about.”

“No matter.” Having found the pillow, she slid it under her head and stretched out in the hammock, drawing a deep breath of relief. She was not a haughty or over-dainty woman. She did not often lie in the hammock, and when she did, there was nothing cat-like or voluptuous about it. It was a kindly rest that seemed to spread through her whole body.
“Shall I stay with you until Mr. Pontellier comes?” asked Robert, sitting down on the outer edge of one of the steps and taking hold of the hammock rope tied to the post.
“If you wish. Don’t swing the hammock. Will you get my white shawl that I left on the window-sill over at the house?”
“No; but I shall be presently.”
“Presently?” he laughed. “Do you know what time it is? How long are you going to stay out here?”
“I don’t know. Will you get the shawl?”
“Of course I will,” he said, and stood up. He crossed the grass to the house. She watched his figure pass in and out of the strips of moonlight. It was past midnight, and very quiet.
When he came back with the shawl, she took it and held it in her hand. She did not put it around her.
“Did you say I should stay until Mr. Pontellier came back?”
“I said you might if you wished to.”

He sat down again, rolled a cigarette and smoked it in silence. Mrs. Pontellier said nothing either. No flood of words could have said more than those silent moments, or been fuller of the first-felt throbbings of desire.

When the voices of the bathers came nearer, Robert said good night. She did not answer. He thought she was asleep. Once more she watched his figure pass in and out of the strips of moonlight as he walked off.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: “What are you doing out here, Edna? I thought you would be in bed,” said her husband when he found her lying there. He had walked up with Madame Lebrun and left her at the house. His wife did not answer.
“Are you asleep?” he asked, bending down close to look at her.
“No.” Her eyes gleamed bright and intense as they looked into his, with no shadow of sleep in them.
“Do you know it is past one o’clock? Come on,” and he climbed the steps and went into their room.
“Edna!” called Mr. Pontellier from inside, after a few moments had passed.
“Don’t wait for me,” she answered. He stuck his head out the door.
“You will catch cold out there,” he said irritably. “What folly is this? Why don’t you come in?”
“It isn’t cold; I have my shawl.”
“The mosquitoes will eat you alive.”
“There are no mosquitoes.”

She heard him moving around the room, every sound showing impatience and irritation. At another time she would have gone in when he asked. Out of habit she would have given in to what he wanted. She would not have felt any submission or obedience to his commanding wishes; she would have done it without thinking, the way we walk, move, sit and stand, and go through the daily treadmill of the life that has been portioned out to us.
“Edna, dear, are you not coming in soon?” he asked again, this time tenderly, with a note of entreaty.
“No; I am going to stay out here.”
“This is more than folly,” he burst out. “I can’t let you stay out there all night. Come into the house this instant.”

She settled herself deeper into the hammock with a writhing movement. She knew that her will had flared up, stubborn and resistant. At that moment she could not have done anything but refuse and resist. She wondered whether her husband had ever spoken to her like that before, and whether she had given in to his order. Of course she had; she remembered that she had. But feeling as she felt now, she could not see why, or how, she could ever have given in.
“Léonce, go to bed,” she said. “I mean to stay out here. I don’t want to go in, and I won’t. Don’t speak to me that way again; I will not answer you.”

Mr. Pontellier had got ready for bed, but he put on one more garment. He opened a bottle of wine from the small, select supply he kept in a cabinet of his own, drank a glass, and went out on the gallery to offer his wife one. She did not want it. He pulled up the rocker, put his slippered feet up on the rail, and went on to smoke a cigar. He smoked two. Then he went in and drank another glass of wine. Again Mrs. Pontellier refused the glass he held out. Mr. Pontellier sat down once more with his feet up, waited a reasonable while, and smoked a few more cigars.

Edna began to feel like someone slowly waking from a dream, a delicious, grotesque, impossible dream, and feeling reality press into her soul again. The physical need for sleep began to overtake her. The exuberance that had held up and exalted her spirit left her helpless, ready to yield to the circumstances that crowded in on her.

The stillest hour of the night had arrived, the hour before dawn, when the world seems to hold its breath. The moon hung low in the sleeping sky, and silver had turned to copper. The old owl hooted no more, and the water-oaks no longer moaned as they bowed their heads.
Edna got up, stiff from lying so long and so still in the hammock. She stumbled up the steps, grasping feebly at the post before she went inside.
“Are you coming in, Léonce?” she asked, turning her face toward her husband.
“Yes, dear,” he answered, his eyes following a misty puff of smoke. “As soon as I have finished my cigar.”

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: She slept only a few hours, troubled and feverish ones, full of dreams without substance that slipped from her, leaving on her half-awakened senses only the impression of something she could not reach. She was up and dressed in the cool of early morning. The air was bracing and steadied her faculties a little. Still, she was not seeking refreshment or help from anywhere, outside or within. She followed blindly whatever impulse moved her, as if she had put herself in strangers’ hands to be directed and had freed her soul of all responsibility.

Most people were still in bed asleep at that hour. A few who planned to cross to the Chênière for mass were stirring. The lovers, who had made their plans the night before, were already strolling toward the wharf. Behind them, at no great distance, came the lady in black with her Sunday prayer-book, velvet and gold-clasped, and her Sunday silver beads. Old Monsieur Farival was up and was more than half inclined to do whatever came to mind. He put on his big straw hat, took his umbrella from the stand in the hall, and set off after the lady in black, never catching her.
The little Black girl who ran Madame Lebrun’s sewing-machine was sweeping the galleries, with long, absent-minded strokes of the broom. Edna sent her up to the house to wake Robert.
“Tell him I am going to the Chêniere. The boat is ready; tell him to hurry.”

He joined her soon. She had never sent for him before. She had never asked for him. She had never seemed to want him before. She did not seem to realize that she had done anything unusual in summoning him. He seemed just as unaware of anything extraordinary in it. But when he met her, a quiet glow filled his face.

They went back together to the kitchen for coffee. There was no time to wait for proper service. They stood outside the window, and the cook passed them coffee and a roll, which they took at the window-sill. Edna said it tasted good.
She had not thought of coffee, or of anything. He told her he had often noticed that she lacked foresight.

“Wasn’t it enough to think of going to the Chênière and waking you? Do I have to think of everything?” she laughed. “That is what Léonce says when he’s in a bad humor. I don’t blame him; he’d never be in a bad humor if it weren’t for me.”

They cut across the sands. Far off they could see the curious procession making for the wharf: the lovers creeping along shoulder to shoulder; the lady in black, gaining on them steadily; old Monsieur Farival, losing ground inch by inch; and at the rear a young barefooted Spanish girl, a red kerchief on her head and a basket on her arm.

Robert knew the girl and talked to her a little in the boat. Nobody else there could follow what they said. Her name was Mariequita. Her face was round, sly and piquant, her black eyes pretty. Her hands were small, and she kept them folded on the handle of her basket. Her feet were broad and coarse, and she did not try to hide them. Edna looked at them and noticed the sand and slime between her brown toes.

Beaudelet grumbled that Mariequita was there taking up so much room. What really annoyed him was having old Monsieur Farival aboard, who thought himself the better sailor. But he would not quarrel with a man as old as Monsieur Farival, so he quarreled with Mariequita. At one moment the girl was apologetic and appealed to Robert. At the next she was saucy, nodding her head up and down, making “eyes” at Robert and “mouths” at Beaudelet.

The lovers were quite alone. They saw nothing and heard nothing. The lady in black was telling her beads for the third time. Old Monsieur Farival kept talking, about all he knew of handling a boat and all Beaudelet did not know.
Edna liked it all. She looked Mariequita up and down, from her rough brown toes to her pretty black eyes, and back again.
“Why does she look at me like that?” the girl asked Robert.
“Maybe she thinks you are pretty. Shall I ask her?”
“No. Is she your sweetheart?”
“She’s a married lady, and has two children.”
“Oh! well! Francisco ran away with Sylvano’s wife, who had four children. They took all his money and one of the children and stole his boat.”
“Does she understand?”
“Are those two married over there — leaning on each other?”
“Of course not,” laughed Robert.
“Of course not,” echoed Mariequita, with a serious, confirming nod of the head.

The sun stood high and had begun to bite. The quick breeze seemed to Edna to drive its sting into the pores of her face and hands. Robert held his umbrella over her. The boat went slicing sideways through the water, its sails bellied tight, the wind filling them and running over. Old Monsieur Farival laughed sardonically at something as he looked up at the sails, and Beaudelet swore at the old man under his breath.

Sailing across the bay to the Chênière Caminada, Edna felt carried away from an anchorage that had held her fast. Its chains had been loosening, and the night before, with the mystic spirit abroad, they had snapped, leaving her free to drift wherever she chose to set her sails. Robert talked to her constantly and no longer noticed Mariequita. In her bamboo basket the girl had shrimps covered with Spanish moss. She pressed the moss down impatiently and muttered sullenly to herself.
“Let’s go to Grande Terre tomorrow?” said Robert in a low voice.
“What shall we do there?”
“Climb the hill to the old fort, look at the little wriggling gold snakes, and watch the lizards sun themselves.”

She gazed off toward Grande Terre. She thought she would like to be there alone with Robert, in the sun, hearing the ocean roar and watching the slimy lizards writhe in and out among the ruins of the old fort.
“And the next day or the next we can sail to the Bayou Brulow,” he went on.
“What shall we do there?”
“Anything — cast bait for fish.”
“No; we’ll go back to Grande Terre. Let the fish alone.”
“We’ll go wherever you like,” he said. “I’ll have Tonie come over and help me patch up and trim my boat. We won’t need Beaudelet or anyone else. Are you afraid of the pirogue?”

“Then I’ll take you some night in the pirogue when the moon shines. Maybe your Gulf spirit will whisper to you which of these islands the treasures are hidden on — direct you to the very spot, perhaps.”

“And in one day we should be rich!” she laughed. “I’d give it all to you, the pirate gold and every bit of treasure we could dig up. I think you would know how to spend it. Pirate gold isn’t something to hoard or put to use. It is for squandering, for throwing to the four winds, for the fun of watching the golden specks fly.”
“We’d share it, and scatter it together,” he said. His face flushed.
All of them climbed together to the quaint little Gothic church of Our Lady of Lourdes, which gleamed brown and yellow with paint in the glare of the sun.
Only Beaudelet stayed behind, tinkering with his boat. Mariequita walked off with her basket of shrimps, giving Robert a look of childish ill humor and reproach out of the corner of her eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
