paragraphs: The service left Edna oppressed and drowsy. Her head began to ache, and the altar lights swayed before her eyes. On another day she might have tried to pull herself together, but now she wanted only to get out of the stifling church into the open air. She got up and climbed over Robert’s feet, muttering an apology. Old Monsieur Farival, flustered and curious, rose too, but seeing that Robert had followed Mrs. Pontellier, he sank back into his seat. He whispered an anxious question to the lady in black, who neither noticed nor answered, but kept her eyes fixed on the pages of her velvet prayer-book.

“I felt giddy and almost overcome,” Edna said, lifting her hands instinctively to her head and pushing her straw hat up from her forehead. “I couldn’t have stayed through the service.” They were outside, in the shadow of the church. Robert was full of concern.

“It was folly to think of coming in the first place, never mind staying. Come over to Madame Antoine’s; you can rest there.” He took her arm and led her off, watching her face anxiously the whole way.

How still it was, with only the sea’s voice whispering through the reeds in the salt-water pools! The long row of little gray, weather-beaten houses lay peacefully among the orange trees. It must always have been God’s day on that low, drowsy island, Edna thought. They stopped at a jagged fence made of driftwood and leaned on it to ask for water. A youth, a mild-faced Acadian, was drawing it from the cistern, which was only a rusty buoy, open on one side, sunk in the ground. He handed them the water in a tin pail. It did not taste cold, but it felt cool on her heated face, and it revived and refreshed her greatly.

Madame Antoine’s cot stood at the far end of the village. She welcomed them with all the hospitality of the place, the way she would throw open her door to the sunlight. She was fat and crossed the floor with a heavy, clumsy walk. She spoke no English, but when Robert made her understand that the lady with him was ill and needed rest, she was eager to make Edna feel at home and settle her comfortably.

The whole place was spotlessly clean, and the big four-posted bed, snow-white, invited rest. It stood in a small side room that looked out over a narrow grass plot to the shed, where a disabled boat lay keel upward.

Madame Antoine had not gone to mass. Her son Tonie had, but she supposed he would soon be back, and she invited Robert to sit down and wait for him. He went and sat outside the door and smoked instead. Madame Antoine busied herself in the large front room, getting dinner ready. She was boiling mullets over a few red coals in the huge fireplace.

Alone in the little side room, Edna loosened her clothes and took off most of them. She washed her face, neck and arms in the basin between the windows. She took off her shoes and stockings and lay down in the very middle of the high, white bed. What luxury it was to rest in a strange, quaint bed, the sweet country smell of laurel still in the sheets and mattress! She stretched her strong limbs, which ached a little, and for a while ran her fingers through her loosened hair. She held her round arms straight up and rubbed them one after another, studying the fine, firm quality and texture of her flesh as if she were seeing it for the first time. She folded her hands easily above her head, and in that position she fell asleep.

At first she slept lightly, half awake, drowsily aware of what went on around her. She could hear Madame Antoine’s heavy, scraping tread as she went back and forth across the sanded floor. A few chickens clucked outside the windows, scratching in the grass for bits of gravel. Later she half heard Robert and Tonie talking under the shed. She did not stir. Even her eyelids lay numb and heavy over her sleepy eyes. The voices went on, Tonie’s slow Acadian drawl and Robert’s quick, soft, smooth French. She understood French only imperfectly unless she was spoken to directly, and the voices were just part of the other drowsy, muffled sounds that lulled her senses.

When Edna woke, she was sure she had slept long and soundly. The voices under the shed had hushed. Madame Antoine’s step no longer sounded in the next room. Even the chickens had gone elsewhere to scratch and cluck. The mosquito bar had been drawn over her; the old woman must have come in and let it down while she slept. Edna rose quietly and looked out between the window curtains. The slanting rays of the sun told her the afternoon was far gone. Robert was out under the shed, leaning in the shade against the sloping keel of the overturned boat, reading from a book. Tonie was no longer with him. She wondered where the rest of the party had gone. As she stood washing in the little basin between the windows, she peeped out at him two or three times.

Madame Antoine had put out some coarse, clean towels on a chair and set a box of poudre de riz within reach. Edna dabbed the powder on her nose and cheeks, studying herself in the little distorted mirror that hung over the basin. Her eyes were bright and wide awake, and her face glowed.

When she had dressed, she walked into the next room. She was very hungry. Nobody was there, but a cloth lay on the table against the wall, with a place laid for one: a crusty brown loaf and a bottle of wine beside the plate. Edna tore off a piece of the loaf with her strong, white teeth and bit into it. She poured some wine into the glass and drank it down. Then she went softly outdoors, picked an orange from a low-hanging bough and threw it at Robert, who had no idea she was awake and up.
A light broke over his whole face when he saw her, and he joined her under the orange tree.

“How many years have I slept?” she asked. “The whole island seems changed. A new race of beings must have sprung up and left only you and me as relics of the past. How many ages ago did Madame Antoine and Tonie die? And when did our people from Grand Isle vanish from the earth?”
He adjusted a ruffle on her shoulder, with an easy familiarity.

“You have slept exactly one hundred years. I was left here to guard your sleep, and for one hundred years I have sat under the shed reading a book. The one evil I couldn’t prevent was a broiled fowl drying up.”
“If it has turned to stone, I will still eat it,” said Edna, going with him into the house. “But really, what has become of Monsieur Farival and the others?”
“Gone hours ago. When they saw you were asleep, they thought it best not to wake you. Anyway, I wouldn’t have let them. What was I here for?”
“I wonder if Léonce will be uneasy!” she speculated, as she sat down at the table.
“Of course not; he knows you are with me,” Robert answered, busy among assorted pans and covered dishes left standing on the hearth.
“Where are Madame Antoine and her son?” asked Edna.
“Gone to Vespers, and to visit some friends, I believe. I am to take you back in Tonie’s boat whenever you are ready to go.”

He stirred the smoldering ashes until the broiled fowl sizzled again. The meal he put before her was a good one; he brewed the coffee fresh and shared it with her. Madame Antoine had cooked little but the mullets, but while Edna slept, Robert had foraged all over the island. He was childishly pleased to find her hungry and to watch her enjoy what he had got for her.
“Shall we go right away?” she asked, after she had drained her glass and brushed the crumbs of the crusty loaf together.
“The sun isn’t as low as it will be in two hours,” he answered.
“The sun will be gone in two hours.”
“Well, let it go; who cares!”

They waited a good while under the orange trees, until Madame Antoine returned, panting and waddling, with a thousand apologies for being gone. Tonie did not dare come back. He was shy and would face no woman if he could help it, except his mother.

It was very pleasant to stay under the orange trees while the sun sank lower and lower and turned the western sky to flaming copper and gold. The shadows grew long and crept across the grass like stealthy, grotesque monsters.
Edna and Robert both sat on the ground — or rather, he lay on the ground beside her, now and then picking at the hem of her muslin gown.
Madame Antoine lowered her fat body, broad and squat, onto a bench by the door. She had talked all afternoon and was wound up to the pitch for storytelling.

And what stories she told them! Twice in her life she had left the Chênière Caminada, and then only for the briefest time. All her years she had squatted and waddled on that island, gathering legends of the Baratarians and the sea. Night came on, with the moon to light it. Edna could hear the whispering voices of dead men and the click of muffled gold.
When she and Robert stepped into Tonie’s boat with its red lateen sail, misty spirit forms were prowling in the shadows and among the reeds, and phantom ships were speeding to cover across the water.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Etienne, the youngest boy, had been very naughty, Madame Ratignolle said as she handed him over to his mother. He had not wanted to go to bed and had made a scene, so she had taken him in hand and calmed him as best she could. Raoul had been in bed and asleep for two hours.

The little boy wore his long white nightgown, which kept tripping him as Madame Ratignolle led him along by the hand. With his other chubby fist he rubbed his eyes, heavy with sleep and bad temper. Edna took him in her arms and sat down in the rocker. She began to coddle and caress him, calling him every tender name she could think of, and soothed him to sleep.
It was not yet nine o’clock. Nobody had gone to bed except the children.

At first Léonce had been very uneasy, Madame Ratignolle said, and had wanted to head for the Chênière right away. Monsieur Farival had assured him, though, that his wife was merely worn out and sleepy, and that Tonie would bring her back safely later in the day. That talked him out of crossing the bay. He had gone over to Klein’s in search of a cotton broker, whom he wanted to consult about securities, exchanges, stocks, bonds, or some such thing; Madame Ratignolle could not recall which. He had promised not to stay late. She herself was suffering from the heat and a heavy, oppressive feeling, she said. She had brought a bottle of salts and a large fan. She refused to stay on with Edna, because Monsieur Ratignolle was by himself, and above all things he hated to be left alone.

Once Etienne was asleep, Edna carried him to the back room. Robert went in first and lifted the mosquito bar so she could settle the child comfortably in his bed. The quadroon was nowhere to be seen. As they stepped out of the cottage, Robert said good-night to Edna.
“Do you realize we have spent the whole livelong day together, Robert—ever since early this morning?” she said as they parted.
“All but the hundred years when you were sleeping. Good night.”
He pressed her hand and left, heading toward the beach. He joined none of the others. He walked by himself down toward the Gulf.

Edna stayed outside to wait for her husband. She wanted neither to sleep nor to go in, and she had no urge to sit with the Ratignolles or to join Madame Lebrun and the group in front of the house, whose animated voices reached her as they talked. Her mind wandered back over her time at Grand Isle. She tried to work out how this summer had been different from every other summer she had known. All she could grasp was that she herself—her present self—was in some way unlike the other self. That she was seeing through different eyes, and getting acquainted with new conditions in herself that colored and changed her surroundings, she did not yet suspect.

She wondered why Robert had gone and left her. It never crossed her mind that he might be tired of her company after the livelong day. She was not tired, and she felt he was not either. She was sorry he had gone. It was so much more natural for him to stay when nothing absolutely required him to leave her.
As Edna waited for her husband, she hummed a little song that Robert had sung while they crossed the bay. It opened with “Ah! si tu savais,” and every verse closed on “si tu savais.”
Robert’s voice made no show of itself. It was musical and true. The voice, the notes, the whole refrain stayed in her memory and haunted her.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Edna was a little late, as usual, when she walked into the dining-room one evening, and a more animated conversation than ordinary seemed to be under way. Several people were talking at once, and Victor’s voice carried over the others, even his mother’s. Edna had come back late from her bath and dressed in a hurry, and her face was flushed. Against her dainty white gown, her head looked like a rich, rare blossom. She sat down at the table between old Monsieur Farival and Madame Ratignolle.

She sat down and was about to start on her soup, which had been served when she came in, when several people told her at once that Robert was going to Mexico. She put her spoon down and looked around her, bewildered. He had been with her all morning, reading to her, and had never once mentioned a place like Mexico. She had not seen him during the afternoon; someone had said he was at the house, upstairs with his mother. She had thought nothing of this, though she was surprised that he did not join her later in the afternoon when she went down to the beach.

She looked across to where he sat next to Madame Lebrun, who presided. Bewilderment showed plainly on Edna’s face, and she never thought to hide it. He raised his eyebrows in a show of a smile as he returned her glance. He seemed embarrassed and uneasy. “When is he going?” she asked, addressing everybody in general, as if Robert were not there to speak for himself.
“Tonight!” “This very evening!” “Did you ever!” “What has got into him!” were some of the replies she caught, called out all together in French and English.
“Impossible!” she cried. “How can anyone just start out from Grand Isle for Mexico on a moment’s notice, as though he were walking over to Klein’s, or the wharf, or down to the beach?”
“I have said all along that I was going to Mexico! I’ve been saying it for years!” Robert cried, excited and irritable, like a man beating off a swarm of stinging insects.
Madame Lebrun rapped on the table with the handle of her knife.

“Let Robert explain, please, why he is going, and why he is going tonight,” she called. “Really, this table gets more like Bedlam every day, with everybody talking at once. Sometimes—God forgive me for saying it—but truly, sometimes I wish Victor would lose his voice altogether.”

Victor laughed sardonically and thanked his mother for her holy wish. He failed to see how it would benefit anyone, except that it might give her a better chance, and more license, to do all the talking herself.

Monsieur Farival thought they ought to have taken Victor out to mid-ocean in his earliest youth and drowned him. Victor thought it would be more logical to get rid of old people that way, since they had earned a reputation for being obnoxious to everybody. Madame Lebrun became a little hysterical, and Robert called his brother some sharp, hard names.

“There’s nothing much to explain, mother,” he said. Yet he explained anyway, looking mostly at Edna. He could only meet the gentleman he meant to join at Vera Cruz by taking such and such a steamer, which left New Orleans on such a day. Beaudelet was going out that night with his lugger-load of vegetables, and that gave him a chance to reach the city and catch his ship in time.
“And when did you decide all this?” demanded Monsieur Farival.
“This afternoon,” Robert answered, with a shade of annoyance.
“What time this afternoon?” the old gentleman pressed him, as doggedly as if he were cross-examining a criminal in a court of justice.
“Four o’clock this afternoon, Monsieur Farival,” Robert answered, his voice high and his air lofty, like some gentleman on the stage, Edna thought.
With an effort she had finished most of her soup. Now she was picking with her fork at the flaky pieces of a court bouillon.

The lovers were taking advantage of the general talk about Mexico to whisper about matters that they rightly considered of interest to no one but themselves. The lady in black had once been sent a pair of prayer-beads of curious workmanship from Mexico, with a very special indulgence attached to them. She had never been able to find out whether the indulgence held outside the Mexican border. Father Fochel of the Cathedral had tried to explain it, but not to her satisfaction. So she begged Robert to take an interest in the matter and find out, if he could, whether she was entitled to the indulgence that came with her remarkably curious Mexican prayer-beads.

Madame Ratignolle hoped Robert would be extremely careful in his dealings with the Mexicans. In her opinion they were a treacherous people, unscrupulous and revengeful. She trusted she was not being unjust in condemning them as a race. Only one Mexican had she known personally, a man who made and sold excellent tamales, and she would have trusted him completely, he spoke so softly. Then one day he was arrested for stabbing his wife. She never learned whether he was hanged or not.

Victor had become hilarious and was trying to tell an anecdote about a Mexican girl who served chocolate one winter in a restaurant on Dauphine Street. Nobody would listen to him except old Monsieur Farival, who went into convulsions over the droll story.
Edna wondered whether everyone had gone mad, talking and clamoring at such a pitch. She could think of nothing at all to say about Mexico or Mexicans.
“What time do you leave?” she asked Robert.
“At ten,” he said. “Beaudelet wants to wait for the moon.”
“Are you all ready to go?”
“Quite ready. All I’ll take is a hand-bag; I will pack my trunk in the city.”
He turned to answer a question from his mother. Edna finished her black coffee and left the table.

She went straight to her room. After the open air, the little cottage felt close and stuffy. But she did not mind; a hundred different things seemed to need her attention indoors. She began to put the toilet-stand in order, grumbling at the carelessness of the quadroon, who was in the next room putting the children to bed. She gathered up the stray garments hanging over the backs of chairs and put each one where it belonged, in the closet or a bureau drawer. She changed her gown for a more comfortable, roomier wrapper. She did her hair over, combing and brushing it with unusual energy. Then she went in and helped the quadroon get the boys to bed.

The boys were very playful and wanted to talk—to do anything except lie quiet and go to sleep. Edna dismissed the quadroon to her supper and said she need not come back. Then she sat down and told the children a story. It excited them instead of soothing them, and made them still more wide awake. She left them arguing hotly over how the tale would end. Their mother had promised to finish it the next night.

The little black girl came in to say that Madame Lebrun would like Mrs. Pontellier to come and sit with them at the house until Mr. Robert left. Edna sent back word that she had already undressed and did not feel quite well, but that perhaps she would come over to the house later. She started to dress again and got as far as taking off her peignoir. But she changed her mind once more, put the peignoir back on, and went outside to sit in front of her door. She was overheated and irritable, and she fanned herself vigorously for a while. Madame Ratignolle came down to find out what was the matter.

“I suppose all that noise and confusion at the table upset me,” said Edna, “and besides, I hate shocks and surprises. Imagine Robert setting off in such a ridiculously sudden, dramatic way! As if it were life or death! And not a word about it all morning, while he was with me.”

“Yes,” Madame Ratignolle agreed. “I think he showed very little consideration for any of us—for you most of all. In one of the others it wouldn’t have surprised me; those Lebruns are all given to heroics. But I must say I never expected it of Robert. Won’t you come down? Come, dear; it doesn’t look friendly.”
“No,” said Edna, a little sullenly. “I can’t be bothered dressing again; I don’t feel like it.”
“You needn’t dress; you look quite all right. Put a belt around your waist. Just look at me!”
“No,” Edna insisted, “but you go on. If we both stay away, Madame Lebrun may take offense.”
Madame Ratignolle kissed Edna good-night and went off, in truth rather eager to join the general lively conversation still going on about Mexico and the Mexicans.
Some time later Robert came up, carrying his hand-bag.
“Aren’t you feeling well?” he asked.
“Oh, well enough. Are you going right away?”

He struck a match and glanced at his watch. “Twenty minutes,” he said. For a while the quick, short flare of the match made the darkness seem darker. He sat down on a stool the children had left on the porch.
“Get a chair,” said Edna.
“This will do,” he said. He put on his soft hat, nervously took it off again, wiped his face with his handkerchief and complained of the heat.
“Take the fan,” said Edna, holding it out to him.
“Oh, no! Thank you. It doesn’t help; sooner or later you have to stop fanning, and then you feel all the more uncomfortable.”
“That is one of those ridiculous things men always say. Not one of them has ever told me anything different about fanning. How long will you be gone?”
“Forever, perhaps. I don’t know. A good many things decide it.”
“Well, in case it shouldn’t be forever, how long will it be?”

“This seems to me perfectly preposterous and uncalled for. I don’t like it. I don’t understand why you have kept it all so secret and mysterious, never saying a word to me about it this morning.” He stayed silent and made no attempt to defend himself. After a moment he only said:
“Don’t let us part in bad feeling. I’ve never known you to be out of patience with me before.”

“I don’t want to part in any ill humor,” she said. “But can’t you see? I’ve become used to seeing you and having you with me all the time, and what you are doing seems unfriendly, even unkind. You don’t even give a reason. Why, I had been planning for us to be together, imagining how pleasant it would be to see you in the city next winter.”

“So had I,” he blurted. “Perhaps that’s the—” He suddenly rose and held out his hand. “Good-by, my dear Mrs. Pontellier; good-by. You won’t—I hope you won’t forget me altogether.” She clung to his hand and tried to keep him there.
“Write to me when you arrive, won’t you, Robert?” she pleaded.
“I will, thank you. Goodbye.”
How unlike Robert! Even the slightest acquaintance would have given a more emphatic answer than “I will, thank you; good-by” to such a request.

Evidently he had already said his farewells to the people at the house, because he went down the steps to meet Beaudelet, who was waiting out there with an oar over his shoulder. They walked off into the darkness. She could hear only Beaudelet’s voice; apparently Robert had not even said a word of greeting to his companion.

Edna bit down hard on her handkerchief, trying to hold back and conceal—even from herself, as she would have hidden it from someone else—the emotion that was troubling, tearing, her. Her eyes were brimming with tears.

For the first time she knew the signs of infatuation, which she had felt in their beginnings as a child, as a girl in her early teens, and again as a young woman. Knowing them did not make the reality or the poignancy of the revelation any less, nor did any hint or promise that the feeling might not last. The past meant nothing to her and offered no lesson she was willing to heed. The future was a mystery she never tried to solve. Only the present counted. It was hers, and it tormented her now with a biting conviction: that she had lost what she once held, and been refused what her impassioned, newly awakened being demanded.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: “Do you miss your friend very much?” asked Mademoiselle Reisz one morning, creeping up behind Edna just as she left her cottage for the beach. Edna spent much of her time in the water now that she had finally learned to swim. With their stay at Grand Isle nearly over, she felt she could not give too much time to the one pastime that brought her any real pleasure. When Mademoiselle Reisz touched her shoulder and spoke, she seemed to echo the thought that was always in Edna’s mind, or better, the feeling that never left her.

Robert’s going had somehow drained the brightness, the color and the meaning out of everything. Nothing in her life had changed, yet her whole existence had gone dull, like a faded garment that no longer seems worth wearing. She looked for him everywhere—in other people, whom she coaxed into talking about him. In the mornings she went up to Madame Lebrun’s room, braving the clatter of the old sewing-machine. She sat there and chatted by fits and starts, as Robert used to do. She gazed around the room at the pictures and photographs on the wall, and in a corner she found an old family album. She went through it with the keenest interest, asking Madame Lebrun to tell her about the many figures and faces on its pages.

One picture showed Madame Lebrun with baby Robert in her lap, a round-faced infant with his fist in his mouth. Only the eyes hinted at the man. And here he was again in kilts, five years old, with long curls and a whip in his hand. That made Edna laugh, and she laughed at the portrait of him in his first long trousers too. Another one caught her interest, taken as he left for college: thin and long-faced, his eyes full of fire, ambition and great intentions. But there was no recent picture, none that suggested the Robert who had left five days ago and left a void and a wilderness behind him.

“Oh, Robert quit having his picture taken as soon as he had to pay for it himself! He says he found better uses for his money,” Madame Lebrun explained. She had a letter from him that he wrote before leaving New Orleans. Edna asked to see it, and Madame Lebrun told her to look on the table or the dresser, or perhaps on the mantelpiece.

The letter was on the bookshelf. For Edna it held the greatest interest and attraction: the envelope, its size and shape, the post-mark, the handwriting. Before she opened it she examined every detail of the outside. It ran to only a few lines. They said that he would leave the city that afternoon, that his trunk was well packed, that he was well, and that he sent his love and wished to be affectionately remembered to everyone. For Edna there was no particular message, only a postscript: if Mrs. Pontellier wanted to finish the book he had been reading aloud to her, his mother could find it in his room, among the other books on the table. Edna felt a pang of jealousy that he had written to his mother instead of to her.
Everyone seemed to take it for granted that she missed him. Even her husband, when he came down the Saturday after Robert left, said he was sorry Robert had gone.
“How do you get on without him, Edna?” he asked.

“It’s very dull without him,” she admitted. Mr. Pontellier had seen Robert in the city, and Edna put a dozen questions or more to him. Where had they met? On Carondelet Street, in the morning. They had gone “in” together for a drink and a cigar. What had they talked about? Mostly his prospects in Mexico, which Mr. Pontellier thought were promising. How had he looked? How had he seemed—grave, or gay, or what? Quite cheerful, and completely taken up with the idea of his trip, which Mr. Pontellier found altogether natural in a young fellow about to go and seek his fortune and adventure in a strange, queer country.

Edna tapped her foot in impatience and wondered why the children kept on playing in the sun when they could be under the trees. She went down and led them out of the sun, scolding the quadroon for not watching them more carefully.

It did not strike her as in the least grotesque that she should be making Robert the topic of conversation and getting her husband to talk about him. Her feeling for Robert bore no resemblance to what she felt for her husband, or had ever felt, or ever expected to feel. All her life she had been used to harboring thoughts and emotions that never found words. They had never turned into struggles. They belonged to her and were her own, and she was convinced that she had a right to them and that they were nobody’s concern but hers. Edna had once told Madame Ratignolle that she would never sacrifice herself for her children, or for anyone. A rather heated argument had followed, in which the two women did not seem to understand each other or to be speaking the same language. Edna had tried to smooth things over and explain.

“I would give up the unessential; I would give my money, I would give my life for my children; but I wouldn’t give myself. I can’t put it any more clearly; it is only something I am starting to understand, something that is revealing itself to me.”

“I don’t know what you count as essential, or what you mean by unessential,” Madame Ratignolle said cheerfully, “but a woman who would give her life for her children could do no more than that—your Bible tells you so. I’m sure I couldn’t do more.”
“Oh, yes you could!” laughed Edna.
So it did not surprise her when Mademoiselle Reisz, who had followed her down to the beach, tapped her on the shoulder that morning and asked whether she did not miss her young friend very much.
“Oh, good morning, Mademoiselle; is that you? Why, of course I miss Robert. Are you going to bathe?”
“Why would I go bathe at the very end of the season, when I haven’t set foot in the surf all summer?” the woman answered, disagreeably.

“I beg your pardon,” Edna offered, somewhat embarrassed, for she should have remembered that Mademoiselle Reisz’s avoiding the water had been the subject of a good deal of joking. Some of them thought it was because of her false hair, or her fear of wetting the violets. Others put it down to the natural aversion to water that is sometimes supposed to go with an artistic temperament. To show she held no grudge, Mademoiselle drew some chocolates in a paper bag from her pocket and gave Edna some. She habitually ate chocolates for their staying power, she said; they packed a great deal of nourishment into a small space. They saved her from starvation, since Madame Lebrun’s table was utterly impossible, and only a woman as impertinent as Madame Lebrun could think of offering such food to people and making them pay for it.
“She must feel very lonely without her son,” Edna said, wishing to change the subject. “Her favorite son, besides. It must have been rather hard to let him go.”
Mademoiselle laughed, not kindly.

“Her favorite son! Oh, dear! Who has been telling you such a tale? Aline Lebrun lives for Victor, and for Victor alone. She has spoiled him into the worthless creature he is. She worships him and the ground he walks on. Robert is well enough in his way, giving the family every cent he can earn and keeping the barest pittance for himself. Favorite son, indeed! I miss the poor fellow myself, my dear. I liked having him around and hearing him about the place—the only Lebrun worth a pinch of salt. He often comes to see me in the city. I like to play for him. That Victor! Hanging would be too good for him. It’s a wonder Robert hasn’t beaten him to death long ago.”
“I always thought he was very patient with his brother,” Edna offered, glad to be talking about Robert, whatever was said.

“Oh! He gave him a good thrashing a year or two ago,” said Mademoiselle. “It was over a Spanish girl that Victor thought he had some sort of claim on. He came upon Robert one day talking to the girl, or walking with her, or bathing with her, or carrying her basket—I don’t remember what;—and Victor became so insulting and abusive that Robert thrashed him on the spot. That has kept him in comparative order for a good while. It’s about time he had another.”
“Was her name Mariequita?” asked Edna.
“Mariequita — yes, that was it; Mariequita. I had forgotten. Oh, she’s a sly one, and a bad one, that Mariequita!”

Edna looked down at Mademoiselle Reisz and wondered how she had listened to her venom for so long. For some reason she felt depressed, almost unhappy. She had not meant to go in the water, but she put on her bathing suit and left Mademoiselle seated alone in the shade of the children’s tent. As the season advanced, the water was growing cooler. Edna plunged in and swam about with an abandon that thrilled and invigorated her. She stayed in a long while, half hoping Mademoiselle Reisz would not wait for her.

But Mademoiselle did wait. She was very amiable on the way back and raved about how Edna looked in her bathing suit. She talked about music. She hoped Edna would visit her in the city, and with the stub of a pencil she wrote out her address on a card she found in her pocket.
“When do you leave?” asked Edna.
“Next Monday; and you?”
“The following week,” answered Edna, adding, “It has been a pleasant summer, hasn’t it, Mademoiselle?”
“Well,” Mademoiselle Reisz agreed with a shrug, “rather pleasant, except for the mosquitoes and the Farival twins.”

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The Pontelliers had a very charming home on Esplanade Street in New Orleans. It was a large double cottage with a broad front veranda, its sloping roof held up by round, fluted columns. The house was painted a dazzling white, and the outside shutters, or jalousies, were green. The yard was kept scrupulously neat, and every kind of flower and plant that grows in South Louisiana flourished there. Inside, the furnishings were perfect in the conventional style. The softest carpets and rugs covered the floors, and rich, tasteful draperies hung at the doors and windows. The walls held paintings chosen with judgment and discrimination. The cut glass, the silver and the heavy damask that appeared on the table every day were the envy of many women whose husbands were less generous than Mr. Pontellier.

Mr. Pontellier liked to walk through his house examining its furnishings and details, to make sure nothing was out of order. He valued his possessions highly, mainly because they were his. He took real pleasure in looking at a painting, a statuette or a rare lace curtain — it made no difference which — once he had bought it and set it among his household gods.

On Tuesday afternoons — Tuesday was Mrs. Pontellier’s reception day — a constant stream of callers arrived. They were women who came in carriages or on the street cars, or who walked when the air was soft and the distance allowed. A light-colored mulatto boy in a dress coat, carrying a tiny silver tray for their cards, let them in. A maid in a white fluted cap offered them liqueur, coffee or chocolate, as they preferred. Mrs. Pontellier, dressed in a handsome reception gown, stayed in the drawing-room all afternoon to receive her visitors. Men sometimes called in the evening with their wives.
Mrs. Pontellier had followed this routine faithfully since her marriage six years earlier. On certain evenings of the week she and her husband went to the opera, or sometimes to the theater.
Mr. Pontellier went out of the house each morning between nine and ten o’clock. He seldom got back before half-past six or seven in the evening, and dinner came at half-past seven.

One Tuesday evening, a few weeks after their return from Grand Isle, he and his wife sat down to dinner. They were alone together. The boys were being put to bed. Every so often the patter of their bare, escaping feet could be heard, along with the quadroon’s voice as she chased them, raised in mild protest and pleading. Mrs. Pontellier was not wearing her usual Tuesday reception gown; she had on an ordinary house dress. Mr. Pontellier, who noticed such things, saw it as he served the soup and handed it to the boy waiting at the table.
“Tired out, Edna? Who came? Did you have many callers?” he asked. He tasted his soup and began to season it with pepper, salt, vinegar, mustard — everything within reach.
“Quite a good many,” replied Edna, who was plainly enjoying her soup. “Their cards were waiting when I got home. I had gone out.”

“Out!” cried her husband, sounding almost truly dismayed. He set down the vinegar cruet and stared at her through his glasses. “Why, what could possibly have taken you out on a Tuesday? What was there to do?”
“Nothing. I simply felt like going out, so I went.”
“Well, I hope you at least left a proper excuse,” said her husband, calmer now, while he shook a dash of cayenne pepper into the soup.
“No, no excuse. I only told Joe to say I was out. That was all.”

“Why, my dear, by this time I should think you would see that people don’t do such things. If we ever hope to get on and keep up with the procession, we have to observe les convenances. When you felt you had to leave home this afternoon, you ought to have left a proper explanation of where you were.
“This soup is really impossible. It’s odd that woman has never learned to make a decent one. Any free-lunch stand in town does better. Did Mrs. Belthrop come?”
“Bring the tray with the cards, Joe. I don’t remember who was here.”
The boy went out and returned in a moment with the tiny silver tray, heaped with ladies’ visiting cards. He offered it to Mrs. Pontellier.
“Give it to Mr. Pontellier,” she said.
Joe held out the tray to Mr. Pontellier and took away the soup.
Mr. Pontellier ran his eye over the names of his wife’s callers. He read some of them aloud, commenting as he went.

“‘The Misses Delasidas.’ This morning I worked a big deal in futures for their father. Nice girls; it’s time they married. ‘Mrs. Belthrop.’ Let me tell you something, Edna: you can’t afford to snub Mrs. Belthrop. Why, Belthrop could buy and sell the two of us ten times over. His business is worth a good, round sum to me. You had better write her a note. ‘Mrs. James Highcamp.’ Hugh! The less you have to do with Mrs. Highcamp, the better. ‘Madame Laforcé.’ She came all the way from Carrolton, too, poor old soul. ‘Miss Wiggs,’ ‘Mrs. Eleanor Boltons.’” He pushed the cards aside.
“Mercy!” cried Edna, who had been fuming. “Why do you take the thing so seriously? Why such a fuss?”
“I’m not making any fuss over it. But it’s just these seeming trifles we have to take seriously. Such things count.”

The fish was scorched, and Mr. Pontellier would not touch it. Edna said she did not mind a little scorched taste. The roast somehow did not suit him either, and he did not like the way the vegetables were served.
“It seems to me,” he said, “that we spend enough money in this house to get at least one meal a day that a man can eat and still keep his self-respect.”
“You once thought the cook was a treasure,” Edna returned, without interest.

“Maybe she was, when she first came. But cooks are only human. You have to keep an eye on them, like anyone else you hire. Suppose I never watched the clerks in my office and let them run things as they pleased. Before long they’d make a fine mess of me and my business.”
“Where are you going?” asked Edna, as her husband rose from the table having eaten nothing but a taste of the highly seasoned soup.
“To the club, for my dinner. Good night.” He went out to the hall, took his hat and stick from the stand and left the house.

She knew such scenes fairly well. They had often made her very unhappy. A few times before, they had taken away all her wish to finish her dinner. Sometimes she had gone into the kitchen to give the cook a belated scolding. Once she went to her room and studied the cookbook for a whole evening, and at last wrote out a menu for the week. It left her harassed with the feeling that she had accomplished nothing, after all, that was worth the name.

That evening, though, Edna finished her dinner alone, deliberately, forcing herself to go slowly. Her face was flushed, and her eyes burned with some inward fire. When she was done she went to her room, having told the boy to tell any further callers that she was indisposed.

It was a large, beautiful room, rich and picturesque in the soft, dim light, which the maid had turned low. She went and stood at an open window and looked out on the deep tangle of the garden below. All the mystery and witchery of the night seemed to have gathered there, among the perfumes and the dusky, twisting outlines of flowers and leaves. She was seeking herself, and finding herself, in just such sweet half-darkness, which suited her moods. But the voices that came to her from the darkness, from the sky above and from the stars were not soothing. They jeered, and sounded mournful notes without promise, empty even of hope. She turned back into the room and began to walk up and down its whole length, without stopping, without resting. In her hands she held a thin handkerchief. She tore it into ribbons, rolled it into a ball and flung it from her. Once she stopped, took off her wedding ring and threw it onto the carpet. When she saw it lying there, she stamped her heel on it, trying to crush it. But her small boot heel made no dent, not a mark, on the little glittering circle.
In a rush of passion she snatched a glass vase from the table and hurled it at the tiles of the hearth. She wanted to destroy something. She wanted to hear the crash and clatter.
A maid, alarmed by the din of breaking glass, came into the room to find out what was the matter.
“A vase fell on the hearth,” said Edna. “Never mind. Leave it till morning.”
“Oh! You could get glass in your feet, ma’am,” the young woman insisted, gathering up the pieces of the vase scattered across the carpet. “And here’s your ring, ma’am, under the chair.”
Edna held out her hand, took the ring and slipped it onto her finger.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: The next morning, as he left for his office, Mr. Pontellier asked Edna whether she would meet him in town to look at some new fixtures for the library.
“I hardly think we need new fixtures, Léonce. Let’s not buy anything new. You’re too extravagant. I don’t believe saving or putting by ever crosses your mind.”

“You get rich by making money, my dear Edna, not by saving it,” he said. He was sorry she did not feel like going with him to pick out the new fixtures. He kissed her good-by. He told her she looked unwell and must take care of herself. She was unusually pale and very quiet.

She stood on the front veranda as he left the house, and absently picked a few sprays of jessamine growing on a trellis nearby. She breathed in the scent of the blossoms and tucked them into the bosom of her white morning gown. The boys were dragging a small “express wagon” along the banquette, filled with blocks and sticks. The quadroon followed them with quick little steps, putting on a false liveliness and eagerness for the occasion. A fruit vender was crying his wares in the street.

Edna looked straight ahead with a self-absorbed expression. Nothing around her interested her. The street, the children, the fruit vender, the flowers growing there under her eyes — all were part and parcel of an alien world that had suddenly turned hostile.

She went back into the house. She had thought of speaking to the cook about her blunders the night before, but Mr. Pontellier had spared her that disagreeable task, for which she was so poorly suited. His arguments were usually convincing to the people he employed. He had left home quite sure that he and Edna would sit down that evening, and perhaps for a few evenings after, to a dinner that deserved the name.

Edna spent an hour or two going over some of her old sketches. Their shortcomings and flaws, which seemed glaring to her, were easy to see. She tried to work a little, but she was not in the humor. At last she picked out a few of the sketches, those she thought least discreditable, and when she dressed a little later and left the house, she took them with her. In her street gown she looked handsome and distinguished. Her face had lost the tan of the seashore, and beneath her heavy, yellow-brown hair her forehead was smooth, white and polished. A few freckles dotted her face. A small, dark mole sat near her lower lip, and another on her temple, half hidden in her hair.

As Edna walked along the street she was thinking of Robert. She was still under the spell of her infatuation. She had tried to forget him, knowing there was no use in remembering. But the thought of him was like an obsession, always pressing itself on her. She did not dwell on details of their acquaintance, or recall his personality in any special or peculiar way. It was his being, his mere existence, that dominated her thoughts. Sometimes it faded, as if it would melt into the mist of the forgotten; then it revived with an intensity that filled her with an incomprehensible longing.

Edna was on her way to Madame Ratignolle’s. Their intimacy, which had begun at Grand Isle, had not cooled, and they had seen each other fairly often since returning to the city. The Ratignolles lived not far from Edna’s home, on the corner of a side street. There Monsieur Ratignolle owned and ran a drug store with a steady, prosperous trade. His father had been in the business before him, and Monsieur Ratignolle stood well in the community and had an enviable reputation for integrity and clearheadedness. His family lived in roomy apartments over the store, with an entrance at the side inside the porte cochère. Edna thought there was something very French, very foreign, about their whole way of living. Every two weeks the Ratignolles entertained their friends in the large, pleasant salon that stretched across the width of the house, with a soirée musicale, sometimes varied with card-playing. One friend played the cello. One brought his flute and another his violin, while some sang and a number played the piano with varying degrees of taste and agility. The Ratignolles’ soirées musicales were widely known, and being invited to them was considered a privilege.
Edna found her friend busy sorting the clothes that had come back that morning from the laundry. She dropped the task at once on seeing Edna, who had been shown in without ceremony.

“’Cité can do it as well as I can; it is really her business,” she explained to Edna, who apologized for interrupting. And she called in a young black woman and told her, in French, to be very careful in checking off the list she handed her. She told her to see in particular whether a fine linen handkerchief of Monsieur Ratignolle’s, missing last week, had been returned, and to be sure to set aside the pieces that needed mending and darning.
Then she put an arm around Edna’s waist and led her to the front of the house, to the salon, where it was cool and sweet with the scent of great roses standing in jars on the hearth.
At home Madame Ratignolle looked more beautiful than ever, in a negligé that left her arms almost wholly bare and showed the rich, melting curves of her white throat.

“Perhaps I shall be able to paint your picture some day,” said Edna, smiling, once they were seated. She drew out the roll of sketches and began to unroll them. “I believe I ought to work again. I feel as if I wanted something to do. What do you think of these? Would it be worth taking up again and studying some more? I might study for a while with Laidpore.”

She knew that Madame Ratignolle’s opinion in such a matter would be next to worthless, and that she herself had not merely decided but determined. Still, she wanted the words of praise and encouragement that would help her take heart for her venture.
“Your talent is immense, dear!”
“Nonsense!” protested Edna, well pleased.

“Immense, I tell you,” Madame Ratignolle insisted. She studied the sketches one at a time, first close up, then at arm’s length, with narrowed eyes and her head cocked to one side. “Surely this Bavarian peasant deserves a frame; and this basket of apples! I have never seen anything so lifelike. One could almost be tempted to put out a hand and pick one up.”

Edna could not help a feeling that bordered on complacency at her friend’s praise, though she knew what it was really worth. She kept a few of the sketches and handed the rest to Madame Ratignolle. Madame Ratignolle prized the gift far above its value, and when her husband came up from the store a little later for his midday dinner, she proudly showed him the pictures.

Monsieur Ratignolle was one of those men people call the salt of the earth. His cheerfulness knew no limit, and his good heart, wide charity and common sense matched it. He and his wife spoke English with an accent that showed only in an un-English stress and a certain care and deliberation. Edna’s husband spoke English with no accent at all. The Ratignolles understood each other perfectly. If anywhere on this earth two human beings have ever become one, it was surely in their marriage.

When Edna sat down at table with them she thought, “Better a dinner of herbs.” It did not take her long to find that this was no dinner of herbs at all but a delicious meal, simple, choice and satisfying in every way.

Monsieur Ratignolle was delighted to see her, though he thought she did not look as well as she had at Grand Isle, and he recommended a tonic. He talked at length on all sorts of subjects: a little politics, some news of the city and gossip of the neighborhood. His animation and earnestness lent every syllable an exaggerated importance. His wife was keenly interested in all he said. She laid down her fork to listen better, put in a word here and there, and took the words from his mouth.

When she left them Edna felt depressed rather than soothed. The little glimpse of domestic harmony she had been given stirred in her no regret and no longing. It was not a life that fitted her, and all she could see in it was an appalling, hopeless ennui. A kind of commiseration for Madame Ratignolle moved her — pity for that colorless existence, which never raised its owner above blind contentment, where no moment of anguish ever visited her soul and she would never taste life’s delirium. Edna vaguely wondered what she meant by “life’s delirium.” The phrase had crossed her mind like some unsought, extraneous impression.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: It struck Edna as very foolish, very childish, that she had stamped on her wedding ring and smashed the crystal vase on the tiles. No further outbursts came over her to drive her to such useless expedients. She began to do as she liked and to feel as she liked. Her Tuesdays at home she dropped altogether, and she did not return the calls of those who had visited her. She made no ineffectual attempt to run her household en bonne ménagère. She came and went whenever it pleased her, and as far as she could, she gave herself over to any passing caprice.

As long as he met a certain tacit submissiveness in his wife, Mr. Pontellier had been a fairly courteous husband. Her new and unexpected behavior left him utterly bewildered. It shocked him. Then her complete neglect of her duties as a wife made him angry. As Mr. Pontellier turned rude, Edna turned insolent. She had resolved never to step backward again.
“It seems to me the height of folly for a woman who heads a household and has children to pass her days in an atelier. She would do better to spend them contriving for her family’s comfort.”
“Painting is what I feel like doing,” Edna answered. “I may not always feel like it.”

“Then paint, in God’s name! But don’t let the family go to the devil. Look at Madame Ratignolle: she keeps up her music, and yet she doesn’t let everything else fall into chaos. And she is more of a musician than you are a painter.”
“She is no musician, and I am no painter. And it isn’t painting that makes me let things go.”
“Because of what, then?”
“Oh! I don’t know. Leave me alone—you bother me.”

It sometimes occurred to Mr. Pontellier to wonder whether his wife was not becoming a little unbalanced in mind. He could plainly see she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself, and day by day throwing off that fictitious self we put on like a garment to appear before the world.

Her husband left her alone, as she had asked, and went to his office. Edna climbed to her atelier, a bright room at the top of the house. She worked with great energy and interest, but nothing she produced satisfied her in the least. For a while she pressed the whole household into the service of art. The boys sat for her. At first they found it amusing, but the work lost its charm as soon as they saw it was not a game set up for their entertainment. The quadroon sat for hours before Edna’s palette, as patient as a savage. Meanwhile the house-maid watched the children, and nobody dusted the drawing-room. Then the house-maid had her turn as model too, once Edna noticed that the young woman’s back and shoulders had classic lines and that her hair, freed from its confining cap, gave her inspiration. As she worked, Edna sometimes sang the little air “Ah! si tu savais!” under her breath.

The song brought memories back to her. Again she heard the ripple of the water and the flapping of the sail. She saw the moon glinting on the bay and felt the soft, gusty beat of the hot south wind. A subtle current of desire ran through her body. Her grip on the brushes went slack, and her eyes burned.

Some days she was very happy and could not have said why. Just to be alive and breathing made her happy; her whole being seemed one with the sunlight, the color, the scents and the lush warmth of some perfect Southern day. On those days she liked to wander alone into strange, unfamiliar places. She came upon many a sunny, sleepy corner that seemed shaped for dreaming. And it felt good to dream, to be alone and left in peace.

Some days she was unhappy and did not know why — days when it seemed not worth the effort to be glad or sorry, alive or dead; when life looked to her like a grotesque pandemonium, and humankind like worms struggling blindly toward certain annihilation. On a day like that she could not work, or spin fancies to quicken her pulse and warm her blood.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Edna was in just such a mood when she went in search of Mademoiselle Reisz. The rather disagreeable impression of their last talk had not faded. Still she wanted to see her, and above all to hear her play the piano. Early in the afternoon she set off to find the pianist. Unfortunately she had mislaid or lost Mademoiselle Reisz’s card. She looked the address up in the city directory, which gave Bienville Street, some distance off. But the directory in her hands was a year or more out of date. At the number given, Edna found a respectable family of mulattoes living in the house, with chambres garnies to let. They had been there six months and had never heard of a Mademoiselle Reisz. In fact they knew nothing of any of their neighbors; their lodgers, they assured Edna, were all people of the highest distinction. She did not stay to talk class distinctions with Madame Pouponne. She hurried to a grocery store nearby, sure that Mademoiselle would have left her address with the proprietor.

Mademoiselle Reisz, he told his questioner, was known to him a good deal better than he cared to know her. The truth was he did not want to know her at all, or anything about her — the most disagreeable, most unpopular woman who ever lived on Bienville Street. He thanked heaven she had left the neighborhood, and he was just as thankful that he had no idea where she had gone.

Since these unlooked-for obstacles had risen to thwart her, Edna’s longing to see Mademoiselle Reisz had grown tenfold. She was wondering who could tell her what she wanted to know when it suddenly struck her that Madame Lebrun would most likely be able to. It was no use asking Madame Ratignolle, she knew. Madame Ratignolle was on the coolest terms with the musician and preferred to know nothing about her. She had once spoken on the subject almost as emphatically as the corner grocer.
It was the middle of November, so Edna knew Madame Lebrun had come back to the city. She also knew where the Lebruns lived: on Chartres Street.

Seen from outside, their house looked like a prison, with iron bars across the door and the lower windows. The bars dated from the old régime, and no one had ever thought of removing them. A high fence along the side enclosed the garden. A gate or door in it, giving onto the street, was locked. Edna rang the bell at this side garden gate and waited on the banquette to be admitted.

Victor was the one who opened the gate. A black woman wiping her hands on her apron stood right behind him. Edna had heard them squabbling before she saw them. The woman — plainly an anomaly — insisted on her right to do her own duties, and answering the bell was one of them.

Victor was surprised and delighted to see Mrs. Pontellier, and he did not try to hide either feeling. He was a dark-browed, good-looking youngster of nineteen. He greatly resembled his mother but had ten times her impetuosity. He ordered the black woman to go at once and tell Madame Lebrun that Mrs. Pontellier wanted to see her. The woman muttered that she would not do part of her duty when she had not been allowed to do all of it, and she started back to the weeding she had been interrupted at. Victor answered with a volley of abuse, so rapid and incoherent that Edna could scarcely make it out. Whatever he said, it worked. The woman dropped her hoe and went into the house, mumbling.

Edna did not want to go inside. The side porch, with its chairs, wicker lounge and small table, was very pleasant. She sat down, since her long walk had tired her, and began to rock gently while she smoothed the folds of her silk parasol. Victor pulled up a chair beside her. The black woman’s offensive manner, he explained at once, came entirely from poor training, because he was not around to take her in hand. He had only come up from the island the morning before and expected to go back the next day. He spent the whole winter on the island, living there, keeping the place in order and getting it ready for the summer visitors.

A man needed to unwind once in a while, though, he told Mrs. Pontellier, and every so often he drummed up an excuse to come to the city. My! the time he had had the evening before! He would not want his mother to know, and he dropped to a whisper. Memories fairly sparkled in him. Of course he could not think of telling Mrs. Pontellier everything, since she was a woman and would not understand such things. But it had started with a girl who peeped and smiled at him through the shutters as he walked by. Oh! she was a beauty! Naturally he smiled back, and went up and talked to her. If Mrs. Pontellier supposed he was a man to let such a chance slip, she did not know him. The youngster amused her, in spite of herself. Her look must have shown some interest or entertainment, for the boy grew bolder. In a little while Mrs. Pontellier might well have been listening to a highly colored story, if Madame Lebrun had not appeared in the nick of time.

That lady still wore white, as she did every summer. Her eyes beamed a gushing welcome. Would Mrs. Pontellier not come inside? Would she have some refreshment? Why had she not come sooner? How was dear Mr. Pontellier, and how were those sweet children? Had Mrs. Pontellier ever known so warm a November?

Victor went and stretched out on the wicker lounge behind his mother’s chair, from where he could see Edna’s face. While talking to her he had taken her parasol from her hands. Now, lying on his back, he held it up and twirled it above him. Madame Lebrun complained: it was so dull to be back in the city; she saw so few people now; even Victor, when he came up from the island for a day or two, had so much to do that he had no time for her. At this the youth began writhing on the lounge and winked mischievously at Edna. She somehow felt like an accomplice in crime, and tried to look severe and disapproving.

There had been only two letters from Robert, with little in them, they told her. When his mother begged him to go in and look for the letters, Victor said it was really not worth going inside for them. He remembered what they said, and in truth he rattled it off very glibly when put to the test.

One letter came from Vera Cruz and the other from the City of Mexico. He had met Montel, who was doing all he could to advance him. For now, his money situation was no better than the one he had left in New Orleans, but of course his prospects were far better. He wrote about the City of Mexico: its buildings, its people and their habits, and the conditions of life he found there. He sent love to the family. He enclosed a check for his mother and hoped she would give his affectionate regards to all his friends. That was roughly all the two letters said. Edna felt sure that if there had been a message for her, she would have been given it. The despondent frame of mind in which she had left home began to settle on her again, and she remembered she wanted to find Mademoiselle Reisz.

Madame Lebrun did know where Mademoiselle Reisz lived. She gave Edna the address, and was sorry Edna would not stay for the rest of the afternoon and visit Mademoiselle Reisz another day. The afternoon was already well along.

Victor saw her out onto the banquette, raised her parasol and held it over her as he walked with her to the car. He begged her to keep in mind that what he had disclosed that afternoon was strictly confidential. She laughed and teased him a little, remembering too late that she ought to have been dignified and reserved.
“How handsome Mrs. Pontellier looked!” said Madame Lebrun to her son.
“Ravishing!” he agreed. “The city air has done her good. Somehow she doesn’t seem like the same woman.”

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Some people said Mademoiselle Reisz always took rooms up under the roof so that beggars, peddlers and callers would not come looking for her. Her little front room had plenty of windows. Most were dingy, but they were nearly always open, so it hardly mattered. Through them came a good deal of smoke and soot, and also every bit of light and air the room had. From them she could see the bend of the river, the masts of ships and the big chimneys of the Mississippi steamers. A magnificent piano crowded the place. She slept in the next room. The third and last held a gasoline stove, on which she cooked her meals whenever she did not feel like going down to the restaurant nearby. She ate in that room too, and kept her belongings in a rare old buffet, dingy and battered from a hundred years of use.

Edna knocked at the door of Mademoiselle Reisz’s front room and went in. She found the woman standing by the window, busy mending or patching an old prunella gaiter. The little musician laughed all over when she saw Edna. Her laugh was a contortion of the face and of every muscle in her body. She looked strikingly homely standing there in the afternoon light. She still wore the shabby lace and the artificial bunch of violets at the side of her head.
“So you remembered me at last,” Mademoiselle said. “I told myself, ‘Ah, bah! she will never come.’”
“Did you want me to come?” Edna asked with a smile.

“I had not thought much about it,” answered Mademoiselle. The two had sat down on a little lumpy sofa against the wall. “I am glad you came, though. I have water boiling back there, and I was just going to make coffee. You will have a cup with me. And how is la belle dame? Always handsome! always healthy! always contented!” She took Edna’s hand in her strong, wiry fingers and held it loosely, without warmth, playing a sort of double theme on the back and the palm.

“Yes,” she went on, “there were times I thought: ‘She will never come. She promised the way society women always do, without meaning a word. She will not come.’ I really don’t believe you like me, you see, Mrs. Pontellier.”
“I don’t know whether I like you or not,” Edna answered, looking down at the little woman with a quizzical expression.

Mademoiselle Reisz was greatly pleased by the candor of Mrs. Pontellier’s answer. To show it, she went straight over to the gasoline stove and rewarded her guest with the promised cup of coffee. The coffee and the biscuit that came with it were very welcome to Edna, who had refused refreshment at Madame Lebrun’s and was now getting hungry. Mademoiselle put the tray she had brought in on a small table close by, and sat down once more on the lumpy sofa.
“I have had a letter from your friend,” she said, pouring a little cream into Edna’s cup as she handed it over.
“Yes, your friend Robert. He wrote to me from Mexico City.”
“Wrote to you?” Edna repeated in amazement, stirring her coffee without thinking.
“Yes, to me. Why not? Don’t stir all the warmth out of your coffee; drink it. The letter might just as well have gone to you, though. From start to finish it was nothing but Mrs. Pontellier.”
“Let me see it,” the young woman begged.
“No. A letter concerns no one but the person who writes it and the person it is written to.”
“Didn’t you just say it concerned me from beginning to end?”

“It was about you, not to you. ‘Have you seen Mrs. Pontellier? How is she looking?’ he asks. Then it is ‘as Mrs. Pontellier says,’ or ‘as Mrs. Pontellier once said.’ ‘If Mrs. Pontellier should visit you, play her that Impromptu of Chopin’s, my favorite. I heard it here a day or two ago, but it was not the way you play it. I would like to know what it does to her,’ and so on. He writes as though he thought we were always in each other’s company.”
“Let me see the letter.”
“Have you answered it?”
“Let me see the letter.”
“Then play the Impromptu for me.”
“It is getting late. What time must you be home?”
“Time is no concern of mine. Your question is a little rude. Play the Impromptu.”
“But you have told me nothing about yourself. What do you do with your days?”
“Painting!” Edna laughed. “I am becoming an artist. Imagine it!”
“Ah! an artist! You have pretensions, Madame.”
“Why pretensions? Do you think I could not become an artist?”

“I do not know you well enough to say. I do not know your talent or your temperament. To be an artist takes a great deal. One must have many gifts — absolute gifts — that no effort of one’s own can acquire. And besides, to succeed, the artist must have the courageous soul.”
“What do you mean by the courageous soul?”
“Courageous, ma foi! The brave soul. The soul that dares and defies.”
“Show me the letter and play me the Impromptu. You see how persistent I am. Does that count for anything in art?”
“It counts with a foolish old woman whom you have charmed,” Mademoiselle said, with her wriggling laugh.

The letter was right there, in the drawer of the little table where Edna had just set down her coffee cup. Mademoiselle opened the drawer and took out the letter, the topmost one. She put it in Edna’s hands and, without another word, got up and went to the piano.

Mademoiselle played a soft interlude, an improvisation. She sat low at the instrument, and the lines of her body settled into ungraceful curves and angles that made her look deformed. Gradually, without a break anyone could notice, the interlude melted into the soft opening minor chords of the Chopin Impromptu.

Edna could not have said when the Impromptu began or ended. She sat in the corner of the sofa and read Robert’s letter as the light faded. Mademoiselle had slipped from the Chopin into the quivering love notes of Isolde’s song, then back to the Impromptu and its soulful, poignant longing.

The shadows grew deeper in the little room. The music turned strange and fantastic — turbulent, insistent, plaintive, soft with entreaty. The shadows deepened. The music filled the room, then drifted out into the night, over the housetops and the bend of the river, until it was lost in the silence of the upper air.
Edna was sobbing, as she had wept one midnight at Grand Isle, when strange new voices woke in her. Rather agitated, she stood up to go. At the threshold she asked, “May I come again, Mademoiselle?”
“Come whenever you like. Be careful, the stairs and landings are dark; don’t stumble.”

Mademoiselle went back in and lit a candle. Robert’s letter was on the floor. She stooped and picked it up. It was crumpled and damp with tears. Mademoiselle smoothed it out, put it back in its envelope, and returned it to the table drawer.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: One morning, on his way into town, Mr. Pontellier stopped at the house of his old friend and family physician, Doctor Mandelet. The Doctor was semi-retired, resting, as the saying goes, on his laurels. His reputation was for wisdom rather than skill. He left the day-to-day practice of medicine to his assistants and younger colleagues, and many people sought him out for consultations. A few families were tied to him by friendship, and when they needed a physician he still attended them. The Pontelliers were among those.

Mr. Pontellier found the Doctor reading at the open window of his study. The house stood well back from the street, in the middle of a delightful garden, so the old gentleman’s study window was quiet and peaceful. He was a great reader. When Mr. Pontellier came in, he looked up disapprovingly over his eyeglasses, wondering who had the nerve to disturb him at that hour of the morning.

“Ah, Pontellier! Not sick, I hope. Come in and sit down. What news this morning?” He was quite portly, with a mass of gray hair and small blue eyes. Age had dulled their brightness a good deal, but not their penetration.

“Oh! I’m never sick, Doctor. You know what tough fiber I come from — the old Creole Pontelliers, who dry up and finally blow away. I came to consult — no, not exactly consult — I came to talk to you about Edna. I can’t tell what ails her.”
“Madame Pontellier not well,” the Doctor marveled. “Why, I saw her — a week ago, I think — walking along Canal Street, the picture of health, it seemed to me.”

“Yes, yes; she looks quite well,” said Mr. Pontellier, leaning forward and twirling his stick between his hands. “But she doesn’t act well. She’s odd, she’s not herself. I can’t make her out, and I hoped you might help.”
“How does she act?” the Doctor asked.
“Well, it’s not easy to explain,” said Mr. Pontellier, throwing himself back in his chair. “She lets the housekeeping go to the dickens.”
“Well, well; women are not all alike, my dear Pontellier. We have to consider —”

“I know that. I told you I couldn’t explain. Her whole attitude has changed — toward me, toward everybody and everything. You know I have a quick temper, but I don’t want to quarrel with a woman or be rude to her, least of all my wife. Still, I’m driven to it, and when I’ve made a fool of myself I feel like ten thousand devils. She’s making life devilishly uncomfortable for me,” he went on nervously. “She’s got some notion in her head about the eternal rights of women. And — you understand — we meet every morning at the breakfast table.”
The old gentleman raised his shaggy eyebrows, pushed out his thick lower lip, and drummed on the arms of his chair with his cushioned fingertips.
“What have you been doing to her, Pontellier?”
“Has she,” the Doctor asked with a smile, “been mixing lately with a circle of pseudo-intellectual women — super-spiritual superior beings? My wife has been telling me about them.”

“That’s the trouble,” Mr. Pontellier broke in. “She hasn’t been mixing with anyone. She has given up her Tuesdays at home and dropped all her acquaintances. She goes tramping about alone, moping in the street-cars, getting in after dark. I tell you, she’s peculiar. I don’t like it, and it worries me a little.”
The Doctor had not looked at it this way before. “Nothing hereditary?” he asked gravely. “Nothing peculiar in her family background, is there?”

“Oh, no, indeed! She comes from sound old Presbyterian Kentucky stock. I’ve heard that her father, the old gentleman, made up for his weekday sins with his Sunday devotions. I know for a fact that his race horses literally ran away with the prettiest bit of Kentucky farmland I ever saw. Margaret — you know Margaret — has her Presbyterianism undiluted. And the youngest is something of a vixen. By the way, she’s getting married in a couple of weeks.”
“Then send your wife up for the wedding,” the Doctor cried, seeing a happy solution. “Let her stay among her own people for a while. It will do her good.”

“That’s just what I want. But she won’t go to the wedding. She says a wedding is one of the most lamentable spectacles on earth. Nice thing for a woman to tell her husband!” Mr. Pontellier exclaimed, fuming again at the memory.

“Pontellier,” said the Doctor, after thinking a moment, “let your wife alone for a while. Don’t pester her, and don’t let her pester you. Woman, my dear friend, is a most peculiar and delicate organism, and a sensitive, highly organized woman like Mrs. Pontellier, as I know her to be, is more peculiar still. Dealing with them successfully would take an inspired psychologist. When ordinary men like you and me try to manage their idiosyncrasies, we only bungle it. Most women are moody and whimsical. What you describe is some passing whim of your wife’s, caused by one thing or several, which you and I needn’t try to fathom. It will pass happily enough, especially if you leave her be. Send her around to see me.”
“Oh! I couldn’t do that. There’d be no reason for it,” Mr. Pontellier objected.
“Then I’ll go and see her,” said the Doctor. “I’ll come to dinner one evening, en bon ami.”
“Do! by all means,” Mr. Pontellier urged. “Which evening? Make it Thursday. Can you come Thursday?” he asked, getting up to go.
“Very well; Thursday. My wife may possibly have some engagement for me that night. If she has, I’ll send word. If not, expect me.”
Before leaving, Mr. Pontellier turned to say:

“I’m going to New York on business very soon. I’ve got a big scheme under way, and I want to be right there, pulling the ropes and handling the ribbons. We’ll let you in on the inside, Doctor, if you say the word,” he laughed.
“No, thank you, my dear sir,” the Doctor answered. “I leave ventures like that to you younger men, who still have the fever of life in your blood.”
“What I wanted to say,” Mr. Pontellier went on, his hand on the knob, “is that I may be away a good while. Would you advise taking Edna along?”

“By all means, if she wants to go. If she doesn’t, leave her here. Don’t contradict her. I assure you the mood will pass. It may take a month, two, three — possibly longer — but it will pass. Be patient.”
“Well, good-by, à jeudi,” said Mr. Pontellier, showing himself out.
During the conversation the Doctor would have liked to ask, “Is there any man in the case?” But he knew his Creole too well to make a blunder like that.
He did not go back to his book right away. He sat for a while, looking out into the garden, lost in thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Edna’s father was in the city and had been staying with them for several days. She was not warmly or deeply attached to him, but they had certain tastes in common, and they were good company for each other. His visit was a welcome disturbance; it seemed to give her emotions a new direction.

He had come to buy a wedding gift for his daughter Janet, and an outfit for himself so that he could make a creditable appearance at her marriage. Mr. Pontellier had chosen the bridal gift, since everyone close to him always deferred to his taste in such matters. His suggestions about clothes, which too often become a problem, were of inestimable value to his father-in-law. But for the past few days the old gentleman had been left on Edna’s hands, and in his company she was getting to know a new set of sensations. He had been a colonel in the Confederate army, and along with the title he still kept the military bearing that had always gone with it. His hair and mustache were white and silky, which brought out the rugged bronze of his face. He was tall and thin, and he wore his coats padded, which gave a false breadth and depth to his shoulders and chest. Edna and her father looked very distinguished together, and they drew a good deal of notice on their walks. When he arrived, she began by showing him her atelier and making a sketch of him. He took the whole thing very seriously. Had her talent been ten times greater than it was, it would not have surprised him. He was convinced that he had passed on to all his daughters the seeds of masterful ability, which needed only their own effort to grow into success.

He sat rigid and unflinching before her pencil, as he had once faced the mouth of a cannon. He resented the children’s intrusion, as they gaped at him with wondering eyes, sitting so stiff in their mother’s bright atelier. When they came near, he waved them off with an expressive motion of his foot, unwilling to disturb the fixed lines of his face, his arms or his rigid shoulders.

Edna wanted to entertain him. She asked Mademoiselle Reisz to meet him, having promised him a treat in her piano playing, but Mademoiselle refused. So the two of them went to a soirée musicale at the Ratignolles’ instead. Monsieur and Madame Ratignolle made a great fuss over the Colonel. They installed him as guest of honor and at once got him to promise to dine with them the next Sunday, or on any day he liked. Madame flirted with him in the most captivating, naive way, with her eyes, her gestures and a flood of compliments, until the Colonel’s old head felt thirty years younger on its padded shoulders. Edna marveled and did not understand. She herself had almost no coquetry in her.

She noticed one or two men at the soirée musicale. But she would never have felt moved to put on a kittenish display to catch their eye, or to use feline or feminine wiles to show herself to them. Their personalities drew her in an agreeable way. Her fancy picked them out, and she was glad when a lull in the music gave them the chance to meet her and talk. On the street, the glance of strange eyes had often stayed in her memory, and sometimes it had troubled her.

Mr. Pontellier did not go to these soirées musicales. He thought them bourgeois and had a better time at the club. He told Madame Ratignolle that the music at her soirées was too “heavy” and beyond his untrained understanding. This excuse flattered her. But she disapproved of Mr. Pontellier’s club, and she was frank enough to say so to Edna.
“It’s a pity Mr. Pontellier doesn’t stay home more in the evenings. I think you two would be more — well, forgive my saying so — more united if he did.”
“Oh! dear no!” said Edna, with a blank look in her eyes. “What would I do with him at home? We would have nothing to say to each other.”

She had not much to say to her father either, for that matter, but he did not antagonize her. She found that he interested her, though she realized he might not interest her for long. And for the first time in her life she felt she knew him thoroughly. He kept her busy serving him and attending to his needs. It amused her to do it. She would not let a servant or one of the children do anything for him that she could do herself. Her husband noticed, and took it for the sign of a deep devotion to her father, which he had never suspected.

The Colonel drank numerous “toddies” in the course of the day, but they left him unruffled. He was an expert at mixing strong drinks. He had even invented some and given them fantastic names, and making them took assorted ingredients that it fell to Edna to get for him.
