When Doctor Mandelet dined with the Pontelliers on Thursday, he could see in Mrs. Pontellier no trace of the morbid condition her husband had described to him. She was excited and, in a way, radiant. She and her father had been to the race course, and when they sat down at the table their minds were still on the events of the afternoon, and they were still talking about the track. The Doctor had not kept up with turf affairs. He had some memories of racing in what he called “the good old times,” when the Lecompte stables flourished, and he drew on this store of memories so as not to be left out or seem wholly without the modern spirit. But he did not fool the Colonel, and he was far from impressing him with this made-up knowledge of bygone days. Edna had bet on her father’s last choice, with gratifying results for them both. Besides, according to the Colonel, they had met some very charming people. Mrs. Mortimer Merriman and Mrs. James Highcamp, who were there with Alcée Arobin, had joined them and livened up the hours in a way that warmed him to think of.

Mr. Pontellier himself had no particular liking for horseracing. He was even rather inclined to discourage it as a pastime, especially when he thought of the fate of that blue-grass farm in Kentucky. He tried to voice a general disapproval, and succeeded only in rousing the anger and opposition of his father-in-law. A fine dispute followed, in which Edna warmly took her father’s side and the Doctor stayed neutral.

From under his shaggy brows he watched his hostess closely. He noted a subtle change that had turned the listless woman he had known into a being who, for the moment, seemed to throb with the forces of life. Her speech was warm and energetic. There was no restraint in her glance or her gestures. She reminded him of some beautiful, sleek animal waking up in the sun.
The dinner was excellent. The claret was warm and the champagne was cold. Under their kindly influence the threatened unpleasantness melted away, and vanished with the fumes of the wine.

Mr. Pontellier warmed up and began to reminisce. He told some funny stories of plantation life, and memories of old Iberville and his youth, when he went hunting ’possum with a friendly Black companion, beat down pecans from the trees, shot grosbec, and wandered the woods and fields in mischievous idleness.

The Colonel, with little sense of humor or of what suited the occasion, told a somber story from those dark and bitter days, in which he had played a conspicuous part and always been a central figure. The Doctor was no happier in his choice. He told the old, ever new and curious story of a woman’s love fading, seeking strange new channels, and returning to its rightful source only after days of fierce unrest. It was one of the many little human documents that had been opened to him during his long career as a physician. The story did not seem to make much impression on Edna. She had one of her own to tell, about a woman who paddled away one night in a pirogue with her lover and never came back. They were lost among the Baratarian Islands, and from that day to this no one has heard of them or found a trace of them. It was pure invention. She said Madame Antoine had told it to her. That, too, was an invention. Perhaps it was a dream she had had. But every glowing word seemed real to those who listened. They could feel the hot breath of the Southern night. They could hear the long sweep of the pirogue through the glistening, moonlit water, and the beating of wings as birds rose startled from the reeds in the salt-water pools. They could see the faces of the lovers, pale, close together, rapt in oblivious forgetfulness, drifting into the unknown.
The champagne was cold, and that night its subtle fumes played fantastic tricks on Edna’s memory.

Outside, away from the glow of the fire and the soft lamplight, the night was chill and murky. The Doctor crossed his old-fashioned cloak over his chest as he strode home through the dark. He knew his fellow-creatures better than most men do, and knew the inner life that so seldom opens itself to unanointed eyes. He was sorry he had accepted Pontellier’s invitation. He was getting old and beginning to need rest and a spirit left in peace. He did not want other people’s secrets forced on him.
“I hope it isn’t Arobin,” he muttered to himself as he walked. “I hope to heaven it isn’t Alcée Arobin.”

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Edna and her father had a hot, almost violent quarrel over her refusal to go to her sister’s wedding. Mr. Pontellier would not step in, either with his influence or with his authority. He was taking Doctor Mandelet’s advice and letting her do as she pleased. The Colonel scolded his daughter for her lack of filial kindness and respect, and her want of sisterly affection and womanly consideration. His arguments were labored and unconvincing. He doubted Janet would accept any excuse, forgetting that Edna had given none. He doubted Janet would ever speak to her again, and he was sure Margaret never would.
Edna was glad to see the last of her father when he finally left, taking his wedding clothes and bridal gifts, his padded shoulders, his Bible reading, his “toddies” and his ponderous oaths.

Mr. Pontellier left right behind him. He meant to stop at the wedding on his way to New York, and to try every means that money and love could devise to make up in part for Edna’s incomprehensible conduct.

“You are too lenient, Léonce, far too lenient,” the Colonel insisted. “What’s needed is authority and coercion. Put your foot down good and hard; that is the only way to manage a wife. Take my word for it.”
The Colonel perhaps did not know that he had coerced his own wife into her grave. Mr. Pontellier vaguely suspected it, and thought it pointless to mention it so long afterward.

Her husband’s leaving did not please Edna as consciously as her father’s had. As the day drew near when he would leave her for a comparatively long stay, she grew tender and affectionate. She remembered his many considerate acts and his repeated expressions of ardent attachment. She fretted over his health and welfare. She bustled about seeing to his clothes and thinking of heavy underwear, exactly as Madame Ratignolle would have done in her place. When he left she cried, and called him her dear, good friend, and felt quite sure that before long she would be lonely and would go to join him in New York.

But when she finally found herself alone, a radiant peace settled over her after all. Even the children were gone. Old Madame Pontellier had come in person and taken them off to Iberville with their quadroon. The old madame did not dare say she feared they would be neglected while Léonce was away; she hardly dared think it. She longed for them, and her attachment was even a little fierce. She did not want them to be wholly “children of the pavement,” as she always put it when she begged to have them for a time. She wanted them to know the country, with its streams, fields, woods and freedom, so delicious to the young. She wanted them to taste something of the life their father had lived, known and loved when he too was a little child.

Left at last to herself, Edna breathed a big, genuine sigh of relief. A feeling came over her that she did not know, and it was very delicious. She walked through the whole house, from room to room, as if she were inspecting it for the first time. She tried out the chairs and lounges as though she had never sat or lain on them. Then she went around the outside of the house, investigating, checking whether the windows and shutters were secure and in order. The flowers seemed like new acquaintances; she approached them as friends and made herself at home among them. The garden walks were damp, so Edna called to the maid to bring out her rubber sandals. She stayed out there, stooping to dig around the plants, trimming, picking off dead, dry leaves. The children’s little dog came out and got in her way. She scolded him, laughed at him and played with him. The garden smelled so good and looked so pretty in the afternoon sunlight. Edna picked every bright flower she could find, and went back into the house with them, she and the little dog.

Even the kitchen took on a sudden interest she had never noticed. She went in to tell the cook that the butcher would have to bring much less meat, and that they would need only half the usual bread, milk and groceries. She said she herself would be very busy while Mr. Pontellier was away, and asked the cook to take all thought and responsibility for the larder on her own shoulders.

That night Edna dined alone. The candelabra, with a few candles in the middle of the table, gave all the light she needed. Outside the circle where she sat, the big dining-room looked solemn and shadowy. The cook, put on her mettle, served a delicious meal: a luscious tenderloin, broiled à point. The wine tasted good, and the marron glacé seemed to be just what she wanted. It was pleasant, too, to dine in a comfortable peignoir.

She thought a little sentimentally of Léonce and the children, and wondered what they were doing. She gave the doggie a dainty scrap or two, and talked to him intimately about Etienne and Raoul. He was beside himself with astonishment and delight at these friendly advances, and showed his appreciation with quick, snappy little barks and a lot of excited wriggling.

After dinner Edna sat in the library and read Emerson until she grew sleepy. She saw that she had neglected her reading, and made up her mind to begin a course of improving studies now that her time was entirely her own to spend as she liked.
After a refreshing bath Edna went to bed. As she snuggled comfortably under the eiderdown, a sense of restfulness came over her, such as she had never known.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Edna could not work on dark, cloudy days. She needed the sun to soften her mood and bring her to the sticking point. She had reached a stage where she no longer seemed to be feeling her way; when she was in the humor, she worked with sureness and ease. Since she had no ambition and was not striving to accomplish anything, she took her satisfaction from the work itself.

On rainy or melancholy days Edna went out to find the company of the friends she had made at Grand Isle. Otherwise she stayed home and nursed a mood she was getting to know too well for her own comfort and peace of mind. It was not despair. It only seemed to her that life was passing her by and leaving its promise broken and unfulfilled. Yet on other days she listened to the fresh promises her youth held out to her, was led on by them, and was deceived.

She went to the races again, and again. One bright afternoon Alcée Arobin and Mrs. Highcamp called for her in Arobin’s drag. Mrs. Highcamp was a worldly but unaffected woman in her forties: intelligent, slim, tall and blonde, with an indifferent manner and blue eyes that stared. Her daughter served as her pretext for keeping up with young men of fashion, and Alcée Arobin was one of them. Everyone at the race course, the opera and the fashionable clubs knew him by sight. His eyes held a perpetual smile, and it rarely failed to rouse a matching cheerfulness in anyone who looked into them and listened to his good-humored voice. His manner was quiet and sometimes a little insolent. He had a good figure and a pleasing face, not burdened with much depth of thought or feeling. He dressed as any conventional man of fashion would.

He had admired Edna extravagantly ever since he met her at the races with her father. They had met on other occasions, but until that day she had struck him as unapproachable. It was at his instigation that Mrs. Highcamp came to invite her to the Jockey Club, to see the turf event of the season.

Out there, a few track men might have known the race horse as well as Edna did, but not one knew it better. She sat between her two companions like a woman entitled to an opinion. She laughed at Arobin’s pretensions and despaired of Mrs. Highcamp’s ignorance. The race horse had been a friend and close companion in her childhood. The atmosphere of the stables and the breath of the blue grass paddock rose in her memory and lingered in her nostrils. As the sleek geldings ambled in review before them, she did not notice that she was talking like her father. She played for very high stakes, and luck was with her. The fever of the game flamed in her cheeks and eyes and got into her blood and her brain like an intoxicant. People turned to look at her. More than one leaned in to catch her remarks, hoping to pick up the elusive but ever-desired “tip.” Arobin caught the contagion of her excitement, and it pulled him toward Edna like a magnet. Mrs. Highcamp, as usual, stayed unmoved, with her indifferent stare and raised eyebrows.
When Mrs. Highcamp urged her, Edna stayed to dine. Arobin stayed as well and sent his drag away.

The dinner was quiet and uninteresting, apart from Arobin’s cheerful efforts to enliven it. Mrs. Highcamp lamented that her daughter had missed the races, and tried to make her understand what she had lost by going to the “Dante reading” rather than coming with them. The girl held a geranium leaf to her nose and said nothing, looking knowing and noncommittal. Mr. Highcamp, a plain, bald-headed man, talked only when he had to, and he was unresponsive. His wife treated him with delicate courtesy and consideration, and she directed most of her conversation at him across the table. After dinner the two of them sat in the library and read the evening papers together under the droplight. The younger people went into the drawing-room next door and talked. Miss Highcamp played some selections from Grieg on the piano. She seemed to have taken in all of the composer’s coldness and none of his poetry. As Edna listened, she could not help wondering whether she had lost her taste for music.

When it was time for her to go home, Mr. Highcamp grunted a lame offer to take her, looking down at his slippered feet with tactless concern. It was Arobin who took her. The car ride was long, and by the time they reached Esplanade Street it was late. Arobin asked leave to come in for a second and light his cigarette, since his match safe was empty. He filled the match safe, but he did not light the cigarette until he left her, after she had said she would be willing to go to the races with him again.

Edna was neither tired nor sleepy. She was hungry again, because the Highcamp dinner, though of excellent quality, had not been plentiful. She rummaged in the larder and came back with a slice of Gruyere and some crackers, and she opened a bottle of beer she found in the icebox. She felt extremely restless and excited. She hummed a fantastic tune without thinking, poking at the wood embers on the hearth and munching a cracker.

She wanted something to happen — something, anything; she did not know what. She was sorry she had not kept Arobin for half an hour to talk over the horses with her. She counted the money she had won. There was nothing else to do, though, so she went to bed and tossed there for hours in a sort of monotonous agitation.

In the middle of the night she remembered that she had forgotten her regular letter to her husband. She resolved to write it the next day and tell him about her afternoon at the Jockey Club. Wide awake, she lay composing a letter that was nothing like the one she actually wrote. In the morning the maid woke her from a dream. In it Mr. Highcamp was playing the piano at the entrance of a music store on Canal Street, while his wife, boarding an Esplanade Street car with Alcée Arobin, said:
“What a pity that so much talent has been neglected! But I must go.”

A few days later Alcée Arobin called for Edna again in his drag, but this time Mrs. Highcamp was not with him. He said they would pick her up. She had not been told he meant to pick her up, though, so she was not at home. The daughter was just leaving for a meeting of a branch of the Folk Lore Society, and she was sorry she could not go with them. Arobin looked nonplused and asked Edna whether there was anyone else she wanted to invite.

She did not think it worth the trouble to hunt up any of the fashionable acquaintances she had withdrawn from. She thought of Madame Ratignolle, but knew her fair friend never left the house, except for a languid walk around the block with her husband after nightfall. Mademoiselle Reisz would have laughed at such a request from Edna. Madame Lebrun might have enjoyed the outing, but for some reason Edna did not want her. So she and Arobin went alone.

She found the afternoon intensely interesting. The excitement came back over her like a recurring fever. Her talk turned familiar and confidential. It was no work to grow intimate with Arobin, whose manner invited easy confidence. Whenever a pretty and engaging woman was involved, he always tried to skip the first stage of becoming acquainted.

He stayed and dined with Edna. He stayed and sat by the wood fire. They laughed and talked, and before he left he was telling her how different life might have been if he had known her years ago. He spoke with ingenuous frankness of what a wicked, ill-disciplined boy he had been. Then, on impulse, he pulled up his cuff to show her the scar of a saber cut on his wrist, which he had gotten in a duel outside Paris when he was nineteen. She touched his hand while she looked over the red scar on the inside of his white wrist. A quick, somewhat spasmodic impulse made her fingers close on his hand in a sort of clutch. He felt her pointed nails pressing into the flesh of his palm.
She got up quickly and walked to the mantel.
“The sight of a wound or a scar always upsets me and turns my stomach,” she said. “I shouldn’t have looked at it.”
“I beg your pardon,” he pleaded, following her. “It never occurred to me that it might be repulsive.”

He stood close to her. The effrontery in his eyes repelled the old self in her, which was fading, yet it drew out all of her awakening sensuousness. What he saw in her face was enough to make him take her hand and hold it while he said his lingering good night.
“Will you go to the races again?” he asked.
“No,” she said. “I’ve had enough of the races. I don’t want to lose all the money I’ve won, and when the weather is bright I have to work, instead of—”
“Yes, work; of course. You promised to show me your work. Which morning may I come up to your atelier? Tomorrow?”
“Oh, please don’t say no! I know a thing or two about such matters. I might help you with a suggestion or two.”

“No. Good night. Why don’t you go, now that you’ve said good night? I don’t like you,” she went on, in a high, excited pitch, trying to pull her hand away. She felt that her words lacked dignity and sincerity, and she knew he felt it too.

“I’m sorry you don’t like me. I’m sorry I offended you. How did I offend you? What have I done? Can’t you forgive me?” And he bent and pressed his lips to her hand as if he never wanted to take them away.

“Mr. Arobin,” she protested, “the excitement of the afternoon has upset me a great deal; I’m not myself. My manner must have misled you somehow. I want you to go, please.” Her tone was dull and monotonous. He took his hat from the table and stood with his eyes turned away from her, gazing into the dying fire. For a moment or two he kept up an impressive silence.

“It was not your manner that misled me, Mrs. Pontellier,” he said at last. “My own feelings did that. I couldn’t help it. How could I help it, when I’m near you? Don’t think anything of it; don’t trouble yourself, please. You see, I go when you order me to. If you want me to stay away, I will. If you let me come back, I—oh! you will let me come back?”
He cast one appealing glance at her, and she gave no answer. Alcée Arobin’s manner was so genuine that it often took in even himself.

Whether it was genuine or not, Edna neither cared nor wondered. Alone, she looked mechanically at the back of the hand he had kissed so warmly. Then she rested her head against the mantelpiece. She felt a little like a woman who, in a moment of passion, is betrayed into an act of infidelity, and who grasps what the act means without having quite woken from its glamour. The thought drifted vaguely through her mind: “What would he think?”
She did not mean her husband. She was thinking of Robert Lebrun. Her husband now seemed like someone she had married without love, as an excuse.

She lit a candle and went up to her room. Alcée Arobin was absolutely nothing to her. And yet his presence, his manners, the warmth of his glances, and above all the touch of his lips on her hand had worked on her like a narcotic.
She slept a languorous sleep, interwoven with vanishing dreams.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Alcée Arobin wrote Edna an elaborate note of apology, quivering with sincerity. It embarrassed her. In a cooler, quieter moment it seemed absurd to her that she had taken what he did so seriously, so dramatically. She felt sure that the whole meaning of the incident had lain in her own self-consciousness. Ignoring his note would give a trivial affair too much weight. Answering it in a serious spirit would still leave him thinking that, in a susceptible moment, she had given in to his influence. After all, having one’s hand kissed was no great matter. She was provoked that he had written the apology at all. She replied in as light and teasing a spirit as she thought it deserved, saying she would be glad to have him look in on her at work whenever he felt like it and his business allowed.

He answered at once by turning up at her home with all his disarming naïveté. From then on, scarcely a day passed when she did not see him or was not reminded of him. He had pretexts in abundance. He took up an attitude of good-humored subservience and silent adoration, ready at any time to put up with her moods, which were as often kind as they were cold. She grew used to him. They became intimate and friendly by imperceptible degrees, and then by leaps. At first he sometimes talked in a way that astonished her and brought the crimson into her face. In the end it pleased her, because it appealed to the animalism stirring impatiently inside her.

Nothing calmed the turmoil of Edna’s senses like a visit to Mademoiselle Reisz. Then, in the presence of a personality she found offensive, the woman seemed, by her divine art, to reach Edna’s spirit and set it free.

One afternoon it was misty, with a heavy, lowering sky, when Edna climbed the stairs to the pianist’s rooms under the roof. Her clothes were dripping wet. She felt chilled and pinched as she went in. Mademoiselle was kneeling at a rusty stove, poking it. It smoked a little and warmed the room only indifferently, and she was trying to heat a pot of chocolate on it. To Edna the room looked cheerless and dingy. From the mantelpiece a bust of Beethoven, hooded in dust, scowled down at her.
“Ah! here comes the sunlight!” cried Mademoiselle, getting up from her knees in front of the stove. “Now it will be warm and bright enough; I can leave the fire alone.”
She banged the stove door shut, came over, and helped Edna out of her dripping mackintosh.

“You are cold; you look miserable. The chocolate will be hot soon. But would you rather have a taste of brandy? I have hardly touched the bottle you brought me for my cold.” Mademoiselle had a piece of red flannel wrapped around her throat, and a stiff neck made her hold her head to one side.

“I will have some brandy,” said Edna, shivering as she pulled off her gloves and overshoes. She drank the liquor from the glass the way a man would. Then she flung herself on the uncomfortable sofa and said, “Mademoiselle, I am going to move out of my house on Esplanade Street.”

“Ah!” said the musician, neither surprised nor especially interested. Nothing ever seemed to astonish her much. She was trying to fix the bunch of violets that had worked loose from its fastening in her hair. Edna pulled her down beside her on the sofa, took a pin from her own hair, and pinned the shabby artificial flowers back in their usual place.
“Aren’t you astonished?”
“Passably. Where are you going? To New York? To Iberville? To your father in Mississippi? Where?”

“Just two steps away,” laughed Edna, “in a little four-room house around the corner. Every time I pass it looks so cozy and inviting and restful, and it’s for rent. I’m tired of looking after that big house. It never felt like mine, anyway — never like home. It’s too much trouble. I have to keep too many servants, and I’m tired of bothering with them.”
“That is not your real reason, ma belle. It is no use telling me lies. I don’t know your reason, but you have not told me the truth.” Edna did not protest or try to defend herself.
“The house, and the money that pays for it, are not mine. Isn’t that reason enough?”
“They are your husband’s,” said Mademoiselle, with a shrug and a malicious lift of her eyebrows.

“Oh! I see there is no fooling you. Then let me tell you: it is a caprice. I have a little money of my own from my mother’s estate, which my father sends me in driblets. This winter I won a large sum at the races, and I am starting to sell my sketches. Laidpore is more and more pleased with my work. He says it is growing in force and individuality. I can’t judge that myself, but I feel I have gained in ease and confidence. In any case, as I said, I have sold a good many through Laidpore. I can live in the tiny house for next to nothing, with one servant. Old Celestine, who does some work for me now and then, says she will come to stay with me and do my housework. I know I shall like it, like the feeling of freedom and independence.”
“What does your husband say?”
“I haven’t told him yet. The idea only came to me this morning. He will think I have lost my mind, no doubt. Perhaps you think so too.”
Mademoiselle slowly shook her head. “Your reason is not yet clear to me,” she said.

It was not quite clear to Edna herself, but it unfolded as she sat for a while in silence. Instinct had told her to put away her husband’s bounty as she threw off her allegiance. She did not know how things would stand when he returned. There would have to be an understanding, an explanation. Somehow things would adjust themselves, she felt. Whatever came, she had resolved never again to belong to anyone but herself.

“I shall give a grand dinner before I leave the old house!” Edna exclaimed. “You will have to come, Mademoiselle. I will give you everything you like to eat and drink. For once we shall sing and laugh and be merry.” And she gave a sigh that came from the very depths of her being.

If Mademoiselle had a letter from Robert that arrived between Edna’s visits, she would hand it over without being asked. Then she would sit at the piano and play as the mood took her while the young woman read it.

The little stove was roaring, red-hot, and the chocolate in its tin sizzled and sputtered. Edna went over and opened the stove door. Mademoiselle got up, took a letter from under the bust of Beethoven, and gave it to Edna.
“Another! so soon!” she exclaimed, her eyes full of delight. “Tell me, Mademoiselle, does he know I see his letters?”

“Never in the world! He would be angry, and he would never write to me again, if he thought so. Does he write to you? Never a line. Does he send you a message? Never a word. It is because he loves you, poor fool, and is trying to forget you, since you are not free to listen to him or to belong to him.”
“Then why do you show me his letters?”

“Haven’t you begged for them? Can I refuse you anything? Oh! you cannot fool me,” and Mademoiselle went over to her beloved instrument and began to play. Edna did not read the letter right away. She sat holding it while the music poured through her whole being like a radiance, warming and brightening the dark places of her soul. It prepared her for joy and exultation.

“Oh!” she cried, letting the letter drop to the floor. “Why didn’t you tell me?” She went and seized Mademoiselle’s hands and pulled them up off the keys. “Oh! unkind! malicious! Why didn’t you tell me?”
“That he was coming back? Hardly news, ma foi. I wonder he did not come long ago.”
“But when, when?” cried Edna impatiently. “He doesn’t say when.”
“He says ‘very soon.’ You know as much about it as I do; it is all in the letter.”
“But why? Why is he coming? Oh, if I thought—” and she snatched the letter off the floor and turned its pages this way and that, hunting for the reason, which was left untold.

“If I were young and in love with a man,” said Mademoiselle, turning on the stool and pressing her wiry hands between her knees, looking down at Edna, who sat on the floor holding the letter, “it seems to me he would have to be some grand esprit: a man with lofty aims and the ability to reach them, one who stood high enough to draw the notice of his fellow men. It seems to me that if I were young and in love, I should never think a man of ordinary caliber worth my devotion.”

“Now it is you who are telling lies and trying to deceive me, Mademoiselle. Or else you have never been in love and know nothing about it. Why,” went on Edna, clasping her knees and looking up into Mademoiselle’s twisted face, “do you suppose a woman knows why she loves? Does she choose? Does she say to herself: ‘Go to! Here is a distinguished statesman with presidential possibilities; I shall proceed to fall in love with him.’ Or, ‘I shall set my heart on this musician, whose fame is on every tongue?’ Or, ‘This financier, who controls the world’s money markets?’
“You are misunderstanding me on purpose, ma reine. Are you in love with Robert?”
“Yes,” said Edna. It was the first time she had admitted it, and a glow spread across her face, blotching it with red spots.
“Why?” asked her companion. “Why do you love him when you ought not to?”
Edna dragged herself forward on her knees, with a motion or two, to Mademoiselle Reisz, who took the glowing face between her two hands.

“Why? Because his hair is brown and grows back from his temples; because he opens and shuts his eyes, and his nose is a little out of drawing; because he has two lips and a square chin, and a little finger he can’t straighten, from playing baseball too hard in his youth. Because—”
“Because you do, in short,” laughed Mademoiselle. “What will you do when he comes back?” she asked.
“Do? Nothing, except be glad and happy to be alive.”

At the mere thought of his return she was already glad and happy to be alive. The murky, lowering sky that had weighed on her a few hours earlier now seemed bracing and invigorating as she splashed through the streets on her way home.

She stopped at a confectioner’s and ordered a huge box of bonbons for the children in Iberville. She slipped a card into the box, with a tender message scribbled on it, and sent along an abundance of kisses.

Before dinner that evening Edna wrote her husband a charming letter. In it she told him she meant to move for a while into the little house around the block and give a farewell dinner before she left. She was sorry he was not there to share it, to help with the menu and to assist her in entertaining the guests. Her letter was brilliant and brimming with cheerfulness.

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: “What is the matter with you?” Arobin asked that evening. “I have never seen you in such a happy mood.” By then Edna was tired, and she lay back on the lounge in front of the fire.
“Haven’t you heard? The weather prophet says we’ll see the sun pretty soon.”

“Well, that ought to be reason enough,” he agreed. “You wouldn’t give me another if I sat here all night begging.” He sat close to her on a low tabouret. As he spoke, his fingers lightly touched the hair that had fallen a little over her forehead. She liked the feel of his fingers in her hair and closed her eyes, sensitive to every touch.

“One of these days,” she said, “I’m going to pull myself together and think — try to decide what kind of woman I am, because frankly I don’t know. By every code I’m acquainted with, I am a devilishly wicked specimen of the sex. But somehow I can’t convince myself that I am. I must think about it.”

“Don’t. What’s the use? Why trouble yourself thinking about it, when I can tell you what kind of woman you are?” Now and then his fingers strayed down to her warm, smooth cheeks and her firm chin, which was growing a little full and double.
“Oh, yes! You will tell me that I am adorable, that I am everything captivating. Save yourself the effort.”
“No, I shan’t tell you anything of the kind, though it wouldn’t be a lie if I did.”
“Do you know Mademoiselle Reisz?” she asked, out of nowhere.
“The pianist? I know her by sight. I’ve heard her play.”
“Now and then she says odd things in a teasing way. You don’t notice them at the time, and afterward you find yourself thinking about them.”

“Well, for instance, when I left her today, she put her arms around me and felt my shoulder blades, to see if my wings were strong, she said. ‘The bird that would soar above the level plain of tradition and prejudice must have strong wings. It is a sad sight to see the weaklings bruised, exhausted, fluttering back to earth.’”
“Where would you soar to?”
“I’m not thinking of any extraordinary flights. I only half understand her.”
“I’ve heard she is partly out of her mind,” said Arobin.
“To me she seems wonderfully sane,” Edna replied.
“I’m told she is extremely disagreeable and unpleasant. Why bring her up just when I wanted to talk about you?”
“Oh! talk about me if you like,” cried Edna, clasping her hands under her head, “but let me think of something else while you do.”

“I’m jealous of your thoughts tonight. They’re making you a little kinder than usual, but somehow I feel they’re wandering, as if they weren’t here with me.” She only looked at him and smiled. His eyes were very near. He leaned on the lounge with one arm stretched over her, his other hand still resting on her hair. They went on gazing silently into each other’s eyes. When he leaned forward and kissed her, she clasped his head and held his lips against hers.
It was the first kiss of her life to which her nature had truly responded. It was a flaming torch that kindled desire.

chapters.title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: After Arobin left that night, Edna cried a little. It was only one phase of the many emotions that had fallen on her. She felt an overwhelming irresponsibility. She felt the shock of the unexpected and the unaccustomed. Her husband’s reproach looked back at her from the outward things around her that he had provided for her outward existence. Robert’s reproach made itself felt as well, in a quicker, fiercer, more overpowering love for him that had awakened in her. Above all there was understanding. It was as if a mist had been lifted from her eyes and she could look at life, that monster made up of beauty and brutality, and grasp what it meant. Yet among the conflicting sensations that came over her, there was neither shame nor remorse. There was a dull pang of regret, because the kiss that had inflamed her was not a kiss of love, and because it was not love that had held this cup of life to her lips.

chapters.title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Edna did not wait for her husband’s answer, or even for his opinion or wishes on the matter. She hurried to make ready to leave her home on Esplanade Street and move into the little house around the block. A feverish anxiety went with every step she took toward it. She allowed no moment of deliberation and no pause for rest between the thought and its fulfillment. Early on the morning after the hours she had spent in Arobin’s company, Edna set about securing her new home and rushing her arrangements to move in. Within her own house she felt like someone who has gone in and lingered at the doors of a forbidden temple, where a thousand muffled voices told her to begone.

Whatever in the house was her own, everything she had acquired apart from her husband’s bounty, she had carried over to the other house. Where simple, meager needs remained, she made them up from her own resources.

When Arobin looked in that afternoon, he found her with her sleeves rolled up, working beside the housemaid. She looked splendid and robust, and she had never been handsomer than in the old blue gown, with a red silk handkerchief knotted at random around her head to keep the dust off her hair. She was up on a high stepladder, unhooking a picture from the wall, as he came in. He had found the front door open and, after ringing, had simply walked in.
“Come down!” he said. “Do you want to kill yourself?” She greeted him with feigned carelessness, as if absorbed in her work.
If he had expected to find her languishing, reproachful or indulging in sentimental tears, he must have been greatly surprised.
No doubt he was prepared for anything, ready for any one of those attitudes, just as he adapted himself easily and naturally to the situation he actually faced.
“Please come down,” he insisted, holding the ladder and looking up at her.

“No,” she answered. “Ellen is afraid to climb the ladder. Joe is working over at the ‘pigeon house’ — that’s what Ellen calls it, because it’s so small and looks like a pigeon house — and someone has to do this.”

Arobin took off his coat and declared himself ready and willing to tempt fate in her place. Ellen brought him one of her dust-caps. When she saw him put it on in front of the mirror, as grotesquely as he could, she went into contortions of laughter that she could not control. Edna herself could not help smiling as she fastened it for him, at his request. So he was the one who went up the ladder, unhooking pictures and curtains and lifting down ornaments as Edna directed. When he had finished, he took off his dust-cap and went out to wash his hands.
By the time he came in again, Edna was sitting on the tabouret, idly brushing the tips of a feather duster along the carpet.
“Is there anything more you will let me do?” he asked.
“That is all,” she answered. “Ellen can manage the rest.” She was keeping the young woman busy in the drawing-room, unwilling to be left alone with Arobin.
“And the dinner?” he asked. “The grand event, the coup d’état?”

“It’s the day after tomorrow. Why do you call it the ‘coup d’état’? Oh! it will be very fine: all my best of everything — crystal, silver and gold, Sèvres, flowers, music, and champagne to swim in. I’ll let Léonce pay the bills. I wonder what he’ll say when he sees them.”

“And you ask why I call it a coup d’état?” Arobin had put his coat on again. Standing in front of her, he asked whether his cravat was straight. She said it was, looking no higher than the tip of his collar.
“When do you go to the ‘pigeon house’? — with all due acknowledgment to Ellen.”
“The day after tomorrow, after the dinner. I shall sleep there.”
“Ellen, would you be so kind as to get me a glass of water?” asked Arobin. “The dust in the curtains, if you’ll pardon my hinting at such a thing, has parched my throat to a crisp.”
“While Ellen gets the water,” said Edna, rising, “I will say good-by and let you go. I have to get rid of this grime, and I have a million things to do and think about.”
“When shall I see you?” asked Arobin, trying to hold her there now that the maid had left the room.
“At the dinner, of course. You are invited.”
“Not before? Not tonight, or tomorrow morning, or tomorrow noon or night? Or the day after, morning or noon? Can’t you see for yourself, without my telling you, what an eternity that is?”
He had followed her into the hall and to the foot of the stairs, and he looked up at her as she climbed, her face half turned toward him.
“Not a moment sooner,” she said. But she laughed, and she looked at him with eyes that at once gave him courage to wait and made the waiting torture.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Edna had called the dinner a very grand affair, but it was in fact small and select. Few guests had been invited, and each had been chosen with care. She had counted on an even dozen at her round mahogany table. For the moment she had forgotten that Madame Ratignolle was to the last degree souffrante and unpresentable, and she had not foreseen that Madame Lebrun would send a thousand regrets at the last minute. So there were only ten after all, which made a cozy, comfortable number.

Mr. and Mrs. Merriman were there. She was a pretty, lively little woman in her thirties. He was a jovial fellow, something of a shallow-pate, who laughed a good deal at other people’s witticisms, and that had made him extremely popular. Mrs. Highcamp had come along with them. Alcée Arobin was there, naturally, and Mademoiselle Reisz had agreed to come. Edna had sent her a fresh bunch of violets with black lace trimmings for her hair. Monsieur Ratignolle brought himself and his wife’s excuses. Victor Lebrun happened to be in the city, bent on relaxation, and had accepted with alacrity. Then there was a Miss Mayblunt, no longer in her teens, who looked at the world through lorgnettes and with the keenest interest. People thought and said she was intellectual, and suspected her of writing under a nom de guerre. She had arrived with a gentleman named Gouvernail, who was connected with one of the daily papers. Nothing special could be said of him, except that he was observant and seemed quiet and inoffensive. Edna herself made the tenth, and at half-past eight they sat down to table, Arobin and Monsieur Ratignolle on either side of their hostess.
Beside Monsieur Ratignolle sat Mademoiselle Reisz. The order ran from there: Mr. Merriman, Miss Mayblunt, Mr. Gouvernail, Mrs. Merriman, and Mrs. Highcamp, who sat between Victor Lebrun and Arobin.

The table looked extremely gorgeous. A cover of pale yellow satin under strips of lace gave it an air of splendor. Wax candles burned softly in massive brass candelabra under yellow silk shades, and full, fragrant roses, yellow and red, were everywhere. There was silver and gold, as she had said there would be, and crystal that glittered like the gems the women wore.

For the occasion the ordinary stiff dining chairs had been set aside. In their place stood the roomiest and most luxurious chairs that could be collected from all over the house. Mademoiselle Reisz was exceedingly small, so she was raised up on cushions, the way small children are sometimes hoisted onto bulky books at table.
“Something new, Edna?” exclaimed Miss Mayblunt, aiming her lorgnette at a magnificent cluster of diamonds in Edna’s hair, just over the middle of her forehead. They sparkled; they almost sputtered.

“Quite new; ‘brand’ new, in fact. My husband sent it, and it came this morning from New York. I may as well own up that today is my birthday, and I am twenty-nine. In good time I expect you all to drink to my health. For now, let me ask you to start with this cocktail, which was composed — would you say ‘composed?’” and she turned to Miss Mayblunt for help — “composed by my father in honor of Sister Janet’s wedding.”
A tiny glass stood before every guest, and it glowed and sparkled like a garnet.

“Then, all things considered,” said Arobin, “we might do well to begin by drinking the Colonel’s health, in the cocktail he composed, on the birthday of the most charming of women — the daughter he invented.”
Mr. Merriman laughed at this sally so heartily and so infectiously that the dinner got off to a pleasant swing, and the swing never slackened.

Miss Mayblunt asked to be allowed to leave her cocktail untouched, only to look at. What a marvelous color! Nothing she had ever seen compared with it, and the garnet lights it threw off were unspeakably rare. She pronounced the Colonel an artist, and she would not be talked out of it.

Monsieur Ratignolle was disposed to take everything seriously: the mets, the entre-mets, the service, the decorations, even the guests. Looking up from his pompano, he asked Arobin whether he was related to the Arobin of Laitner and Arobin, the lawyers. The young man admitted that Laitner was a warm personal friend. Laitner let Arobin’s name adorn the firm’s letterheads, and a shingle on Perdido Street too.

“These days there are so many inquisitive people and institutions around,” said Arobin, “that one is really forced, for convenience, to take on the virtue of an occupation if he lacks one.” Monsieur Ratignolle stared a little. Then he turned to ask Mademoiselle Reisz whether she judged the symphony concerts equal to those of last winter. She replied to him in French, which struck Edna as a little rude, under the circumstances, but typical. Mademoiselle had nothing to say of the symphony concerts but disagreeable things, and she made insulting remarks about every musician in New Orleans, one by one and all together. Her whole interest seemed to be fixed on the delicacies in front of her.

Mr. Merriman said that Mr. Arobin’s remark about inquisitive people put him in mind of a man from Waco, whom he had met the other day at the St. Charles Hotel. But Mr. Merriman’s stories were always lame and pointless, and his wife rarely let him get to the end of one. She broke in to ask if he remembered the name of the author of the book she had bought the week before, to send to a friend in Geneva. She was talking “books” with Mr. Gouvernail and trying to coax out of him what he thought of current literary topics. So her husband told the story of the Waco man privately to Miss Mayblunt, who pretended to be greatly amused and to think it extremely clever.

Mrs. Highcamp hung, languidly but with unaffected interest, on the warm and impetuous flow of talk from Victor Lebrun, her neighbor on the left. After taking her seat she never once took her attention from him. When he turned to Mrs. Merriman, who was prettier and livelier than she was, Mrs. Highcamp waited with easy indifference for a chance to win him back. From time to time came the sound of mandolins, far enough off to be an agreeable accompaniment to the talk and not an interruption. Outside, a fountain splashed softly and monotonously. The sound drifted into the room through the open windows, together with the heavy odor of jessamine.

Edna’s satin gown shimmered golden, falling in rich folds on both sides of her. A soft drift of lace circled her shoulders. It matched the color of her skin but lacked the glow, the myriad living tints that one can sometimes find in vibrant flesh. As she leaned her head back against the high-backed chair with her arms spread, there was something in her attitude and her whole appearance that suggested the regal woman, the one who rules, who looks on, who stands alone.

But sitting there among her guests, she felt the old ennui overtaking her. It was the hopelessness that so often assailed her and came upon her like an obsession, like something from outside herself, independent of her will. It announced itself beforehand, a chill breath that seemed to blow from some vast cavern where discords waited. Then she was seized by the acute longing that always called up to her spiritual vision the presence of the beloved one, and at once overpowered her with a sense of the unattainable.

The moments glided on. Good fellowship passed around the circle like a mystic cord, and held these people together with jest and laughter. Monsieur Ratignolle was the first to break the pleasant charm. He excused himself at ten o’clock, since Madame Ratignolle was waiting for him at home. She was bien souffrante and full of vague dread, and only her husband’s presence could calm it.

Monsieur Ratignolle offered to take Mademoiselle Reisz to the car, and she got up with him. She had eaten well and tasted the good, rich wines, which must have gone to her head, because she bowed pleasantly to everyone as she left the table. She kissed Edna on the shoulder and whispered: “Bonne nuit, ma reine; soyez sage.” Getting up, or rather climbing down from her cushions, she had been a little bewildered, and Monsieur Ratignolle gallantly took her arm and led her off.

Mrs. Highcamp had been weaving a garland of roses, yellow and red. As soon as it was done, she set it lightly on Victor’s black curls. He lay back far in the luxurious chair, holding a glass of champagne up to the light.
It was as if a magician’s wand had touched him. The garland of roses turned him into a vision of Oriental beauty, with cheeks the color of crushed grapes and dusky eyes aglow with a languishing fire.
“Sapristi!” exclaimed Arobin.

But Mrs. Highcamp had one more touch to add to the picture. Earlier in the evening she had covered her shoulders with a white silken scarf, and now she took it from the back of her chair. She draped it over the boy in graceful folds, hiding his black, conventional evening dress. He did not seem to mind what she did with him. He only smiled, with a faint gleam of white teeth, and kept gazing through narrowing eyes at the light in his glass of champagne.
“Oh! if only one could paint in color instead of words!” exclaimed Miss Mayblunt, lost in a rhapsodic dream as she gazed at him.
“‘There was a graven image of Desire / Painted with red blood on a ground of gold.’”
murmured Gouvernail, under his breath.
The wine had an effect on Victor: it turned his usual chatter into silence. He seemed to have given himself up to a reverie, and to be seeing pleasing visions in the amber bead.
“Sing,” entreated Mrs. Highcamp. “Won’t you sing to us?”
“Let him alone,” said Arobin.
“He’s posing,” offered Mr. Merriman. “Let him have it out.”

“I believe he’s paralyzed,” laughed Mrs. Merriman. She bent over the youth’s chair, took the glass out of his hand and held it up to his lips. He sipped the wine slowly. Once the glass was empty, she put it on the table and wiped his lips with her little filmy handkerchief.

“Yes, I’ll sing for you,” he said, turning in his chair toward Mrs. Highcamp. With his hands clasped behind his head and his eyes on the ceiling, he began to hum a little, trying out his voice the way a musician tunes an instrument. Then he looked at Edna and began to sing:

“Stop!” she cried. “Don’t sing that. I don’t want you to sing it.” In her haste she set her glass down so blindly that it broke against a carafe. Wine spilled over Arobin’s legs, and some of it ran down onto Mrs. Highcamp’s black gauze gown. Either Victor had forgotten every notion of courtesy, or he thought his hostess did not mean it, because he laughed and went on:
“Ah! si tu savais / Ce que tes yeux me disent”—
“Oh! you mustn’t! you mustn’t,” cried Edna. She shoved back her chair, stood, and went around behind him to clap her hand over his mouth. He kissed the soft palm pressed against his lips.

“No, no, I won’t, Mrs. Pontellier. I didn’t know you meant it,” he said, looking up at her with caressing eyes. His lips touched her hand like a pleasing sting. She lifted the garland of roses off his head and flung it across the room.
“Come, Victor; you’ve posed long enough. Give Mrs. Highcamp her scarf.”

With her own hands Mrs. Highcamp unwound the scarf from him. All at once Miss Mayblunt and Mr. Gouvernail got the idea that it was time to say good night. And Mr. and Mrs. Merriman wondered how it could possibly be so late.

Before she parted from Victor, Mrs. Highcamp asked him to visit her daughter. She knew the girl would be charmed to meet him and to talk French and sing French songs with him. Victor said he wished to call on Miss Highcamp, and meant to, the first chance he got. Then he asked Arobin if he was going his way. Arobin was not.

Long ago the mandolin players had slipped away. A deep stillness lay over the broad, beautiful street, and the voices of Edna’s scattering guests jarred on the quiet harmony of the night like a discordant note.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: “Well?” asked Arobin, who had stayed with Edna after the others left.
“Well,” she repeated. She stood up and stretched her arms, feeling the need to loosen her muscles after sitting so long.
“What next?” he asked.

“The servants are gone, every one. They went when the musicians did, because I dismissed them. We must close up and lock the house. Then I shall trot around to the pigeon house, and in the morning I shall send Celestine over to put things in order.”
He glanced around and started putting out some of the lights.
“What about upstairs?” he asked.

“I think it is all right, but a window or two may be unlatched. We had better check. You could take a candle and look. And bring down my wrap and hat, please; they are lying on the foot of the bed in the middle room.”

Arobin went upstairs with the light while Edna began shutting doors and windows. She hated to shut in the smoke and the fumes of the wine. He found her cape and hat and carried them down, and helped her into them.
Once everything was secure and the lights were out, they went out by the front door. Arobin locked it, and he kept the key to carry for Edna. He helped her down the steps.
“A spray of jessamine?” he asked, breaking off a few blossoms as they passed.
“No; I don’t want anything.”

She seemed dispirited and said nothing. She took the arm he offered, while he used his other hand to hold up the weight of her satin train. As she looked down she could see the black line of his leg moving in and out, so near hers, against the yellow shimmer of her gown. Somewhere far off a railway train whistled, and the midnight bells were ringing. On their short walk they met no one.

Behind a locked gate and a shallow flower bed, rather neglected, stood the “pigeon house.” It had a small front porch, where a long window and the front door both opened. The door led directly into the parlor, with no side entry. Out back in the yard was a servants’ room, where old Celestine had been installed.

Edna had left a lamp burning low on the table. She had managed to make the room look livable and homelike. There were books on the table, and a lounge nearby. Fresh matting covered the floor, with a rug or two over it, and a few tasteful pictures hung on the walls. But the whole room was full of flowers, and these surprised her. Arobin had sent them and had had Celestine arrange them while Edna was out. Her bedroom adjoined, and across a small passage lay the dining room and kitchen.
Edna sat down, looking thoroughly uncomfortable.
“Are you tired?” he asked.
“Yes, and chilled, and miserable. I feel as if I had been wound up to a certain pitch — too tight — and something inside me had snapped.” She rested her head on her bare arm against the table.
“You want to rest,” he said, “and be quiet. I’ll go. I’ll leave you to rest.”

He stood beside her and stroked her hair with his soft, magnetic hand. His touch gave her a certain physical comfort. She could have fallen quietly asleep right there if he had kept running his hand over her hair. He swept it upward from the nape of her neck.
“I hope you’ll be better and happier in the morning,” he said. “These last few days you have tried to do too much. The dinner was the last straw. You could have done without it.”
“Yes,” she admitted; “it was stupid.”

“No, it was delightful; but it has worn you out.” His hand had wandered to her beautiful shoulders, and he could feel her flesh answer his touch. He sat down next to her and kissed her lightly on the shoulder.
“I thought you were going away,” she said, in an uneven voice.
“I am, after I have said good night.”
“Good night,” she murmured.
He made no answer, but went on caressing her. He did not say good night until she had grown supple under his gentle, seductive pleading.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Mr. Pontellier heard that his wife intended to abandon her home and set up house elsewhere. He answered at once with a letter of unqualified disapproval and remonstrance. She had given reasons that he was unwilling to acknowledge as adequate. He hoped she had not yet acted on her rash impulse, and he begged her to consider first, foremost and above all else what people would say. In warning her he was not dreaming of scandal, which would never have crossed his mind in connection with his wife’s name or his own. He was thinking simply of his financial integrity. Word might get around that the Pontelliers had met with reverses and had to run their ménage on a humbler scale than before. That might do incalculable mischief to his business prospects.

But he remembered Edna’s whimsical turn of mind lately, and he foresaw that she had already acted on her impetuous decision. So he took hold of the situation with his usual promptness and handled it with his well-known business tact and cleverness.

The same mail that brought Edna his letter of disapproval carried instructions — the most minute instructions — to a well-known architect about remodeling his home. He had long contemplated these changes, and he wanted them carried out during his temporary absence.

Expert and reliable packers and movers were hired to take the furniture, carpets, pictures — everything movable, in short — to places of safekeeping. In an incredibly short time the Pontellier house was turned over to the workmen. There was to be an addition, a small snuggery. There was to be frescoing, and hardwood flooring in any rooms that had not yet received this improvement.

What is more, one of the daily papers ran a brief notice. Mr. and Mrs. Pontellier, it said, were contemplating a summer stay abroad, and their handsome residence on Esplanade Street was undergoing sumptuous alterations and would not be ready to occupy until they returned. Mr. Pontellier had saved appearances!

Edna admired the skill of his maneuver and avoided any occasion to thwart his plans. Once the situation as Mr. Pontellier had set it forth was accepted and taken for granted, she was apparently satisfied to leave it so.

The pigeon house pleased her. At once it took on the intimate character of a home, and she gave it a charm that it reflected back like a warm glow. She had a feeling of having gone down in the social scale, and with it a sense of having gone up in the spiritual. Each step she took to free herself from obligations added to her strength and her growth as an individual. She started to look with her own eyes, to see and understand the deeper undercurrents of life. No longer was she content to “feed upon opinion” when her own soul had invited her.

Then, after a little while, only a few days, Edna traveled up to Iberville and spent a week there with her children. The February days were delicious, with all the summer’s promise hovering in the air.

How glad she was to see the children! She wept for pure pleasure when their little arms closed around her and their hard, ruddy cheeks pressed against her own glowing ones. She searched their faces with hungry eyes that could never have enough of looking. And what stories they had for their mother! Stories of the pigs, the cows, the mules! Of riding to the mill behind Gluglu, of fishing in the back lake with their Uncle Jasper, of picking pecans with Lidie’s little black brood and hauling chips in their express wagon. Hauling real chips for old lame Susie’s real fire was a thousand times more fun than dragging painted blocks along the banquette on Esplanade Street!

She went with them herself to see the pigs and the cows, to watch the darkies laying the cane, to shake the pecan trees and to catch fish in the back lake. For a whole week she lived with them, giving them all of herself and gathering their young existence into herself until she was full. They listened, breathless, as she told them that the house on Esplanade Street was crowded with workmen, who hammered and nailed and sawed and filled the place with clatter. They wanted to know where their bed was, and what had become of their rocking-horse, and where did Joe sleep, and where had Ellen gone, and the cook? But more than anything they burned to see the little house around the block. Was there anywhere to play? Were there boys next door? Raoul, with pessimistic foreboding, was sure there were only girls next door. Where would they sleep, and where would papa sleep? She told them the fairies would set it all right.

The old Madame was charmed by Edna’s visit and showered her with delicate attentions of every kind. She was delighted to learn that the house on Esplanade Street had been torn apart, since it gave her both the promise and the pretext of keeping the children as long as she liked.

Leaving her children cost Edna a wrench and a pang. She took with her the sound of their voices and the touch of their cheeks. All the way home their presence stayed with her, like the memory of a delicious song. But by the time she reached the city the song no longer echoed in her soul. She was alone again.

chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: Sometimes when Edna went to see Mademoiselle Reisz, the little musician was out, giving a lesson or buying some small household necessity. The key was always left in a secret hiding place in the entry, and Edna knew where. If Mademoiselle was away, Edna usually let herself in and waited for her to come back.

One afternoon she knocked at Mademoiselle Reisz’s door and got no answer. She unlocked it as usual and found the apartment empty, as she had expected. Her day had been full already. She had come looking for rest and refuge, and to talk about Robert.

She had spent the whole morning at her canvas, a study of a young Italian, finishing it without the model. But there had been many interruptions, some from her modest housekeeping and others from visitors.

Madame Ratignolle had dragged herself over, steering clear of the busier streets, she said. She complained that Edna had been neglecting her of late. Besides, she was consumed by curiosity to see the little house and how it was run. She wanted to hear everything about the dinner party, since Monsieur Ratignolle had left so early. What had happened once he was gone? The champagne and grapes Edna sent over had been too delicious. Her appetite was so poor, and they had refreshed her stomach and given it strength. Where on earth would Edna put Mr. Pontellier in that little house, and the boys? And then she made Edna promise to come to her when her hour of trial arrived.
“Whenever you like, dear. Any time, day or night,” Edna assured her.
Before leaving, Madame Ratignolle said:

“In some ways you seem like a child to me, Edna. You act without a certain amount of thought that one needs in this life. That is why I hope you won’t mind if I advise you to be a little careful while you are living here alone. Why don’t you have someone come and stay with you? Wouldn’t Mademoiselle Reisz come?”
“No, she wouldn’t want to, and I wouldn’t want her with me all the time.”

“Well, the reason is — you know how evil-minded the world can be — someone was talking about Alcée Arobin coming to see you. Of course it wouldn’t matter if Mr. Arobin didn’t have such a dreadful reputation. Monsieur Ratignolle was telling me that his attentions alone are considered enough to ruin a woman’s name.”
“Does he boast about his conquests?” Edna asked, with no great interest, squinting at her picture.

“No, I don’t think so. I believe he is a decent man as far as that goes. But his character is so well known among the men. I won’t be able to come back and see you. It was very, very unwise of me to come today.”
“Mind the step!” cried Edna.
“Don’t neglect me,” Madame Ratignolle pleaded. “And don’t mind what I said about Arobin, or about having someone stay with you.”
“Of course not,” Edna laughed. “Say anything you like to me.” They kissed goodbye. Madame Ratignolle had a short way to go, and Edna stayed on the porch a while, watching her walk down the street.

Then, in the afternoon, Mrs. Merriman and Mrs. Highcamp had made their “party call.” Edna thought they could have skipped the formality. They had also come to ask her to play vingt-et-un one evening at Mrs. Merriman’s. She was to come early, for dinner, and Mr. Merriman or Mr. Arobin would see her home. Edna agreed without enthusiasm. At times she grew very tired of Mrs. Highcamp and Mrs. Merriman.
Late in the afternoon she took refuge with Mademoiselle Reisz. She stayed there alone, waiting, feeling a kind of calm come over her from the very air of the shabby, unpretentious little room.

Edna sat at the window, which overlooked the rooftops and the river beyond. Flowerpots filled the window frame, and she picked the dry leaves off a rose geranium. The day was warm, and the breeze off the river felt very pleasant. She took off her hat and set it on the piano. She went on picking leaves and digging around the plants with her hat pin. Once she thought she heard Mademoiselle Reisz coming. But it was only a young black girl, who walked in with a small bundle of laundry, put it down in the adjoining room, and left.

Edna sat down at the piano and softly picked out with one hand the notes of a piece of music lying open before her. Half an hour went by. Now and then she heard people coming and going in the lower hall. She was growing interested in picking out the aria when there was a second knock at the door. She vaguely wondered what these people did when they found Mademoiselle’s door locked.

“Come in,” she called, turning her face toward the door. And this time it was Robert Lebrun who appeared. She tried to rise, but she could not have done it without showing the agitation that overpowered her at the sight of him. So she dropped back onto the stool, and only exclaimed, “Why, Robert!”
He came and took her hand, seemingly without knowing what he was saying or doing.
“Mrs. Pontellier! How did you happen — oh! how well you look! Isn’t Mademoiselle Reisz here? I never expected to see you.”
“When did you get back?” Edna asked, her voice unsteady, wiping her face with her handkerchief. She looked uneasy on the piano stool, and he begged her to take the chair by the window.
She did so mechanically, while he sat down on the stool.
“I got back the day before yesterday,” he answered, leaning his arm on the keys and producing a crash of discordant sound.

“The day before yesterday!” she repeated aloud, and went on thinking to herself, “day before yesterday,” without really taking it in. She had pictured him looking for her in the very first hour. Instead he had been living under the same sky since the day before yesterday, and had found her only by accident. Mademoiselle must have lied when she said, “Poor fool, he loves you.”
“Day before yesterday,” she repeated, snapping off a sprig of Mademoiselle’s geranium. “Then if you hadn’t met me here today, you wouldn’t — when — that is, didn’t you mean to come and see me?”

“Of course I would have come to see you. There have been so many things —” He nervously leafed through Mademoiselle’s music. “Yesterday I went straight back to work for the old firm. After all, there’s as much chance for me here as there was there — that is, it might pay off for me someday. The Mexicans weren’t very congenial.”

So he had come back because the Mexicans were not congenial, because business was as profitable here as there, because of any reason at all except that he wanted to be near her. She remembered the day she sat on the floor turning the pages of his letter, searching for the reason that had been left unsaid.

She had not noticed how he looked, only felt that he was there. But now she turned deliberately and studied him. After all, he had been gone only a few months, and he had not changed. His hair, the same color as hers, waved back from his temples as it always had. His skin was no more burned than it had been at Grand Isle. When he looked at her for one silent moment, she found in his eyes the same tender caress, with a new warmth and pleading that had not been there before. It was the same glance that had reached the sleeping places of her soul and awakened them.

A hundred times Edna had pictured Robert’s return and imagined their first meeting. It was usually at her home, where he had come looking for her at once. She always imagined him expressing his love for her, or giving it away in some way. And here was the reality: they sat ten feet apart, she at the window, crushing geranium leaves in her hand and smelling them, he twirling around on the piano stool, saying:

“I was very surprised to hear that Mr. Pontellier is away. It’s a wonder Mademoiselle Reisz didn’t tell me. And your moving — mother told me yesterday. I would think you would have gone to New York with him, or to Iberville with the children, rather than be bothered here with housekeeping. And you’re going abroad too, I hear. We won’t have you at Grand Isle next summer. It won’t seem — do you see much of Mademoiselle Reisz? She often spoke of you in the few letters she wrote.”
“Do you remember that you promised to write to me when you left?” A flush spread over his whole face.
“I couldn’t believe my letters would interest you.”
“That is an excuse. It isn’t the truth.” Edna reached for her hat on the piano. She put it on, pushing the hat pin rather deliberately through the heavy coil of her hair.
“Aren’t you going to wait for Mademoiselle Reisz?” asked Robert.
“No. I’ve found that when she is away this long, she is likely not to come back until late.” She pulled on her gloves, and Robert picked up his hat.
“Won’t you wait for her?” asked Edna.

“Not if you think she won’t be back until late,” he said, and added, as if suddenly aware of some rudeness in what he had said, “and I would miss the pleasure of walking home with you.” Edna locked the door and put the key back in its hiding place.

They went together, picking their way across muddy streets and past sidewalks cluttered with the cheap wares of small shopkeepers. They rode part of the way in the streetcar, and after getting off they passed the Pontellier mansion, which looked broken and half torn apart. Robert had never known the house, and he looked at it with interest.
“I never knew you in your home,” he remarked.
“I am glad you didn’t.”
“Why?” She gave no answer. They walked on around the corner, and it seemed that her dreams were coming true after all when he followed her into the little house.
“You have to stay and have dinner with me, Robert. You see, I’m all by myself, and I haven’t seen you for so long. There is so much I want to ask you.”

She took off her hat and gloves. He stood there, undecided, offering some excuse about his mother, who was waiting for him. He even muttered something about an engagement. She struck a match and lit the lamp on the table, since dusk was coming on. When he saw her face in the lamplight, pained, every soft line gone out of it, he flung his hat aside and sat down.
“Oh! you know I want to stay, if you’ll let me!” he exclaimed. All the softness returned to her face. She laughed, and went over and laid her hand on his shoulder.

“This is the first moment you’ve seemed like the old Robert. I’ll go and tell Celestine.” She hurried off to have Celestine lay an extra place. She even sent her out to look for some added delicacy that she would never have thought of for herself alone. And she stressed the need for care in dripping the coffee and in turning the omelet out just right.
When she came back in, Robert was turning over magazines, sketches and other things lying in great disorder on the table. He picked up a photograph and exclaimed:
“Alcée Arobin! What on earth is his picture doing here?”

“I tried sketching his head one day,” Edna answered, “and he thought the photograph might help. It was at the other house. I thought it had been left there. I must have packed it with my drawing things.”
“I would think you’d give it back to him if you’ve finished with it.”
“Oh! I have plenty of photographs like that. I never think of giving them back. They don’t amount to anything.” Robert went on looking at the picture.
“It seems to me — is his head really worth drawing? Is he a friend of Mr. Pontellier’s? You never told me you knew him.”

“He isn’t a friend of Mr. Pontellier’s. He’s a friend of mine. I always knew him — that is, it’s only lately that I’ve come to know him pretty well. But I’d rather talk about you, and hear what you’ve been seeing and doing and feeling out there in Mexico.” Robert threw the picture aside.

“What I’ve seen is the waves and the white beach of Grand Isle, the quiet, grassy street on the Chênière, the old fort at Grande Terre. I’ve worked like a machine and felt like a lost soul. Nothing was interesting.”
She rested her head on her hand, shading her eyes from the light.
“And what have you seen and done and felt all these days?” he asked.

“What I’ve seen is the waves and the white beach of Grand Isle, the quiet, grassy street on the Chênière Caminada, the old sunny fort at Grande Terre. I’ve worked with a little more understanding than a machine, and I’ve still felt like a lost soul. Nothing was interesting.”
“Mrs. Pontellier, you are cruel,” he said feelingly, shutting his eyes and leaning his head back in his chair. They sat in silence until old Celestine announced dinner.

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: The dining room was very small. Edna’s round mahogany table would almost have filled it. As it was, the little table stood just a step or two from the kitchen, the mantel, the small buffet and the side door that opened onto the narrow, brick-paved yard.

A certain formality settled over them when dinner was announced. They did not go back to personal matters. Robert told stories of his stay in Mexico, and Edna talked about events she thought would interest him that had happened while he was away. The dinner was ordinary, except for the few delicacies she had sent out to buy. Old Celestine, a bandana tignon twisted around her head, hobbled in and out, taking a personal interest in everything. Now and then she lingered to talk patois with Robert, whom she had known as a boy.
He stepped out to a cigar stand nearby for cigarette papers, and on his return he found that Celestine had set out the black coffee in the parlor.
“Maybe I shouldn’t have come back,” he said. “Tell me to go when you get tired of me.”
“You never tire me. Surely you haven’t forgotten those long hours at Grand Isle, when we grew used to each other and to being together.”

“I have forgotten nothing at Grand Isle,” he said, not looking at her, as he rolled a cigarette. The tobacco pouch he laid on the table was a fantastic embroidered silk affair, plainly a woman’s handiwork.
“Your tobacco used to be in a rubber pouch,” said Edna, taking up the pouch and looking over the needlework.
“Where did you buy this one? In Mexico?”
“A Vera Cruz girl gave it to me. They are very generous,” he replied, striking a match and lighting his cigarette.
“I suppose they’re very handsome, those Mexican women. Very picturesque, with their black eyes and lace scarves.”
“Some are. Others are hideous, as you find women everywhere.”
“What was she like, the girl who gave you the pouch? You must have known her very well.”
“She was quite ordinary. She had no importance at all. I knew her well enough.”
“Did you call on her at her home? Was it interesting? I’d like to hear about the people you met and what impression they made on you.”
“Some people leave an impression that fades faster than the mark of an oar on the water.”
“Was she one of those?”
“It would be ungenerous of me to admit she was of that sort.” He shoved the pouch back into his pocket, as if to put the subject away with the trifle that had raised it.
Arobin dropped in bringing a message from Mrs. Merriman. The card party was put off because one of her children was ill.
“How do you do, Arobin?” said Robert, rising out of the shadows.
“Oh! Lebrun. Of course! I heard yesterday that you were back. How did they treat you down in Mexique?”
“Not well enough to keep you there, though. Stunning girls in Mexico, I’ll say that. I thought I’d never tear myself away from Vera Cruz when I was down there a couple of years ago.”
“And did they embroider slippers and tobacco pouches and hatbands and such for you?” asked Edna.
“Oh! my! no! I never got so far into their regard. I’m afraid they made more of an impression on me than I made on them.”
“Then you were less fortunate than Robert.”
“I’m always less fortunate than Robert. Has he been passing on tender confidences?”
“I’ve imposed on you both long enough,” said Robert, getting up and shaking Edna’s hand. “Please remember me to Mr. Pontellier when you write.”
He shook hands with Arobin and went away.
“A fine fellow, that Lebrun,” said Arobin once Robert had gone. “You never mentioned him to me.”
“I met him last summer at Grand Isle,” she answered. “Here’s that photograph of yours. Don’t you want it?”
“What would I do with it? Throw it away.” She tossed it back onto the table.
“I’m not going to Mrs. Merriman’s,” she said. “If you see her, say so. But perhaps I had better write. I’ll do it now. I’ll say I’m sorry her child is ill, and that she shouldn’t count on me.”
“That would be a good idea,” Arobin agreed. “I don’t blame you. Stupid crowd!”
Edna opened the blotter, found paper and a pen, and started the note. Arobin lit a cigar and read the evening paper he had brought in his pocket.
“What is the date?” she asked. He told her.
“Will you mail this for me when you go out?”
“Of course.” He read her scraps from the newspaper while she straightened things on the table.
“What shall we do?” he asked, throwing the paper down. “Would you like a walk, or a drive, or anything? It would be a fine night for a drive.”
“No. I don’t want to do anything except be quiet. Go and amuse yourself. Don’t stay.”
“If I must, I’ll go, but I won’t amuse myself. You know I only live when I’m near you.”
He stood up to say good night.
“Do you say that to all women?”
“I’ve said it before, but I don’t think I ever came so close to meaning it,” he answered with a smile. No warm lights shone in her eyes, only a dreamy, faraway look.
“Good night. I adore you. Sleep well,” he said, kissed her hand, and went away.

She remained alone in a kind of reverie, a sort of stupor. Step by step she relived every moment with Robert since he had come through Mademoiselle Reisz’s door. She went over his words and his looks. How few they had been, and how meager, for her hungry heart! A vision, a transcendently seductive vision of a Mexican girl, rose before her. She writhed with a jealous pang. She wondered when he would return. He had not said he would. She had been with him, had heard his voice and touched his hand. But somehow he had seemed closer to her off there in Mexico.

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: The morning was full of sunlight and hope. Edna could see no refusal ahead of her, only the promise of overwhelming joy. She lay awake in bed, her eyes bright with speculation. “He loves you, poor fool.” If she could only fix that conviction firmly in her mind, what did the rest matter? She felt she had been childish and unwise the night before to give herself up to gloom. She went over the reasons that no doubt explained Robert’s reserve. They were not impossible to overcome. They would not hold if he really loved her, and they could not hold against her own passion, which in time he must come to see. She pictured him going to work that morning. She even saw how he was dressed, how he walked down one street and turned the corner into another. She saw him bent over his desk, talking to people who came into the office, going out to lunch, perhaps watching for her in the street. He would come to her in the afternoon or evening, sit and roll his cigarette, talk a little, and go away as he had the night before. But how delicious it would be to have him there with her! She would have no regrets, and she would not try to break through his reserve if he still chose to wear it.
