Edna ate breakfast only half dressed. The maid brought her a delicious printed scrawl from Raoul. He sent his love, asked for some bonbons, and reported that that very morning they had found ten tiny white pigs lying in a row beside Lidie’s big white pig.

A letter also came from her husband. He hoped to be back early in March, and then they would get ready for the trip abroad he had promised her for so long. He felt he could now fully afford it. Thanks to his recent speculations on Wall Street, he could travel as people should, without any thought of small economies.

To her great surprise she received a note from Arobin, written at midnight at the club. It wished her good morning, hoped she had slept well, and assured her of his devotion, which he trusted she returned in some faintest way.
All these letters pleased her. She answered the children cheerfully, promising them bonbons and congratulating them on their happy discovery of the little pigs.

She answered her husband with friendly evasiveness. She had no fixed plan to mislead him. It was only that all sense of reality had gone out of her life. She had given herself up to Fate and waited for the consequences with indifference.
She made no reply to Arobin’s note. She put it under Celestine’s stove lid.
Edna worked for several hours with great spirit. She saw no one except a picture dealer, who asked her whether it was true that she was going abroad to study in Paris.
She said she possibly might, and he negotiated with her for some Parisian studies, to reach him in time for the holiday trade in December.

Robert did not come that day. She was keenly disappointed. He did not come the next day, or the one after. Each morning she woke with hope, and each night she fell prey to despondency. She was tempted to look for him. But far from giving in to the impulse, she avoided every occasion that might throw her in his way. She did not go to Mademoiselle Reisz’s or pass by Madame Lebrun’s, as she might have done if he had still been in Mexico.

One night Arobin urged her to go driving with him, and she went, out to the lake along the Shell Road. His horses were full of spirit and even a little hard to manage. She liked the rapid pace at which they raced along, and the quick, sharp sound of the hooves on the hard road. They did not stop anywhere to eat or drink. Arobin was not needlessly reckless. But they ate and drank when they got back to Edna’s little dining room, which was comparatively early in the evening.

It was late when he left her. For Arobin, seeing her and being with her was becoming more than a passing whim. He had detected her hidden sensuality, which unfolded under his delicate sense of what her nature required, like a torpid, torrid, sensitive blossom.
There was no despondency when she fell asleep that night, and no hope when she woke in the morning.

chapters.title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: Out in the suburbs there was a garden, a small, leafy corner with a few green tables under the orange trees. An old cat slept all day on the stone step in the sun. An old mulatresse slept away her idle hours in her chair at the open window, until someone happened to knock on one of the green tables. She had milk and cream cheese to sell, and bread and butter. No one could make coffee as good as hers or fry a chicken as golden brown.

The place was too modest to attract people of fashion, and so quiet that those looking for pleasure and dissipation had never noticed it. Edna had found it by accident one day when the high board gate stood ajar. She caught sight of a little green table, blotched with the checkered sunlight that filtered through the quivering leaves overhead. Inside, she had found the sleeping mulatresse, the drowsy cat, and a glass of milk that reminded her of the milk she had tasted in Iberville.

She often stopped there on her rambles, sometimes with a book, and when the place was empty she would sit an hour or two under the trees. Once or twice she dined there quietly alone, having told Celestine ahead of time not to make dinner at home. It was the last place in the city where she would have expected to meet anyone she knew.

Still she was not astonished when Robert came in at the tall garden gate. She was eating a modest dinner late in the afternoon, looking into an open book and stroking the cat, which had made friends with her. She was not greatly astonished to see him.
“I’m destined to see you only by accident,” she said, pushing the cat off the chair next to her. He was startled, uneasy, almost embarrassed to meet her like this.
“Do you come here often?” he asked.
“I almost live here,” she said.
“I used to drop in very often for a cup of Catiche’s good coffee. This is the first time since I came back.”

“She’ll bring you a plate, and you will share my dinner. There’s always enough for two, even three.” Edna had meant to be as indifferent and reserved as he was when she met him. She had reached that decision through a laborious train of reasoning, in one of her despondent moods. But her resolve melted when she saw him, whom a designing Providence had led into her path.
“Why did you stay away from me, Robert?” she asked, shutting the book that lay open on the table.

“Why do you have to be so personal, Mrs. Pontellier? Why do you push me into silly evasions?” he exclaimed with sudden heat. “I suppose it’s no use telling you I’ve been very busy, or ill, or that I called and found you out. Please accept any one of those excuses and let me go.”

“You are selfishness itself,” she said. “You spare yourself something, I don’t know what, but there is some selfish motive. And in sparing yourself you never consider for a moment what I think, or how I feel your neglect and indifference. I suppose you would call this unwomanly, but I have gotten into the habit of saying what I think. It doesn’t matter to me, and you may think me unwomanly if you like.”

“No, I only think you are cruel, as I said the other day. Maybe not intentionally cruel, but you seem to be forcing me into confessions that can lead to nothing. It’s as if you wanted me to bare a wound for the pleasure of looking at it, with no intention or power of healing it.”
“I’m ruining your dinner, Robert. Never mind what I say. You haven’t touched a bite.”
“I only came in for coffee.” Excitement had twisted his sensitive face.

“Isn’t this a lovely place?” she remarked. “I’m so glad no one has really found it. It’s so quiet and sweet here. Do you notice you can hardly hear a sound? It’s so far out of the way, a good walk from the car. But I don’t mind walking. I always feel sorry for women who dislike it. They miss so much, so many rare little glimpses of life. And on the whole we women learn so little of life.

“Catiche’s coffee is always hot. I don’t know how she does it, out here in the open. Celestine’s goes cold on the way from the kitchen to the dining room. Three lumps! How can you drink it so sweet? Try some of the cress with your chop. It’s so sharp and crisp. And out here you can smoke with your coffee, which is a point in its favor. Now, in the city — aren’t you going to smoke?”
“In a while,” he said, laying a cigar on the table.
“Who gave it to you?” she laughed.
“I bought it. I suppose I’m turning reckless. I bought a whole box.” She had made up her mind not to turn personal again and make him uneasy.

The cat made friends with him and climbed into his lap as he smoked his cigar. He stroked her silky fur and said a few words about her. He looked at Edna’s book, which he had already read, and told her how it ended, to save her the trouble of wading through it, he said.

Again he went with her back to her home, and it was after dusk when they reached the little “pigeon house.” She did not ask him to stay, and he was grateful, since it let him stay without the discomfort of fumbling through an excuse he had no intention of taking seriously. He helped her light the lamp. Then she went into her room to take off her hat and wash her face and hands.

When she returned, Robert was no longer going through the pictures and magazines. He sat back in the shadow with his head resting against the chair, as if lost in a reverie. Edna paused for a moment by the table, straightening the books on it. Then she walked over to where he sat. She leaned over the arm of his chair and spoke his name.
“Robert,” she said, “are you asleep?”
“No,” he answered, looking up at her.

She bent down and kissed him, a soft, cool, delicate kiss whose voluptuous sting pierced him through. Then she drew away. He went after her and took her in his arms, simply holding her close. She raised her hand to his face and pressed his cheek to hers. The movement was full of love and tenderness. He sought her lips again. Then he pulled her down onto the sofa beside him and held her hand in both of his.
“Now you know,” he said. “Now you know what I’ve been fighting since last summer at Grand Isle, what drove me away and drove me back.”
“Why have you been fighting against it?” she asked. Her face glowed with soft lights.

“Why? Because you weren’t free. You were Léonce Pontellier’s wife. I couldn’t have helped loving you if you were ten times his wife. But as long as I went away and stayed away, I could keep from telling you.” She raised her free hand to his shoulder, then laid it against his cheek, stroking it gently. He kissed her again. His face was warm and flushed.
“Down in Mexico I thought of you all the time and longed for you.”
“But not writing to me,” she interrupted.
“Something made me believe you cared for me, and I lost my head. I forgot everything except a wild dream that you might somehow become my wife.”
“Religion, loyalty, everything would give way if only you cared.”
“Then you must have forgotten that I was Léonce Pontellier’s wife.”
“Oh! I was out of my mind, dreaming wild, impossible things, remembering men who had set their wives free. We have heard of such things.”
“Yes, we have heard of such things.”
“I came back with vague, mad plans. And when I got here —”
“When you got here you stayed away from me!” She was still stroking his cheek.
“I saw what a cur I was to dream of it, even if you’d been willing.”
She held his face between her hands and gazed into it as if she would never look away again. She kissed him on the forehead, the eyes, the cheeks and the lips.

“You have been a very, very foolish boy, wasting your time on impossible dreams, talking about Mr. Pontellier setting me free! I’m no longer one of Mr. Pontellier’s possessions, to be handed over or kept. I give myself where I choose. If he were to say, ‘Here, Robert, take her and be happy, she’s yours,’ I would laugh at both of you.”
His face went a little pale. “What do you mean?” he asked.

Someone knocked at the door. Old Celestine came in and said that Madame Ratignolle’s servant had come around by the back with a message: Madame had been taken ill and begged Mrs. Pontellier to come to her at once.
“Yes, yes,” said Edna, getting up. “I promised. Tell her yes, she should wait for me. I’ll go back with her.”
“Let me walk over with you,” offered Robert.
“No,” she said. “I’ll go with the servant.” She went into her room to put on her hat, and on coming back she sat down again beside him on the sofa. He had not moved. She put her arms around his neck.
“Goodbye, my sweet Robert. Tell me goodbye.” He kissed her with a passion that had not been in his caresses before, and held her tight against him.

“I love you,” she whispered. “Only you, no one else. You were the one who woke me last summer out of a lifelong, stupid dream. Oh! you made me so unhappy with your indifference. Oh! I suffered, suffered! Now that you’re here we’ll love each other, my Robert. We’ll be everything to each other. Nothing else in the world matters. I have to go to my friend, but will you wait for me? No matter how late, you’ll wait for me, Robert?”
“Don’t go, don’t go! Oh! Edna, stay with me,” he begged. “Why must you go? Stay with me, stay with me.”

“I’ll come back as soon as I can. I’ll find you here.” She buried her face in his neck and said goodbye again. Her seductive voice, together with his great love for her, had enthralled his senses and left him no impulse but the longing to hold her and keep her.

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: Edna looked in at the drug store. Monsieur Ratignolle was carefully mixing a preparation himself, counting drops of a red liquid into a tiny glass. He was grateful that Edna had come, since her presence would comfort his wife. Madame Ratignolle’s sister had always stayed with her through such trying times, but this time she could not leave the plantation. Adèle had been inconsolable until Mrs. Pontellier kindly promised to come. The nurse lived a long way off, so she had been spending the nights there for the past week. Dr. Mandelet had been coming and going all afternoon, and they expected him again at any moment.

Edna hurried up a private stairway that led from the back of the store to the apartments above. The children were all asleep in a back room. In her suffering restlessness, Madame Ratignolle had wandered into the salon. She sat on the sofa in an ample white peignoir, clutching a handkerchief nervously in one hand. Her face was drawn and pinched, and her sweet blue eyes looked haggard and unlike themselves. All her beautiful hair had been pulled back and plaited, and it lay on the sofa pillow in a long braid, coiled like a golden serpent. The nurse, a comfortable-looking Griffe woman in a white apron and cap, was trying to persuade her to go back to her bedroom.

“There is no use, there is no use,” she said to Edna at once. “We must get rid of Mandelet; he is getting too old and careless. He said he would be here at half-past seven, and now it must be eight. See what time it is, Joséphine.”

The woman was cheerful by nature and would not take any situation too seriously, least of all one that was so familiar to her. She urged Madame to have courage and patience. But Madame only pressed her teeth hard into her lower lip, and Edna watched the sweat gather in beads on her white forehead. After a moment or two she let out a deep sigh and wiped her face with the handkerchief, now rolled into a ball. She seemed exhausted. The nurse gave her a fresh handkerchief sprinkled with cologne water.
“This is too much!” she cried. “Mandelet ought to be killed! Where is Alphonse? Am I really to be abandoned like this, neglected by everyone?”

“Neglected, indeed!” exclaimed the nurse. Wasn’t she right there? And wasn’t this Mrs. Pontellier, who had given up what was no doubt a pleasant evening at home to devote herself to her? And wasn’t Monsieur Ratignolle that very instant coming down the hall? Joséphine was quite sure she had heard Doctor Mandelet’s coupé. Yes, there it was, down at the door.
Adèle agreed to go back to her room. She sat down on the edge of a little low couch beside her bed.
Doctor Mandelet took no notice of Madame Ratignolle’s scolding. He was used to it at such times, and he knew her loyalty too well to doubt it.

He was glad to see Edna, and wanted her to come into the salon with him to keep him company. But Madame Ratignolle would not let Edna out of her sight for an instant. In the pauses between the agonizing moments she chatted a little, saying that it took her mind off the pain.

Edna began to feel uneasy, and a vague dread came over her. Her own experiences of the same kind seemed far away and unreal, and she remembered them only in part. She dimly recalled an ecstasy of pain, the heavy smell of chloroform, and a stupor that had deadened all feeling. Then she had awakened to find a little new life, one she had given being to, added to the great unnumbered multitude of souls that come and go.

She began to wish she had not come, since she was not needed. She could have made up some pretext to stay away; she could even make one up now to leave. But Edna did not go. In inward agony, with a flaming, outspoken revolt against the ways of Nature, she watched the scene of torture.

She was still stunned and speechless with emotion when, later, she bent over her friend to kiss her and softly say good-by. Adèle pressed her cheek and whispered, in a voice worn out with exhaustion, “Think of the children, Edna. Oh, think of the children! Remember them!”

chapters.title: Chapter 38
paragraphs: Edna still felt dazed when she came out into the open air. The Doctor’s coupé had returned for him and was waiting in front of the porte cochère. She did not want to get in. She told Doctor Mandelet she would walk, that she was not afraid and would go alone. He ordered his carriage to meet him at Mrs. Pontellier’s, and walked home with her.

Far above the narrow street between the tall houses, the stars were blazing. The air was mild and caressing, though cool with the breath of spring and of the night. They walked slowly. The Doctor’s tread was heavy and measured, and his hands were clasped behind him. Edna walked absent-mindedly, as she had one night at Grand Isle, as if her thoughts had run ahead and she were trying to catch them.

“You shouldn’t have been there, Mrs. Pontellier,” he said. “It was no place for you. Adèle is full of whims at such times. A dozen women could have stayed with her, women who aren’t impressionable. I felt it was cruel, cruel. You shouldn’t have gone.”
“Oh, well!” she answered, indifferently. “I don’t know that it matters, after all. Sooner or later one has to think of the children; the sooner the better.”
“When is Léonce coming back?”
“Quite soon. Sometime in March.”
“And you are going abroad?”

“Perhaps—no, I am not going. I won’t be forced into doing things. I don’t want to go abroad. I want to be left alone. Nobody has any right—except children, perhaps—and even then, it seems to me—or it did seem—” She felt her words voicing the incoherence of her thoughts, and broke off abruptly.

“The trouble is,” sighed the Doctor, understanding her meaning intuitively, “that youth is given over to illusions. Nature seems to provide for it, as a decoy to secure mothers for the race. And Nature takes no account of moral consequences, or of the arbitrary conditions that we create and then feel bound to maintain at any cost.”

“Yes,” she said. “The years that are gone seem like dreams—if one could only keep sleeping and dreaming—but to wake up and find—oh! well! perhaps it is better to wake up after all, even if it means suffering, than to be the dupe of illusions one’s whole life.”

“My dear child,” said the Doctor as they parted, holding her hand, “it seems to me that you are in trouble. I am not going to ask for your confidence. I will only say that if you ever feel moved to give it, perhaps I could help you. I know I would understand. And I tell you there are not many who would—not many, my dear.”

“Somehow I don’t feel moved to talk about the things that trouble me. Don’t think I am ungrateful, or that I don’t value your sympathy. There are periods of despondency and suffering that take hold of me. But all I want is my own way. That is wanting a good deal, of course, when you have to trample on the lives, the hearts, the prejudices of others—but no matter—still, I wouldn’t want to trample on the little lives. Oh! I don’t know what I’m saying, Doctor. Good night. Don’t blame me for anything.”

“Yes, I will blame you if you don’t come to see me soon. We will talk about things you have never dreamed of discussing before. It will do us both good. I don’t want you to blame yourself, whatever comes. Good night, my child.”

She let herself in at the gate, but instead of going inside she sat down on the porch step. The night was quiet and soothing. All the tearing emotion of the last few hours seemed to drop away from her, like a somber, uncomfortable garment she had only to loosen to be rid of it. She went back to the hour before Adèle sent for her, and her senses kindled again at the thought of Robert’s words, the pressure of his arms, and his lips on hers. At that moment she could picture no greater bliss on earth than having the one she loved. His declaration of love had already given him to her in part. When she thought of him close by, waiting for her, she grew numb with the intoxication of expectancy. It was so late; he might be asleep. She would wake him with a kiss. She hoped he would be asleep, so that she could rouse him with her caresses.

Still, she remembered Adèle’s voice whispering, “Think of the children; think of them.” She meant to think of them. That resolve had driven into her soul like a death wound—but not tonight. Tomorrow would be time enough to think of everything.
Robert was not waiting for her in the little parlor. He was nowhere to be found, and the house was empty. But on a piece of paper lying in the lamplight he had scrawled:
“I love you. Good-by—because I love you.”

The words made Edna faint. She went and sat on the sofa, then stretched out on it without a sound. She did not sleep, and she did not go to bed. The lamp sputtered and went out. She was still awake in the morning, when Celestine unlocked the kitchen door and came in to light the fire.

chapters.title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: Victor was mending a corner of one of the galleries, with a hammer, nails and some scraps of scantling. Mariequita sat close by with her legs dangling, watching him work and passing him nails from the tool-box. The sun beat down on both of them, and the girl had folded her apron into a square pad to cover her head. They had been talking for an hour or more. She never got tired of hearing Victor describe the dinner at Mrs. Pontellier’s. He exaggerated every detail until it sounded like a true Lucullean feast. The flowers stood in tubs, he said. The champagne was drunk from huge golden goblets. Venus rising from the foam could not have been a more entrancing sight than Mrs. Pontellier, blazing with beauty and diamonds at the head of the table, while the other women were all youthful houris of incomparable charm. Mariequita got it into her head that Victor was in love with Mrs. Pontellier, and he gave evasive answers that were worded to confirm her belief. She turned sullen and cried a little, and threatened to leave him to his fine ladies. A dozen men at the Chênière were crazy about her. And since it was the fashion to be in love with married people, why, she could run off to New Orleans any time she liked with Célina’s husband.

Célina’s husband was a fool, a coward and a pig. Victor meant to prove it to her by hammering his head into a jelly the next time they met. Mariequita found this promise very consoling. She dried her eyes and cheered up at the thought.

They were still on the subject of the dinner and the attractions of city life when Mrs. Pontellier herself slipped around the corner of the house. The two youngsters were struck dumb with amazement, for they took her for an apparition. But it was really she, in flesh and blood, looking tired and a little travel-stained.

“I walked up from the wharf,” she said, “and I heard the hammering. I guessed it was you, mending the porch. That’s a good thing. Last summer I was always tripping over those loose planks. How dreary and deserted everything looks!”
Victor needed a little time to take it in: she had come in Beaudelet’s lugger, she had come alone, and she had no purpose except to rest.
“You see, nothing is fixed up yet. I’ll give you my room, since it’s the only place.”
“Any corner will do,” she assured him.
“And if you can stand Philomel’s cooking,” he went on, “though I could try to get her mother while you’re here. Do you think she would come?” He turned to Mariequita.
Mariequita thought Philomel’s mother might come for a few days, if she was paid enough.

The moment Mrs. Pontellier appeared, the girl had suspected a lovers’ rendezvous. But Victor’s astonishment was so real, and Mrs. Pontellier’s indifference so obvious, that the disturbing idea did not stay in her head for long. She looked with the keenest interest at this woman who gave the most sumptuous dinners in America and had every man in New Orleans at her feet.
“When will dinner be ready?” asked Edna. “I’m very hungry, but don’t go to any extra trouble.”
“It’ll be ready in no time,” he said, bustling about and packing up his tools. “Go to my room and freshen up and rest. Mariequita will show you.”
“Thank you,” said Edna. “But do you know, I have a notion to go down to the beach before dinner and wash well, and even have a little swim?”
“The water is too cold!” they both exclaimed. “Don’t even think of it.”

“Well, I might go down and try—just dip my toes in. Why, the sun seems hot enough to have warmed the ocean to its depths. Could you bring me a couple of towels? I should go right now, to be back in time. If I waited until this afternoon it would be a little too chilly.”
Mariequita ran over to Victor’s room and came back with some towels, which she handed to Edna.
“I hope you have fish for dinner,” said Edna, starting to walk away; “but if you haven’t, don’t go to any extra trouble.”
“Go and find Philomel’s mother,” Victor ordered the girl. “I’ll go to the kitchen and see what I can do. By Gimminy! Women have no consideration! She could have sent me word.”

Edna walked on down to the beach rather mechanically. She noticed nothing special, except that the sun was hot, and she followed no particular train of thought. All the thinking she needed to do had been done after Robert went away, while she lay awake on the sofa until morning.

Over and over she had told herself: “Today it is Arobin; tomorrow it will be someone else. It makes no difference to me, it doesn’t matter about Léonce Pontellier—but Raoul and Etienne!” Now she saw clearly what she had meant, long ago, when she told Adèle Ratignolle that she would give up the unessential but would never sacrifice herself for her children.

Despondency had settled on her during that wakeful night and had not lifted since. There was nothing in the world that she wanted. There was no one she wished to have near her but Robert, and she even saw that the day would come when he too, and the thought of him, would melt out of her life and leave her alone. The children appeared before her like antagonists who had beaten her, who had overpowered her and tried to drag her into the soul’s slavery for the rest of her days. But she knew a way to escape them. She was not thinking of any of this as she walked down to the beach.

The water of the Gulf stretched out before her, gleaming with a million lights from the sun. The voice of the sea is seductive. It never ceases, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander in abysses of solitude. Up and down the white beach, nothing living was in sight. A bird with a broken wing beat the air overhead, reeling, fluttering, circling disabled down, down to the water.
Edna found her old bathing suit still hanging, faded, on its usual peg.

She put it on and left her clothes in the bath-house. But when she stood beside the sea, completely alone, she flung off the unpleasant, pricking garments. For the first time in her life she stood naked in the open air, at the mercy of the sun, the breeze beating on her, and the waves that invited her.
How strange and awful it seemed to stand naked under the sky! How delicious! She felt like some newborn creature opening its eyes on a familiar world that it had never known.

The foamy wavelets curled up around her white feet and coiled like serpents about her ankles. She walked out. The water was chill, but she kept walking. The water was deep, but she lifted her white body and reached out in a long, sweeping stroke. The touch of the sea is sensuous. It wraps the body in its soft, close embrace.

She went on and on. She remembered the night she had swum far out, and the terror that gripped her when she feared she could not get back to shore. Now she did not look back. She went on and on, thinking of the blue-grass meadow she had crossed as a little child, believing it had no beginning and no end.
Her arms and legs were growing tired.

She thought of Léonce and the children. They were a part of her life. But they need not have imagined that they could possess her, body and soul. How Mademoiselle Reisz would have laughed, perhaps sneered, if she had known! “And you call yourself an artist! What pretensions, Madame! The artist must have a courageous soul, one that dares and defies.”
Exhaustion was pressing in on her and overpowering her.

“Good-by—because I love you.” He did not know; he did not understand. He would never understand. Perhaps Doctor Mandelet would have understood, if she had gone to see him—but it was too late. The shore was far behind her, and her strength was gone.

She looked into the distance, and the old terror flared up for an instant, then sank again. Edna heard her father’s voice and her sister Margaret’s. She heard the barking of an old dog chained to the sycamore tree. The cavalry officer’s spurs clanged as he walked across the porch. Bees hummed, and the musky scent of pinks filled the air.
